OUT THE UNITED KINGDOM. Who are Lewis's? Well, Lewis's are as well known in Liver- pool as the Bank of England is known in London. Lewis's began business in Liverpool thirty years ago, and Lewis's have at this present time dma of the very largest businesses In Eng- land.

Lewis's have not always sold Tea, but having a very large number of employ& to provide with an afternoon meal, Lewis's were struck with the difficulty of prccuring a good drinkable and refreshing Tea for them at a moderate price. The ordinary Teas were perfectly abominable. Tired of the constant and not unreasonable complaints, and of the perpetual changing of their Tea Dealers. Lewis's at last resolved to buy their Tea for the use of their establishment direct from the shippers, and to en- gage a qualified person to make the purchase. Lewis's could hardly believe there could be such a eiaange for the better in the cost and quality of the tea so bought, but "experience teaches." Lewis's thought what was good enough for the use of all their establishments, public and private, would surely be good enough for the general public. Lewis's then began to sell Teas to their friends, and at last were induced to make thesale public in Lancashire, where they soil 20.000 pounds of Tea per week. Lewis's now feel they have benefited only a small pro- portion of the population; they intend in future to make their Tea known all over the United Kingdom. Lewis's pure, splendid Tea, is one stated price, 2s a pound. Lewis a have no other price Tea, neither higher nor lower, and this Two Shilling Tea is fit for the Queen to drink. Two shil- lings is a favourite Drioe with Lewis's. they having been able to supply the public with many excellent things at the price. Not till after much hard work did Lewis's succeed in blending a splendid and most deliciously-flavoured Tea, which they are giving to the public for 2s a pound. Many tea dealers charge the public 3s and 3s ed for a similar quality. Lewis's desire to be the universal suppliers of Tea. Tea is drunk in every house- hold in the United Kingdom; it should therefore be sold at less profit than any other article of consumption, except bread. Lewis's wish particularly to direct the attention of every ' family and every househo!der to the great adva.ntage there is in buying Lewis's Two Shilling Tea. Thellavoar is so good and the strength rei very great, that one pound goes further than 18 ounces of most other Teas, providing always the water boils thoroughly. The proof that Lewis's do not exaggerate the appreciation in which their Two Shilling Tea is held lies in the fact that they receive thousands of orders every day from all parts of the United Kingdom. Lewis's would like members of the Press all over the United Kingdom to write for a pound of Lewis's Two Shilling Tta ; they are sure to be satisfied aed astonished with the rceult. Every hotel-keeper, and every public and private institution throughout the country, should write to Lewis's in Liverpool for a pound of Lewis's Two Shilling Tea. The risk is not great; it is only to send 2s in stamps to Lewis's in Liverpool, and in return they will receive a sound of splendid Tea, packed neatly in a box carriage paid, to any aidress in the United Kingdom. , --Address Lewis'sLewies in Liverpool.

Have I heart? Ton a3k, Blue Eyes— (Were ever eves so bright as thine? How roguishl3. with feigned surprise And a mccked seriousness they shine!) Yes I've a heart, in texture fine. And still almost as good as new; Constant and loyal; in design Somewhat old-fashione& it is true. But e'en in a ballad's .disguise, To tell, with rythmtc line on line— I wonder why site pensive sighs— My heart's sad secret I decline; My I.ve to silence I con,ign. Hearts now are far between and few, And love—such love, at lease, as mine— Somewhat old-fashioned, it is true. My heart, once wounded, still defies Time's healing touch. For one I pine, Who, that I have a heart. denies. If I dared woo one so divine— What! tears? Sweet sympathy's mute sign; Alas Yes. 'tis a lass—and—you! A—something—followed sweet as wine, Somewhat old-fashioned, though, 'tis true. ENVOY.

A judge having fallen asleep during a trial, Lawyer X suddenly ceased pleading and exclaimed: "I will wait until his honour wakes before finishing." "But," answered the opposing counsel, "perhaps his honour will wait until you have finished before waking." "Woman's rights!" exclaimed a Philadelphia man when the inbject was broached. "What more rights do they want? My wife bosses me; our daughters boss us both, and the servant girl bosses the whole family. It's time the men were allowed some rights." A little four-year-old, upon the other night, began to say her evening prayer as usual, and after repeating, "If I should die before I wake," paused a moment and added, "What a rumpus there would be in this house!" Then she'recited the concluding lines of the prayer and scrambled into bed. " notice," said one lady to another, "that at our social gatherings you are always the last one to leave." I know it," was the reply, "I have an object in view." "What is it ?" " I want to prevent the rest of you from slandering me." "0 you mean thing; you never like to see your friends enjoy themselves." Ah! George, isn't it delightful that we are to be mar- ried so soon. To be sure, we are not rich in this world's goods, but With such love as ours we can almost live on bread and water; can't we, dear ?" " Eisilv," said George, with great emotion. " You furnish the bread, love, and I will skirmish around and find the water."

CRYING —Toto is crying very hard. "What is the matter?" asked one of her father's friends. "I have lost two cents that mamma gave me." "That is not a diffi- cult loss to repair," replied the friend, "here are two cents." An instant afterwards Toto was crying harder than ever. "What are you still crying for? " asked the gentleman. "I am crying," said the artful baby, "because if I had not lost tw cents I ebould now have four."

" Yee, same oldconcern, but situated a little differently." "How is that ?" "Well, I've got an interest." "Is that so ? How:long since ?" "Since the first of the month." "Let me congratulate you." LOWERING Parars.—A travelling man for a high-toned New York house pulled up in a small city out West and spread his samples. A slow-going old merchant looked over them, and the high prices almost gave him the hysterics. "Wait a minute," he said, going eat of the room to appear shortly after with a step ladder.—" What's that?" inquired the astonished C. T. "Don't you see it's a step-ladder ?" "But what are yon going to do with it ?"—" Well, your figures are so derned high, that I thought maybe I could reach 'em with this and buy a bill of goods."—He was al- lowed a slight discount for cash. A STATESMAN'S Colsct.rstoxs.—lt was 2 a.m. when Mr. Ginnery tumbled across the threshold of his wife's bedroom, and without making any effort to rise lay there, conducting an animated argument with himself on the subject of reducing taxation. Mrs. Ciinnery was a woman of few words, but her methods were prompt and decisive. She got ' out of bed, removed the wash pitcher from the basin, and dashed the contents over Mr. Ginnery. Then he arose slowly to his feet, dripping at every extremity, and observed with a most solemn and impressive air: "Yeah, Mrs. Gin'ry ; we mush take the tax off whisky (hie), an' put 'er on wazzar." Nor Tile BOOTS.—A soldier of an infantry regiment at N ishville, being in need of a pair of boots, and not being able to draw them from the quartermaster, went into the shop of a Jew dealer, and asked the price of some that were lying on the counter. " Dese pouts ish nine dollars," said the dealer. "Can't give it; they are too dear," said the soldier. "Mv grashus !" says the Jew. "Dey costs me shust eight dollar and seventy-five cents in New York. You must let a pooty make a leetle somethings. Here, Shon " to a boy--,,pring de invoice of dese tine poots, and show de shentlemans de price." The invoice was prodaced, and, after pome higgling, which brought down the price con- siderably, the soldier bought a pair and started off. He had walked only the length of the street however, when the soles came off. He at once returned to the Jew and branded him in strong military language as a swindler and an imposter. The Jew looked up in amazement at his, customer, and, putting on an air of well-feigned astonishment, replied, "Oh, dein ish not infadtry Pouts! I tought you vas a cavalry rnan "

div.head: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.
div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

A small heated bar of iron applied to the head of a rusted :crcar will render its withdrawal as easy as one just in- se.rted. The number of applications at the American Patent Office 4 for patents on electrical inventions in 1882 was about 2,000, , ofwhich about two-thirds were granted. In 1877 electricity was a sub-class in a division; now it is the largest and most important division in the patent office. Dr. A. D. White, President of the Cornell University, is the owner of the MS. of the protocol of the trial for witch- craft at Trier in 1589 of Dr. Dietrich Flack. It ended in the burning of that magistrate. This protocol is to be pub- lished with critical and bibliographical notes. The Antiquarian 21fayazine opens with an account of the curious literary crime of Lauder, who accused Milton of plagiarism, and forged the evidence which he adduced as proofs. His audacity hoaxed Dr. Johnson. Mr. Flood's first chapter gives promise of a full and careful account of this affair. There are other articles of interest. A NEW SPECTROMETEIL—Professor Clifton, of Oxford, has brought out a new spectrometer. In the ordinary in- strument the axis round which the prism turns are generally at an angle to each other; but it is of importance that they should not be inclined in this way, hence Pro- fessor Clifton has made them coincident. There is, in fact, only one axis in the new instrument, the telescope, divided circle, and prism plate being fixed on as one conical axis turned very true.—Engineering. Mr. J. Brander Matthews mentions in Lippincott's a curious American sequel to the failure in England of Lamb's farce, "Mr. H.," the famous play which its own author helped to hiss off the stage. It appears, however, that "Mr. H." was produced both in New York and in Phila- delphia; and in the latter place, for ten years or more, it was one of the stock-pieces acted at the Chestnut-street Theatre. When it was first brought out it met with "extraordinary success." Not only this, but Elliston wanted to act it again in England. FORETELLING FIRE-DAMP ESCAPES.—It is well known that the escape of fire-damp in mines is intimately asso- ciated with the height of the barometer, which thus be- comes'a means of foretelling when such escapes are likeliest to occur. But according to M. de Chaneourtois, who has brought the matter before the French Academy, the danger is also increased by strain in the earth's crust causing or opening fissures in the coal; and he therefore proposes to fix seismographic apparatus at the head of every dangerous mine in order to detect these strains and take additional precautions against the gas.—Engineering. The production of the Nibelungen-cyclus in Italy seems to have proved an unexpected success. In Venice and Bologna, but especially in Rome, the performances a Herr Angelo Neumann's company were received with enthusiasm. A romantic celebration took place at Venice in front of the Palazzo Vendramin, in which Wagner died. The orchestra of 60 members played from a decorated vessel the overture to " Tannhauser " and the Funeral March from the GOtter- dammerung." The Grand Canal was crowded with gondo- las during this uncommon concert, which concluded with the Italian Royal March and a demonstration by the float- ing audience. A NEW MINOR PLANET.—Shortly after nine o'clock on Sunday evening M. Borelly, of the Marseilles Observatory, discovered a new minor planet. At nine hours thirty-seven minutes it was in right ascension fourteen hours twenty miqutes, and south declination fourteen degrees, the daily motion being thirteen seconds in right ascension (decreas- ing) and seven seconds in declination (increasing). It is of the eleventh magnitude, and can therefore only be observed with large telescopes. The number of these bodies known at the present time is 234, the first having been discovered on January Ist, 1801, by the late Guiseppe Piazzi at the Palermo Observatory. We learn from the Athenaitm that the whole of Mr. William George Black's "Folk Medicine," which has been written for the Folk-lore Society, is now through the press, and, with the exception of the index, is ready for the binder's hands. Mr. Black is himself preparing the index, and this will be ready in a day or two. The chapters deal with the origin of disease, transference of disease, sympa- thy and association in ideas, new birth, our Lord and the saints in folk medicine, charms connected with death or the grave, colour, number, influence of the sun and moon, per- sonal cures, animal cures, specific charms, domestic folk medicine.

THE VISTULA AND Tun DNIESTER.—They rise within thirty miles of each other, and each runs, not counting ins and outs, its clear three hundred miles—the Vistula to the north-east, the Dniester to the south-west; the two of them together cut Europe straight across, at the broad neck of it, and more deeply looking at the thing, - they divide Europe, properly so called, Europa's own and Jove's, the small educationable, civilisable, and more or less mentally rational fragment of the globe, from the great Siberian , wilderness, cis-Ural and trans-Ural; the inconceivable chaotic space occupied datelessly by Scythians, Tartars, Huns, Cossacks, bears, ermines, and mammoths, in various thickness of hide, form of brain, and woe of abode—or of lunabiding. Nobody's history worth making out has any- thing to do with them; for the force of Scandinavia never came round by Finland at all, but always sailed or paddled itself across the Baltic or down the rocky west coast ; and the Siberian and Russian ice pressure merely drives the really memorable races into greater concentration, and kneads them up in fiercer and more necessitous exploring masses. But by those exploring masses of true European birth, our own history was fashioned for ever; and, there- fore, these two truncating and guarding rivers are to be marked on your map of Europe with supreme clearness— the Vistula, with Warsaw astride of it half-way down, and embouchure in Baltic • the Dneister, in Euxine ; flowing, each of them, measured arrow-straight, as far as from Edin- burgh to London—with widenings, the Vistula six hun- dred miles, and the Dneister five; count them together for a thousand miles of moat. between Europe and the desert, reaching from Dantzic to Odessa.—" Ott?' Fathers Have Told Us," by Mr. Ruslcin. AN AIR-DRIVEN TRAMCAR.—The direct application of compressed air to the driving of tramcars was successfully demonstrated on Wednesday to a large party of gentlemen interested in such matters by the British Mekarski Air Engine Company. The Mekarski engine is no novelty as an independent engine, in which form it has already done good work in tramway hauling in this country. It is, however, as combined with a tramcar that it is new in Eng- land, although in this form it has been working tramway traffic successfully at Nantes, in France, for the last four years. The engine-house is situated at the depot of the London Street Tramway's Company, in the Camden-road, Holloway, and contains two 20-horse power engines, with compressing cylinders, air receivers, and store tanks for a reserve of compressed air at a pressure of 4501b5. per square inch, steam being supplied to the compressing engines by two double-flued Lancashire boilers. The car is one of the ordinary cars of the London Street Tramways Company (who are the first to adopt the system) adapted for working on t4l WicatelS^FineTie. The car has two pairs of wheels, one pair being used for driving and being connected with the working'cyllnders, which are 511 n. in diameter, with a 10in, stroke' and in which the compressed air is used. This air is stored in a reservoir placed under the body of the car, and in passing thence to the cylinders it is conducted through boiling water and steam at 601bs, per square inch, carried in a vessel called a hot-pot. This vessel is charged at the depat during. the time occupied in charging the. reservoir on the car with compressed air. This application of heat not only causes an ex- pansion of the air, but prevents the formation of snow , in the cylinders and at the exhaust. The moisture picked up also acts as a lubricant for the slide valves and pistons of the driving engines. The working pressure varies from 1201bs. down to 501bs. per square inch, the variation being ' zegulated by a special valve which gives the driver a means of minutely adjusting the pressure and of perfectly con- trolling the engine, and consequently the vehicle. A hot- pot is placed at each end of the car, on the platform, and the driver and conductor have at present to change ends at the close of each run. By adopting a triangle at each end of the line, however, the cars in future will be reversed, so that in adapting the other cars of the company, as is in- tended, a hot-pot will be placed at one end only, and thus expense will be saved. The car is fitted with the ordinary driver's foot brake, besides which there is a powerful air- pressure brake for use in emergencies, which will bring the , car up in a distance slightly exceeding its own length. No ' noise whatever is made by the exhaust air from the en- gines, nor is there any steam visible, nor the smell of fire or engine lubricants. The car runs smoothly and well, as was demonstrated at the trial on Wednesday, which was made upon the company's line, which runs the whole length of the Caledonian-road, between Holloway-road and King's- cross. The length is two miles, and it has several steep gradients and sharp curves on its course. The journey to King's-cross and back. was accomplished in excellent time, and was in other respects a success. It is intended to fit the remaining cars on this line upon the Mekarski princi- ple, and so by degrees to supersede the present horse trac- tion. At the close of the experiments the visitors were entertained at luncheon by the directors of the Mekarski Company.

IT REVIVED Ihm.—Just as a Chicago, Burlington, and Quincy train stopped at Galesburg one day recently, and everything was still for a moment, a man sitting near the forward end of the car was heard to groan as though in terrible anguish. Some of the passengers went over to him and found him speechless. One of the men pulled out a flask of brandy, and two others prying open .his teeth forced about half a pint of the liquor down his diaphragm. He . immediately revived. "Do you feel better now " inquired the man with the brandy. "Yes, sir," was the reply. "What do you think was the matter with you?" "I Wanted a drink."

div.head: I NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, ITORTI-
div.p: I NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, ITORTI-
CIJLTURF, &e.

During the year 1882, 34 horses, 63 beasts and cows, 162 sheep, one donkey, and 15 hounds were run over and killed on our railways. On the 6th September next a valuable selection of short- horns from the herd of the Duke of Devonshire will be sold by Mr. Thornton' embracing at least ten cows and heifers of the celebrated Oxford tribe. A butcher and cattle dealer of Newcastle-under-Lyme, named Edwin Edge, was committed for trial on a charge of defrauding auctioneers. He had obtained valuable cattle from several farms and local auctioneers by cheques, which were subsequently returned dishonoured. Professor J. T. Edwards, Randolph, N.Y., is well pleased with his ensilage experience-200 tons maize from eleven acres, and fed to cattle at the rate of twenty-five pounds twice a day per head, with one ration of hay. He advises the use of meal in connection with the preserved fodder. A shorthorn cow belonging to a Mr. C. Brooks' farmer of Little Horward,Bucks, presented him with a fine heifer calf with five legs, all perfect. The fifth leg was fixed on its back between its shoulders. On the third day after the calf was born, the farrier took the leg off, and the calf is now doing well. The Department of Agriculture has leased a piece of ground in the outskirts of the city of Washington to be used as an experiment farm and hospital in connection with in- vestigations of diseases of animals. Dr. E. B. Salmon, who has ror a number of years been employed by the department in the investigations of diseases of cattle, swine and pOul- try, will take charge of the work. Last week, Mr. Greenhouse, a farmer, near Presteign, lost a cow in a very curious manner. Three of his cows strayed on to the highway, owing to a gate having been left open, and proceeded in the direction of an old quarry, some dis- tance up the road. Eventually two of them fell over the quarry, one being killed, and the other is not expected•to recover. The loss is still greater owing to the cows being in calf. _ _

THE 116YAL SHOW AT READING.—The precise financial results of the Royal Show at Reading last summer are now for the first time made public. The total receipts amounted to £15,822 12s. id., and the expenditure to £15,803 is. 10d., thus leaving a sum of £l9 10s. 3d. standing to the credit of the society. This small balance is in a great measure due to-the large sum of £2,241 2s. appropriated to the trials of hay driers, &c. A LONG FENCE.—The longest line of fence in the world will be the wire fence extending from the Indian Territory west across the Texas Panhandle, and 35 miles into New Mexico. We are informed that eighty-five miles of this fence is already under contract. Its course will be in the line of the Canadian River, and its purpose is to stop the drift of the Northern cattle. It is a bold and splendid enterprise, and will pay large percentage on the investment. The fence will be over 200 miles long.—Land. SALE OF TENANT RIGHT.—Mr. David Wood, auctioneer, Castleblayney, put up for sale, on Monday, the tenant's in- terest in a farm near that town, the property of Miss Har- rison. The farm is about two miles from Castleblayney, and is beautifully situated along the shore of Lough Muckno. It contains 48 acres,and is held under Mrs. Hope, of Blayney Castle, at theyearly rent of £4O. The farm is in a superior state of cultivation, and there is a finely situated residence on it The farm was knocked down to Mr. John Harrisen for 1972. FARM FIRES IN WALES.---A fire, the undoubted work of an incendiary, broke out on Sunday night in the stackyard of Rhosnessney Farm, and the contents of the stackyard were destroyed, but the farm buildings were saved. This is the fourth incendiary fire that has occurred in North Wales during the past few months. A few weeks since the farm was also the scpne of wanton outrage of another character. During the nig,ht the whole of the straps of the threshing machine were cut and rendered useless, and although a re- ward was offered no clue to the miscreant was obtained. LABOURERS' COTTAGES.—III connection with the Cork Industrial Exhibition, Mr. Villiers Stuart, M.P., offers a prize of £5O for the best plans, specification, detailed esti- mate, and model, on the scale of 11 inches to the foot, of a labourer's cottage, the cost of erecting which is not to ex- ceed £52 10s., the winner to undertake to build a full-sized cottage in conformity with the plans, specification, detailed estimate, and model for the specified sum, within a radius of six miles from Cork, or within a reasonable distance, on receiving an order for the same. Plans, specification esti- mate, and model for two cottages at a post of £lO5 will be allowed to compete for this prize. SHORTHORNS IN AMERICA.—A a combined sale of Mr. R. Gibson's and Mr. Huston's shorthorns, held at Dexter Park, Chicago, on Wednesday, April 18th, the seventeen females belonging to the former made 18,760 dol., or an average of £220 a piece. Mr. Huston's eight averaged about £273 each. The highest priced lot in the sale was Duchess of Hilldale Ist, calved in 1881, and in calf. She was sold for 6,000 dol. to Mr. S. Givens. Duke of Hilldale Ist, about the same age fetched 3,500 dol. Lally Barrington 6th, bred by the age, of Lathom, and sold by him to Mr. Gib- son, was knocked down at 3,000 dol. to Mr. A. J. Alexander. ' Business is reported to have been brisk; but some embar- rassment was caused by one or two buyers, who expected the old fashion of payment by bills would be permitted. This was not allowed, and the lots were again put up "for prompt cash," and made an advance in each case. THE FLOCKS IN KENT.—The largeness of the fall of lambs this spring is the subject of general remark. The lambing began badly, and it seemed at first as if there would not be a lamb to every ewe. Subsequently twos and. threes were frequent, and deaths by no means a large per- centage, so that there are reports of flocks in which 160, 150, and 140 strong, healthy lambs have been given per 100 ewes. An extraordinary feature of the lambing, however, is that the male lambs are numerous beyond all proportion to the ewes. It is estimated that of every three lambs two are rams. This is considered wonderful. Particularly is it the case in the Weald of Kent. Another curious fact is, that sheep this year are very little troubled with the tick. Those which have been out at winter keep among the hill districts of West Kent, Surrey, and Sussex have returned home almost free from parasites of this kind. Perhaps the wet winter had something to do with this clearness of the wool from insects.

AN A B C EXPERIMENT ON ENSILAGE.—We take the following from a Banffshire paper. I write to inform you of an experiment I have been making on ensilage. You are aware that there has been a considerable amount of discus- sion about it in this country, and many will not believe that it is possible to prevent wet grass from rotting if put up in that state. I must allow I was very doubtful about it, as I had seen some specimens of it which had been sent to the Secretary of the Highland and Agricultural Society, and which smelt badly, but I have no doubt it was from its having been exposed for a length of time after it was taken out of the pit. Since meeting with a gentleman on his re- turn from America, who described the process, which is a very simple one, I have made the experiment on a very small scale; and which any of your readers may do who are not satisfied of the results. I obtained a jar with a pretty wide mouth, cut some wet grass, sliced some carrots, also turnips, greens, and cabbages; cut each and all into short lengths of an inch, less or more, put them into the jar, pressing them hard down until the jar was full, closed the mouth with a lump of clay, and laid it away for two months. I then, to get the mixture in a solid state, broke the jar, and the whole came out quite fresh—no bad smell whatever. I then took the mixture to the byre (the cows were eating cabbage at the time). I offered the mixture to one of the cows, and she at once left the cabbages and ate the mixture with ev,dent relish. I should think it would be a very great advantage to the farmers in this country to have pits in which they could preserve the second crop of grass in any kicul of weather, or in which, when taking up , their swede turnips, they could save all the tops for spring use; as often both the second crop of clover is lost, and, the turnips having to be taken up without delay, the tops can- not he all used, even by the young cattle.—Ron. WILSON (Durn), in the Banffshire Journal. AGRICULTURAL ENGINEERS' ASSOCIATION.—The annual meeting of this, association, which is one of growing im- portance, was held last week at Midland Grand Hotel, London, the president in the chair. The report for the year states that foreign tariffs have been investigated, pro- posed alterations noted, and, through the Foreign Office, influence has been exerted to modify duties on agricultural implements; railway rates have been attacked, and reducl tions in favour of the purchaser of agricultural machinery secured, local assessment rates have been considered, action taken, and other important matters discussed during the year. The treasurer reported a balance in hand, and alto- gether the association seems in a healthy condition. Col. Griffin, of the firm Walter A. Wood, was unanimously re- elected president for the ensuing year, and Messrs. James Hornsby and Robert Charles Rausome, vice-presidents. Vegetation in general around Preston has improved con- siderably during the past few days. The various seeds that may have been committed to the ground from time to time, and were unable to germinate on account of the cold, will appear to come up all at once, and such things as broccoli, greens, and Savoys are all the better if thinned out a little wherever they appear to crowd each other. Those left will make stronger plants. If it is desirable to make the most of them, prepare a mellow piece of ground, and prick the surplus into it 2in. apart. If the sun is hot they will require some shade, and a few green boughs thrust into the ground amongst them will greatly assist them; so will any kind of wicker basket inverted over them and this should be removed at night after the first night or two, and only placed on in the sunniest part of the day. The aim should be to inure them by degrees to bear full exposure. These remarks will be applicable to celery plants, which some will be pricking out, others trans- planting. Few things suffer on removal so much as this, and anything in the shape of a screen should be resorted to. The trenches should be prepared for the earliest batch. We never plant nearer than 4ft. apart. We mark the trench with the line 18in. in width, and the soil if thrown out 12in. , deep ; Gin, of manure is thrown in and forked with the ' I bottom soil. This leaves only a few inches of real trench, though it is true that it will sink a little. The ridges or the spaces between the trenches we plant with lettuce or coleworts, and sometimes cauliflowers. Some of the trenches will be between the rows of peas; in that case the ground is already cropped. The stumps of winter greens an broccoli should be cleared off the ground as soon as they are of no further use. They seem to be a prey for underground insects, which being supplied with ample food increase rapidly in numbers. Again, though the growth the greens make is of no use for culinary purposes, but is sufficient to assist in exhausting the soil, consequently the sooner they are moved the better. The ground these have occupied should be forked up, and allowed to remain roughly until it is disintegrated by wind, sun, and rain. The hoe can scarcely be applied too frequently amongst crops. Where hoeing is persevered in, weeds cannot grow, and the haunts of insects are being continually disturbed,

div.p: ' - • 91,., r THR -EXAMINER. SATURDAY MAY 26, 1883. COTTAGE GARDENING. THE TURNIP FLY will soon be a source of annoyance in some places, attacking young seedlings of the cabbage tribe as well as the turnip. We have not found a better preven- tative than soot and lime mixed in about equal proportions, and if scattered over the plants in the morning when the plants are usually moist with due, it adheres to the leaves better. Dust off the road will frequently act as a deterrent. For the benefit of those who may not be acquainted with this insect, and the mischief it creates, we may as well state that it is of a dark colour, and if any attempt is made to catch it it jumps from the plant on to another some distance off. On this account it has received the sobriquet turnip " flea," and it is as übiquitous as the little household pest of that name. It is so insidious in its inroads that few are aware that it is the cause of the perforations in the leaves of the turnip and other plants similar to those on a sheet of postage stamps. FRONT GARDEN.—The rain has made the plants in this department look nice and fresh by washing the dust off the foliage. Calceolarias may now be planted. They should be placed in an oblique direction. They are so brittle that if planted upright the wind frequently severs whole branches from the plants. We find as they grow the points of the shoots turn up, and by the time they are in flower they appear as if they had been planted in the usual way. Creepers and roses should be made secure to the walls or fences. There is more danger of their breaking now than at any time. There is a daily increase of foliage, and this in a shower of rain becomes of considerable weight, and weighs the plant down to the ground. We have seen some recently so, and their apparent owners lounging largely on the opposite fence or on the entrance gate. It is not a very laborious undertaking to drive a few nails into the joints of the bricks and attacha piece of string to each of them, and then tie the main branches with it. We like this method equally as well as having cloth or leather shreds round each shoot and attached to the wall with a nail. All kind of annuals should have the last sowing made at once, also Wall- flowers and Sweet William. The two latter may be sown in the vegetable garden, and planted in the front garden in the autumn or spring, and as they do not flower the same year they are sown, they may be made to give way to those things that do. THE WINDOW.—The Arum Lily is a most serviceable window plant. We occasionally observe one here and there. They require a liberal supply of water, and they will soon throw up their spathes„ as their semi-trumpet-shaped flowers are termed. These plants do equally well out of doors during the summer months, and gardeners occasion- ally plant them out in rich ground when they require gigantic specimens, and lift them up and pot tfient in Sep- tember or early in October. We name this to incite the cottager to be courageous, and move his plants outside at the proper time. The pots may be partly plunged in a border or in ashes to counteract the drying influence of the sun. The Hydrangea is another occasional tenant of the window, and will now be forming its buds, which will de- velops into globular, massive heads ere long. This plant has stood the severest winters in some of the southern counties, and on that account there must be no scruple about turning it also out of doors in summer. Like the Arum, it can scarcely receive too much water. Geraniums of the bedding out type may be turned out of doors in the day time, and replaced inside at night, if there is no means of protecting them. Treated in this way for a week, they will be sufficiently hard even to remain outside entirely. Those called Pelargoniums may be stood outside during showery weather to have the dust washed off their foliage and be otherwise refreshed. They will now be showing their flower buds, and if there are any traces of greenfly on any about to expand, fumigate them with to- bacco smoke, according to the instructions given some time back. If they 'lre fumigated after their flowers are developed the petals or the most ornamental part of the flower collapse. The musk plant and musk Mimmulus will now be moving, and should not be allowed to get dry. If there is any room on the surface for any soil, a top dress- ing will be beneficial. About one-eighth of horse excre- ment rubbed fine and mixed with loam and leaf mould will ' prove highly nutritious. Fuchsias that have been properly treated will have advanced sufficiently to have half the soil shook away from their roots, and some of the longest of the latter may be shortened half their length. They may be potted into pots of the same size that they have been occu- pying, which should be thoroughly cleansed inside and out, and efficiently crocked or drained. The soil should consist of decomposed turfy loam and leaf mould, in proportion of three of the former to one of the latter and a tenth of the whole of silver sand. The whole to be thoroughly mixed. Two inches of the rougher portion of this compost must be placed on the crocks in the pot to prevent the smaller par- ticles entering amongst them and obstructing the free pas- sage of the water given to the plants from time to time. In placing the roots in the fresh pot it is necessary to be care- ful to have soil all round them sufficient to prevent them being in contact with the side of the pot. The compost should be well worked amongst the roots, by giving the bottom of the pot sundry taps on a table or any firm base. The surface should be pressed with the thumbs, and soil added until within an inch of the top in a 6in, pot, but a i trifle less in a smaller one.

A TRAIN ON FIRE. 7.,,The occupants (ladies) of a carriage of the elken train from Chester to Shrewsbury on %Vednesday, were horrified soon after leaving Wrexham to find flames coming through the top of the carriage and a red hot bolt apparently ready to fall in their midst. The communication cord was hurriedly pulled. The engine stopped and was after- wards drawn into a colliery siding where the flames were extinguished. It was subsequently ascertained that the workmen at the new iron bridge at Wrexham, had let a red hot bolt fall on the train as it was passing. A Chester correspondent telegraphs the following account of the occurrence :—On Thursday, as the members of the Chester Natural Science Society were proceeding on an ex- cursion to Llangollen, some of the large party who were in a carriage at the rear of the train noticed, after passing Wrexham, that the roof of the compartment was on fire. The train was running rapidly, and as the roof was naturally, during this dry weather, in a very combustible condition, no little alarm prevailed among the occupants, many of whom were ladies. To prevent the flames from playing on the inside of the carriage a gentleman present, Mr. Hickman, of Chester, promptly crushed his hat against the hole which it was making. There being no communication between passengers and guard loud cries were raised which attracted the atten- tion of the other passengers. Handkerchiefs were waved from the windows, and ultimately, after great excitement, some vrerkmen on the line drew the attention of the guard to the fire, and the train was brought to a standstill. The driver first carried a bucket of water to the burning carriage, but this proving useless the engine was run forward to the points burning, and brought back on the down line opposite the carriage, and water was poured upon the flames, which were speedily extinguished. The damage done to the roof of the carriage was fortunately very slight, owing to the promptitude with which the train was stopped.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANA L BILL. The Select Committee of the House of Commons to Which the above bill has been referred met again on Thurs- day, which was the tenth sitting ; Sir Joseph Bailey presid- ing. The other members were Mr. Reginald Yorke, Mr. A. P. Vivian, and Mr. Stafford Howard. It will be remembered that at the last meeting but one of the committee before the Whitsuntide recess the engineering evidence of the pro- moters was closed, after which the chairman declared that there was a priinz facie case on which to proceed, and sub- sequently a legal point was raised by the opponents of the bill as to whether the powers of the Mersey Conservancy Commissioners were sufficiently extensive to allow of the construction of a low water channel in the estuary under their authority without express legislation, but the corn- mittee did not deem the objection to be of such weight as to warrant their interfering with the progress of the measure, and it was arranged that at the next meeting the general case of the promoters should be proceeded with. The commercial aspect of the scheme was laid before the Committee by Mr. Daniel Adamson, chairman of the Pro- visional Committee of the undertaking.—Mr. ADAMSON said that up to September last about £64,000 had been subscribed for the preliminary expenses, and since that time pr4bably £15,000 more had been raised. The total number of sub- scribers was 4,251. The scheme was probably the most popular thing Gince the formation of the Anti-Corn Law League, even if it was not more popular than that. The principal object of the promoters was to cheapen the carriage of goods between Liverpool and Manchester and the surrounding districts. Mr. Adamson then entered into a detailed statement of the grievances of the mercantile community of this district in regard to Liverpool dues and charges and railway rates. He said that the high rates now charged bad seriously affected the Lancashire trades and several works had been stopped as a consequence. With, their present area the Mersey Dock Board could not accom- modate any increased shipping, and he often beard com- plaints that they had not now sufficient accommodation. As an engineer he aid not think there would be any difficulty in making the canal. Subscribers had the option of taking up shares to the amount of 20 times their subscription, and he expected that that option would be largely taken advan- tage of. He himself had subscribed £l,OOO, and inclined to taking up the shares open to him.

Before- the committee rose for the day the chairman, address;ng one of the counsel for the promoters, expressed a hope that when he came to examine the ship engineers, he would not give the committee the same evidence over and over again. He was afraid the committee were already "in" for a very long time.

div.head: PRINTER'S DEVIL.-IV.
div.p: THE PRINTER'S DEVIL.-IV.

[By ANGT.o-Scoirs.] A prominent politician who was charged the other Jay with having a desire to "put his finger into his opponents' pies," was made to appear in print as being of so san- guinary a disposition as to wish to "put his finger into his opponents' pus." Now there is a story on record to the effect that Aldus Manntius, a printer in Venice to the Holy Church and the Doge, at one time employed a negro boy to help him in his office. And it got abroad that this little black boy was an imp of Satan, and the people christened him by the name of the Printer's Devil. Now Manutius must have been a bit of a wag, for in order to protect the young Caxtonian from persecution, and to confute a foolish superstition, the master made a public exhibition of the apprentice, and announced that "any one who doubted him to he flesh and blood might come forward and pinch him." Perhaps the comp. who gave the politician credit for cruelty had read this story, and imagined the pinches in time developed into suppurating wounds, and hence his confusion of metaphor. If he should read this, I hope he will take the allusion to the circumstance good-naturedly and acquit me of any intention to unnecessarily irritate " proud flesh." In a recently published article on the debate on the Ex- plosives Act, for "both the Houses were unanimous," duly came out " both Houses were harmonious." Probably the compositor and reader thought that if as was asserted just previous to the commencement of the Franco-German war Frenchmen were "dancing on the edge of a volcano," the threatened blow-up of London would make British legislators express themselves thereon in musical numbers—possibly in the spirit that When griping grief the heart dot Is wound, And doleful dumps the minc., oppress, Then Afusir with his silver sound, With speedy help doth lend redress."

To take another recent instance, here is the heading given by a well known weekly paper to the St. Denis tragedy : "Terrible Tragedy at a wedding—Murder of the Bridegroom and Suicide of the Assassin." And this is how the account concludes :—"The unfortunate bridegroom is in a very serious condition." I should think 80. In almost as serious and lamentable a condition as the Times critic, who in the same week criticised a play in the morning that was not per- formed till the evening. Clever people, these critics! But it would seem to be in connection with Art that the Printer's Devil or his satellites exercise their power in the most exuberant fashion. The following is delightful:—" If you ask," observes a correspondent in the Church Review, " the editor of Truth, he will tell you that four queens of fashionable society are said to have sat as nude models for the four figures in a picture exhibited by an R.A. in the Academy a few years ago." I wonder if that correspondent is a Scotchman, if he has filled the office of church elder, and penned his "observations " on art after having been " oxtered "home by a buxom waiting-woman from a Sunday night's "toddy meeting!" The reply to the rash assertion is a caution in its way. The answer of the editor of Truth is as follows:—" He certainly will not 'tell you' anything of the kind. The only instance that I know of a fashionable lady sitting in the nude' is that of the Princess Pauline Bonaparte, who sat thus to Canova. Some one asked her how she could have consented to do so? Her answer was, There was a fire in the room, so I did not feel cold.' " I should think the "correspondent " did not feel particularly chilly alter reading the above reply. Even for Royalty itself the Printer's Devil has no respect. The Court Circular, under date of 18th May last, stated that "the Princess Beatrice went to London yesterday. She visited the Royal Academy, and afterwards honoured the Royal Italian Opera with her presence. She then went to the Fisheries Exhibition, and at ten o'clock left Buckingham Palace and went to Esher to be present at a concert.' As " Dagonet " in the Referee says, "This is all very wonder- ful. To leave Windsor in the afternoon, do the Academy and then the Italian Opera, taking the Fisheries Exhibition afterwards, and winding up by going to .Esher, is a slightly jumbled prograinme ; but the conclusion of the day's—[or rather, "Dagonet " should have said the night's; but pos- sibly the P. D. jogged his elbow]—amusement is the most marvellous." According to the Court Circular, the motto of H.R.H. is "Late to bed and early to rise," for in connec- tion with Princess Beatrice's movements next day we are told that "she arrived at Windsor Castle at a quarter before eight this morning, having driven from Claremont." Where- upon " Dagonet " again remarks:—" I knew that the Royal Family were early risers, but I can't for the life of me imagine why the Princess should drive from Claremont to Windsor at such a remarkable hoer as that. I fancy the Court newsman must have got a little mixed somewhere." I quite coincide with this opinion; and I have no doubt so will the readers of The Examiner. Harking back again to Art, the titles or descriptions of pictures, dr.c., in the art ex- hibitions—or the handwriting of the critics—would seem to more than usually bother the compositors. The Cinderella of Mr. Millais was recently described by an art critic as " a child seated in front of a dying fire, with an old broom in her hand." For" broom" the compositor put " horse." A modern Cinderella "with an old horse in her hand," recalls to mind the story about the mischievous infant daughter of one of the Indian gods, who used to throw elephants and camels up on to:the tops of houses for the purpose of getting fun and enjoyment out of the clumsy attempts of the animals themselves, or in the event of their non-success in the attempt, then of the efforts of the owners and inhabi- tants to get the huge brutes down again. Another sentence in the same writer's criticism of the picture alluded to, and which should have been read, "The pose is easy, the back- ground quiet," &e.. was rendered " The horse is easy, the blackguard quiet," Ix

div.head: DYNAMITE PLOT.
div.p: THE DYNAMITE PLOT.
EXAMINATION OF THE LIVERPOOL PRISONERS.

At the Liverpool City Police Court on Saturday, before Mr. Raffles, the prisoners who have been several times re- manded on charges of conspiracy to commit felonies, were brought up for further examination. Their names are Dennis Deasy, 26, and Patrick Flannigan, 32, railway brakesmen (arrested at St. Helens) ; Timothy Featherstone, 30, described as a press correspondent; Daniel O'Herlihy, 36, ink manu- facturer, and Henry Dalton, 39 (alias John O'Connor). Mr. Marks, assistant prosecuting solicitor, appeared to conduct the case; Dr. O'Feely appeared for the two first-named pri- soners; Dr. Commins for Featherstone and O'Herlihy; and Mr. Little for Dalton. Mr. Marks, in opening the case, said that the prisoners, with the exception of Deasy and Flanni- gan, were charged with conspiracy to commit felonies, and with being in the illegal possession of explosives, with intent to blow up public buildings. They had been remanded on different occasions, and it would he remembered that Dennis Deasy and Patrick Flannigan were the two men committed on a former occasion for trial at the assizes on these charges. At the assizes the trial was postponed in order that they might be arraigned with the prisoners who had just then been arrested. Those were nominally the charges on which they were arrested, but he proposed to ask his worship to commit the men on four different charges. The first charge on which he would ask for a committal was treason felony, the second conspiracy to damage, injure, and destroy pnblic and other buildings; the third was being In possession of explosives with intent to commit a felony; and therfourth was conspiracy to murder subjects of her Majesty. His worship was aware that although these men were charged with what was a joint offence, nevertheless they had been arrested under different circum- stances, and there were different sets of facts which applied to each prisoner individually, as well as the general broad facts which connected the whole of the men concerned in the conspiracy. With regard to Deasy and Flannigan, the facts had been pretty well brought out on a former occasion, but they would require observation so far as they bore on the case of the prisoners, who at that time were under arrest. After detail- ing the circumstances as to the arrest of the various prisoners, Mr. Marks proceeded to call evidence.—Sub-In- spector Starkie, of the Royal Irish Constabulary at Cork, proved the arrest of Featherstone at Cork, at a refreshment house, on the 29th March. On being searched an order on Messrs. Montgomery and Co., of Glasgow, for four carboys of sulphuric acid, WAS found upon him, and also a green paper, headed "A Cure for Gout." At his lodgings was found a glass test tube similar to one on a dia- gram on the paper, "A Cure for Gout."—Several other witnesses were examined, amongst them William Dreghorn, a supercargo, in the employment of the Clyde Shipping Company at Cork, who testified to the pri- soner Deasy taking away, on the Bth January last, a carboy of nitric acid, which arrived at Cork from Glasgow, and was addressed to D. O'Herlihy, Cork. Deasy signed for the carboy in the presence of witness, and the book containing his signature was produced. Deasy had previously been inquiring if there were any goods for Mr.O'Herlihy. Another carboy addressed to O'Herlihy, Cork, arrived in Cork from Glasgow on the 22nd February, and was deposited on the quay. On the 24th of February a carboy of sulphuric acid arrived at Cork from Glasgow for the same person. On the sth April two carboys of nitric acid arrived at Glasgow addressed to O'Herlihy, 10, Great George-st., West Cork, and witness sent advice notes to O'Herlihy respect- ing them.—Christian Jacob Danckert, also a supercargo in the service of the Clyde Shipping Company, deposed to Deasy taking away the first carboy mentioned by the pre- vious witness, and to Deasy saying that it was no use send- ing advice notes respecting the arrival of any,carboys to O'Herlihy, because he knew that they were there. Deasy fetched other carboys away. Witness once asked Deasy what O'Herlihy required so much acid for, and he replied for making ink and other purposes.- -On Monday the prisoners were further examined and re- manded. Evidence by means of letters and postcards con- necting the prisoners with one another in the purchasing and transmitting of acids in carboys. as well as scientific evidence on the part of Colonel Majendie and Lieutenant Ford, was given. Inspector Littlechild, of the Metropolitan Police, deposed to finding in Dalton's possession instructions regarding Fenian centres.—The investigation was resumed on Tuesday.—Dr. Campbell Brown, city analyst, repeated the evidence given at the previous trial as to the acids and infernal machines found in the possession of Deasy. Evi- dence followed respecting Dalton's voyage from New York to Liverpool in the Celtic, and his arrest in London. Ser- geant Melville, of the Metropolitan Police, said that on March 24th, he saw Dalton in front of the Charing Cross Hotel with another man. The witness watched them go down Parliament-street and passed the scene of the explo- sion at the Local Government Board Offices, at which they laughed.;They also went to Westminster Abbey, and visited the Clock Tower at the Houses of Parliament, apparently inspecting the base of the building for ten minutes. On March 31st the witness again followed Dalton and another man. He saw them in Sloane Square about midnight, talking together for over an hour. The.other man was ges- ticulating violently, and Dalton said," I would let the swines have a bullet." A few minutes later Dalton drew something from his pocket and showed it to his companion. Afterwards Dalton went in the direction of Chelsea Barracks. The inquiry was further adjourned. The inquiry concluded on Wednesday. Evidence was given as to the arrest of Deasey in Liverpool. Several wit- nesses deposed to the explosion in Glasgow, and at the Times office, London, and stated that the explosives and machines used on these occasions were similar to those found in Liverpool. Prisoners, who reserved their defence, were committed for trial on four charges—namely, treason- felony, and conspiracy to damage, injure, and destroy pub- lic buildings, being in possession of explosives with intent to commit a felony, and conspiracy to murder subjects of her Majesty. Bail was refused. DESIGNS OF DYNAMITERS ON LONDON.

div.head: DERBY DAY.
div.p: THE DERBY DAY.

The race for the Derby Stakes was run under exception- ally favourable circumstances, the weather being all that could be desired. Most people concurred in opinion that the spectators were in number far in excess of anything experienced for a long time. Every element of society, from the Heir Apparent down to the humblest excursionist from the Metropolis, was. represented. The arrivals by road were not so numerous as in previous years, but the rail- ways with termini on the Downs and in the village of Epsom proper were taxed to their utmost resources. There was full and varied provision of all kinds of amusement. It is to be hoped, however, the foreigners who for the first time may have visited the scene of the great race will not too closely interpret the rude devices to amuse and interest the British public as in any way representing either the common sense of the people or the national regard for fun or frolic. Never has Epsom Downs presented a grander scene than on Wed- nesday. An invigorating breeze from the south kept the rising clouds of dust from the Downs and tempered the heat of the glorious sunshine. The massive trees there ought to have been rich in their green dress, but they were ' coated with white dust that clung to the leaves like a hoar frost. The grand stand was crowded to its utmost capacity, and the ring was literally packed with people. There was a fall attendance of members of both Houses of Parliament, Seldom has there been mole uncertainty felt as to the result of the race for the Derby Stakes. As usual, on the day that decides the event there was an abandon- ment of old favourites, such as Galliard, Splendor, and highland Chief. The Prince was thought by some to be 'good enough to win, and many shared the great confidence of Sir F. Johnstone in his chestnut colt St. Blaise, who ran fourth in the Two Thousand, being only four lengths behind. His owner backed St. Blaise for £lO,OOO, with the result now known to all the world. He gave his trainer, J. Porter, instructions to reduce the " beef " of St. Blaise in the firm belief that it would work wonders. Everybody expected a good race, and every- body must have been gratified. The field numbered only elven, the smallest that has started for the race for the last sixty years. The preliminary canter as usual threw little or no light upon the probable victor. All the horses looked in fine condition, except Beau Brummel, who looked worse than many expected. Fully half an hour was occupied in clearing the course. The immense multitude was orderly and amenable to discipline, and the great roar of human voices as the time flew by gradually stilled. In the royal box were the Prince and Princess of Wales, the Duke and Duchess of Connaught, the Duke and Duchess of Albany, the Duke of Cambridge, Prince Christian, Prince George, of Wales. Prince Albert Victor, Prince Edward, of Saxe-Weimar, and the suite of the royal party. Represen- tatives of several Oriental countries travelled to the course with the royal party from Victoria by a special train which arrived shortly before two o'clock. That all were not interested in the exciting moment now fast approaching was evident from the fact that the merry-go-rounds and swing boats on the crest of the hill were in full operation to the delight of their occupants, and close to the grand stand a man with a youth blindfolded was revealing the mysteries of second sight to an appreciative audience. Away behind the booths young men and maidens tripped it to imperfect music, and gipsies in the cocoanut business were everywhere pleading for custom and had it. The lover of contrast might here have seen downright frivolity airing itself side by side with the troubled yearning speculators in turf transactions, in- spiring by their aspect sympathy rather than admiration. Then tte betting men cease to harangue the multitude, and turn. their eyes towards the starting place. The end is not far off. From start to finish the whole race went like clock- work; there was no hitch from beginning to end. At the first attempt a good start was effected. Bon-Jour soon took the lead, Sigmophone and Prince being in attendance. The last two were Highland Chief and Laocoon. The pace through the Furze seemed slow. At the mile-post Bon-jour still led amongst those well up being St. Blaise, Galliard, and Prince. Rounding Tattenham Corner Ladislas had a clear lead of St. Blaise, Galliard, and Goldfield. In the straight Ladislas and Prince gave way, and it now became evident that they were out of the race. St. Blaise now had it all its own way, though Galliard and Goldfield made a des- perate effort to pass him. Highland Chief was the next to show fresh energy. In front of the grand stand it seemed as if Highland Chief would win, and many voices pro- claimed this view. He only succeeded, however, in over- hauling Galliard, whom Archer had evidently pumped out, and allowed St. Blaise to win by a neck. It was a very exciting race' and until the figures were run up those who saw saw the finish could not be positive which horse had won. There were loud cries of "Bravo, Charley," when Wood rode up on the winner into the weighing paddock, Sir Frederick Johnstone proudly leading the way. Rumour has it that a distinguished personage has an Interest in St. Blaise, and the handshaking all round in the royal box after the event strongly supported what on the course seemed to be the general belief. The crowd be- gan to rapidly thin after the principal race, comparatively little interest being apparently taken in the other items on the card. Return appended :

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The death is announced of Colonel Bousfield, whose re- tirement from the command of the Ist Lancashire Volunteers was announced only a fortnight ago. At Scarborough, on Saturday, two farm labourers were remanded for a murderous assault on a farm foreman, named Houseman, after a drunken quarrel. The injured man lies in a very critical condition. The evidences increase of a want of unanimity among tbo coalminers on the question of " restricting the output." The Aberdare ,niners have resolved to take no part in the conference on the subject, and in other parts of South Wales a similar disposition is apparent. It is announced that the Marquis of Lorne is to be Suc- ceeded in the Governor. Generalship of Canada by the Marquis of Lansdowne. It is understood that the new Gaveruor-General will go to the Dominion in October, by which time the Marquis of Lorne will have completed five years' service. A youngY man named William Emery is in custody at Birmingham charged with murdering his sweetheart, Sarah Davis. He tells a singular story as to the girl jumping in- to the canal and dragging him in with her, but he got out, and left his unfortunate companion to drown. Davis's body has been taken from the canal at the place indicated by the Prisoner. FORTHCOMING MARRIAGE OF MR. JOHN BRIGHT, M.P. Mr. John Bright, M.P.,is about to re-enter the married state. Mr. Bright was first married in 1839, to Miss Priestman, of Newcastle-upon-Tyne, who died in 1841 ; and, secondly, in 1847, to Miss Leatham, of Wakefield, who died in 1878; and we understand that the lady to whom he is about to be united is the sister of his first wife. A make-believe "infernal machine" was discovered, on Sunday morning, at the entrance of Peterborough Cathedral. Accompanying it were representations of a skull and cross hones with the words in writing " Beware of the Invincible Army," and "Conscience makes cowards of all men." A genuine fuse was attached, but the contents are believed to be merely sawdust soaked in ink and some innocuous liquids. Following up the acquisition of Eppine, Forest for the people, the Corporation of the City of London have now acquired the Coulston Commons, near Caterharn, in Kent, the area of which is about 340 acres, and on Saturday these Picturesque commons were formally dedicated to the public by Mr. Shaw-Lefevre, the Chief Commissioner of Works, who praised the public-spirited action of the Corporation in thus providing healthy recreation grounds for the people. THE REPORTED PERNERSION OF SIR TATTON SYKES.—A new organ just presented to the Parish Church at Sled- mere is the gift of Sir Tatton Sykes, and this gift is con- strued in the neighbourhood, and we believe correctly, as a public intimation that Sir Tatton still remains a member of the Church of England. The report that Sir Tatton Sykes signed contracts when in Rome for a Roman Catholic Cathedral is we believe, without the slightest foundation.— Yorkshire i ost. DEATH OF DR. WILLIAM CHAMBERS.—Dr. William Chambers, of Glenoriston, editor of Chambers's Journal, died at his residence, 20, Chester-street, Edinburgh, on Sun- day, aged 83 years. He had been confined to the house for the past three or four weeks, and gradually becoming frailer and frailer succumbed at an early hour on Sunday morning. Only about a week ago Dr. Chambers was offered and ac- cepted a baronetcy. Dr. Chambers married Miss Clark, of London,and had a familybut both wife and children are dead. DISORDERLY TORY MEETING AT NORTHAMPTON.—Mr. Richards, Conservative candidate, addressed a large meeting of electors in Northampton Town Hall, on Monday even- ing. Although accorded a favourable reception by the Con- servatives present, a strong contingent of Mr. Bradlaugh's supporters subsequently caused a riot by caterwauling. cock-crowing, and hooting, interspersed with frequent scuffling, which terminated in a free fight. The police were then called in, and the more turbelant disturbers ejected. A vote of confidence in Mr. Richards was declared carried. EXTRAORDINARY MISTAKE: LOCKED UP DURING WHIT- SUNTIDE.—An extraordinary case of mysterious disappear- ance in Birmingham has just come to light. Last Saturday week a working jeweller was missing from home. On Thers- day a policeman heard cries in a warehouse where the miss- ing man is employed, and on forcing an entrance discovered the man, whom he took into custody as a burglar. It turned out, however, that the unfortunate fellow had been locked in the premises, where he had remained a prisoner all Whit- suntide without anything to eat or drink. The two men' Warren and Toner, who were apprehended on Sunday, the 13th instant, en the premises of Mr. Beaver, jeweller, Cross-street, underwent a further examination on Monday before the Manchester Stipendiary Magistrate. The evidence given by police officers and other witnesses showed that the prisoners had made extraordinary efforts to carry off the jewellery, which was evidently their object. They had worked their way through several doors sand walls into the shop, and succeeded in partially opening the safe containing Mr. Beaver's valuable property. Mr. Head- lam again remanded the prisoners for a week. DoenetE EXECUTION AT Terwroer.—George White and. 'Joseph Wedlake were on Monday morning executed by Mar- wood in Taunton Jail—the former for the murder of his Wife at Wincanton, the latter for the murder of Mark Cox. Shortly before eight the prison bell began to toll, and a few minutes after the black flag was hoisted over the entrance to the jail. A small crowd assembled outside. Both the condemned men walked firmly to the drop, and death was instantaneous. They had been attended by the jail chap- lain, and died penitent. The bodies were allowed to hang Ott the scaffold for one hour, after which a formal inquest was held, and a verdict that the sentence of the law had been executed upon the culprits was returned. THE RECENT POISONING CASE AT SHFFIFLD.- —A Sheffield correspondent states that Mrs. Jane Jones, principal witness against Kate Dover, undergoing penal servitude for life for Poisoning Thomas Skinner, artist, died at Sheffield on Saturday, under circumstances which are being investigated. Mrs. Jones, who had been parted from her husband, met him on the 12th inst., and she stated that he kicked and struck her. The husband denies the assault. There was great jealousy between the deceased and Kate Dover. The de- ceased sent the onions in which Dover was said to have put poison. The surgeon who attended her in her last ill- ness says she struggled to make a statement before death, but was unable to do so. ARREST ON A LIVERPOOL MUSIC HALL STAGE.—OR Saturday, Mr. J. Grady, described as a "lion comique," and earning £3O a week, "and worth more," was charged at the Birmingham Police Court with neglecting to support his wife and children, and allowing them to become chargeable to parish. Detective-Inspector Daniells stated that he arrested the defendant on the stage of a Liverpool concert hall, just after he had sung some songs and whilst the audience were applauding for an encore. Counsel for the defence urged that the defendant, who was partner with the " celebrated Pat Feeney," had not the slightest desire to to neglect his responsibilities, and the case was adjourned till Monday, it being understood that a satisfactory settle- ment would be made. TILE Nonni WALES COLLEGE.—At an influential meet- ing held at Chester on Saturday, under the presidency of Lord Pow's, it was reported that the subscriptions in aid of the proposed college for North Wales now amount to a trifle Over £28,000. It was resolved to refer the question of the site for the college to the Lord President of the Privy Coun- cil, the Vice-President of the Committee of Council on Edu- cation, and Lord Bramwell, and that they be asked to give their decision within three months. No fewer than nine towns are desirous of competing for the honour of supplying a site for the college, and it was felt that the only way to decide satisfactorily where the institution shall be located was to leave the matter in the bands of three gentlemen in- terested in education and possessing no local connection with any of the rival towns. ENGLISH PATENTS. The following patents amongst Others published in the Commissioners of Patents Journal Were sealed during the week ending May 19th, 1883 :- -rernes Anderson McFerran, Manchester, improvements in the arrangement and working of clocks or timekeepers for the purpose of exhibiting uniform time at several points ; illiana Haesalwood Carmont, Manchester, consulting en- gineer, improvements in the manufacture of grooved tyres for wheels ; Percy Henry Marriott and James Hall, Stock- Port, for improvements in 'pirn and spool winding machines ; John Maynes, Manchester, improvements in gasometer en- gines; George Walter Dyson, Bolton, a new and improved construction of boiler flues and boiler shells ; Henry Sut- cliffe, Halifax, improvements in the manufacture of metal Cisterns and syphons used therewith ; Arnold Budenberg, Manchester, improvements in regulating apparatus for steam engines ; Richard Longdon Hattersley, Keighley, and Wil- liam Greenwood, of the same place, new or improved ma- chinery far " warps.—List supplied by Mr. George Davies, C.E. Feb. Lag. P.A.. Patent Solicitor, 4, St. Ann'sosquare, Manchester. MR.
