A cotton warehouse in Derby-road, Liverpool, was des- troyed by fire, together with its contents, on Tuesday, the damage being estimated at £lO,OOO. A grocer named Wall, calling on business at Bilston, was on Tuesday fined £2O and costs for using light weights He had previously been heavily fined for a similar offence. Stephen Lewis, a naval pensioner, has died at Southamp- ton, aged one hundred and five years and eleven months. He was born in June, 1777, and the evidence of his age is unimpeachable. He was a retired master gunner, and signed for his pension regularly every quarter. He was present at many- engagements on sea and shore, including that of Tra (al gar. THE PARCELS Posr.—lt is officially announced that the Postmaster-General, with the concurrence of the Treasury, has consented to the employment of time-served soldiers forming part of the first-class army reserve, or army pensioners, as parcel deliverers or as substitutes for letter- carriers and others who may be transferred from letter duties to those connected with the parcels post. ASSIZES AND GAOL DELIVERIES.—The Home Secretary has issued a circular informing clerks of justices of petty sessions that henceforth all commissions of assize will be issued in the form of gaol deliveries. It is said that in some counties this arrangement inflicts considerable hardship, and Mr. Sclater-Booth has undertaken to call attention to the matter on going into Committee of Supply. A DANGEROUS TEST OF A GALLOWS: A WORKMAN NEARLY STRANGLED.—WhiIe the gallows in Duke-street Prison, Glasgow, which was used for the execution of the Port Glasgow murderers, was being tested under the per- sonal direction of Marwoocl, one of the workmen put his head into the noose. Scarcely had he done so, when either his foot slipped or the trap gave way, and unfortunately the man got a drop that almost hanged him. BILLS or SALE AND FAILURES.—In the week ending May 19, 1833, there were 234 bills of sale in England and Wales, a decrease of 710 over those of the corresponding period last year ; and the failures gazetted numbered 149, a decrease of 63. Totals for the portion of year to May 19, 1883, are--bills of sale registered for England and Wales, 4,876, a decrease of 14,696 ; the failures gazetted number 4,241. a decrease of 169.—Stubbs's .7fercantile Gazette. The Standard says it is understood that Mr. Bradlaugh, after the demonstration which he proposes to hold on the 9th of August, will proceed to the House of Commons and again attempt to administer the oath to himself. He will be accompanied hr a great body of his supporters, but care will be taken to prevent them over-running the Houses of Parliament, or oiving any material assistance to Mr. Brad- laugh should he provoke a conflict with the officers of the House. THE ROBBERY AT THE MUNSTER BANE.—At the Dublin Commission, on Tuesday, a clerk named Lodge was charged by the Munster Bank authorities with stealing from the strong room 5,500 sovereigns from bags containing £15,000, which were about to he forwarded to Liverpool. The money !had not been traced, and the only connection established , between it and the accused was the evidence of a fellow- clerk that he saw the prisoner handling several bags of ! sovereigns shortly before the money was missed. Lodge was found "Not guilty." THE COST OF THE SPECIAL MISSION TO MOSCOW.—A supplementary estimate has been issued of the amount re- quired to defray the expenses of the special mission to the Moscow coronation. The items are :-1. Rent of house, £2,000. 2. Expenses of transport and incidental charges for Her Majesty's Ambassador and members of the Embassy and servants, maintenance of ditto, hire of horses and car- riages, and transport of ditto, £2,000. 3. Cost of transport and incidental expenses of special Embassy, £l,OOO. Gratui- ties. illuminations, and unforseen expenses, £l.OOO. Total, £6,000. , A DISPUTE BETWEEN FRENCH AND JERSEY FISHERMEN. ! —A Jersey correspondent says that frequent disputes have of late arisen between the Jersey and French fishermen as to the right to fish and cut seaweed on the Ecrehos, a large bed of rocks, lying midway between France and Jersey. The Frenchmen claim these rocks as neutral, while the Jersey men contend that they have belonged to the English Crown since the twelfth century. The matter has been brought before the States Assembly, and a deputation has been ap- pointed to go to England and lay the case before the Privy Council, with a view to the settlement of the dispute. ALLEGATION OF ASSAULT AGAINST SIGNOR FOLI.—At Westminster, London, on Tuesday, application was made for a process against Signor Fo:i, the well known operatic I singer, for an assault and threats alleged to have taken place at Monte Carlo in March. Mrs. Bradshaw, widow of the late General Bradshaw, deposed that on the day she was at the table d'hote in the same hotel with Signor Foli, and in the course of some dispute he called her a liar and a base born woman. On the following day, while again at dinner, he shook her violently. The magistrate said as the alleged assault had been committed at Monte Carlo he could not grant a process. BRITISH MILLIONAIRES.—The Spectator says:—"A little more than 10 years ago we compiled a list of all British for- tunes exceeding a quarter of a million personality which had been transferred by death within the decade. That list, which was the first of its kind, and excited at the time a preposterous amount of interest, showed that within the 10 years 10 persons had died in Great Britain leaving more than a million, 53 leaving more than half a million, and 161 leav- ing more than a quarter of a million sterling. We promised to repeat the list at the end of anether decade, and here it IS, compiled in the same way." Then follow 216 names and amounts of fortunes. We can but give a summary. Only 13 men have left more than a million, only 56 more than half a million, and only 195 more than a quarter of a million. That is an increase among millionaires of 30 per cent., among half millionaires of six per cent., and among quarter millionaires of 18 per eent. Aer Imsn EUPHEMISM—Mr. James Anderson writes as follows to the Times from the Garrick Club :—" Having been asked whether, as an old actor, any passage in Shakespeare may have suggested to the Irish 'lnvincibles ' the use of the word 'remove' for murder. I immediately answered 'Yes,' and recited the following words from 'Othello':—lago: 'Si-, there is especial commission come from Venice, to depute Cassio in Othello's place, . . . unless his abode be lin- gered here by some accident; wherein none can be so deter- minate as the removing of Cassio! Roderigo : 'How do you mean—removing of him ?' lago : 'Why, by making him uncapable of Othello's place; knocking out his brains.' It i seems probable that the Invincibles' received their directions I to murder from men of much higher culture and position \ than themselves, and that they designedly substituted the I word remove for murder in order the more effectually to se- cure the execution of their sentence."

DOUBLE EXECUTION AT GrAsGow.—Henry Mullen an d Martin Scott, the two poachers convicted of shooting two gamekeepers near Port Glasgow, on the evening of the 3rd February, were executed within Glas- gow prison on Wednesday morning. Marwood was the executioner. Both men slept well on Tuesday night. Only the necessary officials were present at the execution. Death in the case of both culprits was instantaneous. The men made no formal confession of the crime for which they were hanged, but Scott is understood to have made a state- ment to one of the clergymen who were in attendance upon him. The keepers Fyle and M'Caughtrie, he said, came upon him and his companion Mullen. M•Caughtrie de- manded their guns, and seized bold of Mullen wrenching his gun from him. M'Caughtrie then fired one Imre' at Mullen, and next, pointing the muzzle at Scott, said, Here's one for you, too." Scott fired at M`Caughtrie, and killed him. Mullen immediately grasped his own gun from the hands of the dead keeper and shot Fyle, who ran a short dis• tance after receiving the charge, and dropped to the ground mortally wounded. Mullen before going to the scaffold reiterated the statement made in his declaration before the Sheriff that he did not shoot either of the men.

REWARD OF BRAVERY.—One of the most thrilling narra- tives of bravery at sea which Liverpool seamanship has produced was repeated at the meeting of the Local Marine Board, on Tuesday, when Captain Irving, of the steamer Republic, an old "Conway" boy, the first and second officers of that ship, and twelve gallant seamen, were pre- sented with medals and other tokens of the Government's appreciation of their valour in rescuing, during a gale, in mid-Atlantic, 44 persons from the disabled steamer Glamor- gan. of Liverpool. The perilous nature of the enterprise was sufficiently demonstrated by the fact that three of the Republic's boats were sacrificed in the work of rescue, and one seaman named Forrester drowned. With thoughtful consideration, the Government have awarded to Forrester's widow £lOO. Captain Irving, in a few manly words, ex- pressed his pride at haying been a Conway boy, his appre- ciation of the Government reward, and very gracefully ascribed to the owners of his ship a considerable share of the merit of the rescue, and to his seamen high praise for the readiness with which they had volunteered for the perilous expedition. The boats, he said, could have been manned several times over—evidence enough, surely, that the British seaman is still an honour to his country and his race.

CARI)INAL MANNING ON TIIE PREVALENCE OF UNBELIEF. —ln a pastoral to the clergy and laity of the diocese of Westminster, read in the Catholic churches on Sunday, Cardinal Manning says :—" No civil order ift the world ever sank so low as the Christina world is sinking now, and will be sunk, if the name of God be erased from its public laws. You have lately asked of those who make our laws that none should legislate for us except those who believe that there is a divine law-giver, whose law is supreme. Bat it seems as if we were being carried down a stream against which we if prevail, and from which there is no es- cape: as f in a little while the public life and laws of the world will be no longer Catholic nor Christian, nor based upon a belief in God. 'I here are many who see where we are rushing downwards, and desire it. And many who see it with horror, but with folded hands do nothing against it: and many more who see nothing, and are being c irried away unconsciously into a social and political state without God- in the world. For the first time since the world began, it is openly rejscting God. The old world so profusely be- lieved in the Divine, that God was everywhere, and in all things. To them even the world was God, and all things were supernatural. Now God is nowhere, and exists no longer; the world is dead. The men of culture and the i philosophers of this world claim their independence of n- tellect and their independent morality. But the people have not forsaken God, nor has God forsaken them." div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, MAY
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, MAY

Lieutenant-General Stephenson, the new Commander-in- Chief of the British Army of occupation, arrived at Aie.lan- aria by the Brindisi mail on Wednesday. The Queen's birthday was observed in the usual manner throughout the country on Thursday. The Prince and Princess of Wales visited the Queen at Windsor in the afternoon. .

A North Wales paper says of a farmer near Conway that his wife gave birth to a son, a mare of his foaled, one of his cows calved, a sow dropped a litter of pigs, and a hen hatched a brood of chickens all in one day. The Rev. Thomas M'Cullagh, now stationed in Liverpool is mentioned as the probable successor to the Rev. Charles Garrett, as President of the Wesleyan Conference. Mr. M'Cullagh was born in the west of Ireland, and was educated at Athlone. He took his first circuit at Wo!king- ton in 1845. _

At the Epsom Police Court on Thursday there were fifty- two prisoners for trial for gambling and pocket-picking on the Downs during Derby day. The police state that there was more gambling with table § on Thursday than on any previous Derby day. The whole time of a large force of detectives was occupied in chasing gamblers over the _Downs.

_ _ The RIBOLDI CASE —The hearing of the application on behalf of the testamentary guardians of Catherine Mary Riboldi to discharge an order made last December appointing a Jewish gentleman in London, named Brandon, guardian of the child, who is heiress to a French nobleman, was con- cluded on Thursday. Mr. Justice Chitty roserved judg- ment.

The General Committee of the Established Church of Scotland opened its annual sitting in Edinburgh on Thurs- day. The Earl of Aberdeen, her Majesty's Lord High Commissioner, who held the customary leree at Holyrood Palace intimated the Queen's intention again to contribute £2,000 for Christian knowledge extension in the Highlands and the islands of Scotland. _ _ _

On Wednesday night Mrs. Clarkson, wife of John Clark- son, coal merchant, drc., Tottenhall-road, Wolverhampton, placed an infant child, nine months old, in a bath of tepid water. Directly after she was suddenly called out of the bathroom, and awing her temporary absence a little boy she had left in the room turued on the hot water tap into the bath, and the infant received such severe scalds that it died shortly afterwards. The court martial on the commander, the navigating lieu- tenant, and the boatswain of the Wye man-of-war, was con- cluded, on Wednesday, at Portsmouth. The prisoners were charged with negligence in running the vessel ashore in the Gulf of Suez. The Wye ran ashore in a fog, but was sub- sequently got off. The court found that Commander Miller had committed an error of judgment, and they ad- monished him ; the other prisoners were acquitted. An action for breach of promise of marriage, which was commenced in the Queen's Bench Division on Tuesday, was concluded on Wednesday. The plaintiff, Miss Sarah Miller, the daughter of an auctioneer at Stoke Newington, said that she and the defendant, Mr. Abraham Mory Joseph, a drug merchant of St. Mary Axe, had gone through the ceremony of betrothal according to Jewish customs, and that he had never corresponded with her afterwards. The jury found a verdict for the plaintiff —damages,i3so. At the Liverpool Assizes last February, the Blackpool Winter Gardens Company were awarded £l5O for damages sustained through the failure of Madame Bernhardt to com- plete the performance of " La Dame aux Camelias" at the Blackpool Winter Gardens, in August last. M. Meyer, against whom the verdict was given, was not satisfied with the decision, and it now appears that Mr. Justice Williams did not agree with it. In the Queen's Bench Division on Thursday, M. Meyer succeeded in obtaining an order for a new trial.

_ On Thursday morning an inquest was held on an old man who had died in Wolverhampton Hospital after injuries caused by a fall in the street. Great complaints were made that the surgeons at the hospital, without either knowledge of the deceased's friends or the authority of the coroner, had opened the body and made a post-mortem examination. The coroner expressed himself very strongly as to the con- duct of the surgeons referred to, and at the request of the jury he premised to write to the hospital authorities on the subject. Information received at Lloyd's, on Thursday morning, states that the fine iron ship Ghazeepore, 1,557 tons register, owned in Liverpool, is missing with all hands. The vessel sailed from Newcastle for Calcutta several months ago with a valuable cargo, and has never been heard of since. As she has not been reported as having passed through the Downs, underwriters are of opinion that the ship has been lost in the North Sea, and the whole of her crew, 40 in number, are given up as lost. The insurances on the ship were effected with Liverpool companies. Special Lloyd's telegrams received on Thursday morning state that the two first cargoes of the new season's teas have left China for London, the values being upwards of £250,000. The race this year is between the Castle Line steamer Stirling Castle, 4,423 tons register and 1,500 horse power, and the Glen Line steamer Glenogle, 3,743 tons and 700 horse power. Both vessels sailed from Woosung on Tuesday last, and they are expected to make the run home in about forty days to the Thames. Much interest is mani- fested in these steamers, but the Castle boat is the favourite this season.

THE "COUNTS OUT" OF THE SESSION.—On Tuesday night the House of Commons was counted out for the seventh time this session. The discussions which have been thus abruptly stopped are as follows :—Tuesday, February 20, Mr. Gorst's discussion on Kilmainham transaction ; Tuesday, March 6, Mr. Craig Sellar's reform of Private Bill Legislation; Friday, March 16, counted out before business began; Friday, March 30, Mr. Arnold's resolution on Elec- toral Reform ; Friday, April 13, Mr. Monk on the Reform of Marriage Laws; Tuesday, April 24, Dr. Cameron on the case of the Leon XIII.; Tuesday, May 22, Mr. Stevenson's Sunday Closing Bill.—Pall Mall Gazette. An inquest was, on Wednesday, held at Burnley on the body of Mary Wade, aged 19 years, who died on Monday, after l• ing delivered of a stillborn child, It appeared from the cvidence that a fortnight last Saturday the deceased, who WIS of weak intellect, went into the house where a young man named William Swindell, a collier, now in custody, lodged, it being alleged that she had kept company with Swindell. The young fellow ordered her out, and, it is said, rushed at her and kicked her on the back. The medical evidence showed that blood poisoning had brought on pre- mature confinement, and might have been caused by external violence or mental emotion. The jury returned a verdict that the deceased died from blood poisoning, but that there was not sufficient evidence as to how it was caused.

At the Birmingham Police Court, yesterday, Mr. Philip Soloman, a gentleman of considerable means, well-known in Birmingham, and residing at Handsworth, was charged with stealing 103. Od, from the till of Messrs. Canning and Co., wholesale chemists, Great Hampton-street. Defendant was an intimate and trusted friend of the prosecutors, and was in the habit of occasionally serving in their shop. Money had been missed in an unaccountable manner, and a detective was set to watch. Money was marked, and on Thursday defendant was seen to take some money out of the till, place it in his pocket, and leave the premises. The detective arrested him, and in his possession found 103. 01. of the marked money, and £l5O in gold and silver. When apprehended the defendant became tersibly excited, and almost fainted away. SINGULAR CASE OF CarLD DESERTION —Amelia Howard, a domestic servant, was charged at Sheffield Town Hall, on Wednesday, with deserting her child, which was found in one of the Sheffield streets and taken to the union. The girl afterwards sought for it, and told the police that its father, a gentleman in London, had taken it away, promising that his friends would care for the little one. Instead of doing so he sent a letter, saying he was sailing from Liverpool, and that the child had been left in the street. The prisoner's solicitor described the father of the child as a scamp, and her mistress, Mrs. Anderson, a merchant's wife at Leeds, said she believed the girl's story, and was willing to retain her in her service. The stipendiary said the case was a very painful one, and he remanded the girl at large under her mistress's care. Mr. FORSTER ON THE TRANSVAAL CONVENTION.—Mr. Forster, speaking in London, on Wednesday night, at the annual meeting of the Aborigines' Protection Society, re- ferred to the Transvaal question, and said he thought the action of this country had had a great deal to Co with the sxisting state of affairs. It was generally understood, when the Convention was signed, that we were to undertake the protection of the native population. We had failed to do that, but had allowed their lands to be overrun by deser- ters of the English Army, filibusterers and freebooters from the neighbouring States, and, in some cases, by the Queen's subjects in Cape Colony. It had been add that if England had sent an expedition war would have resulted. But there was no necessity for that; a kind of police control was ill that was required, if we had shown the Boers that we were determined to protect the natives. He referred to the amend- ment on the Transvaal question which Mr. Gladstone had placed upon the paper of the House of Commons, and ex- pressed his delight that the Premier was not making any special efforts to obtain a discussion upon it. He hoped that discussion would never take place, but if it did, he should certainly feel bound to oppose the amendment.

SIR R. CROSS ON THE CONSERVATIVE POLICY.—Sir Richard Cress, addressing a meeting of Wolverhampton, Conservatives on Wednesday night, said the Conservative working men, instead of being nnmbered by ones and twos, now numbered thousands in the supposed Radical town of Wolverhampton. One reason why a working man should be a Conservative was because he did not swallow every- thing told 11;in by agitators, but was able to think for him- self. Ho saw there was a good deal which ought to be pre- served in the country. He had learned that the Conserva- tive party had a consistent and steady policy. On the other hand the Liberal party was an aggregate of both par- ties which occasionally united for the purpose of turning out (lei., opponents, and could net agree among themselves when in office. In -4upport of this view he pointed to the secessions of Ministers from the present Administration. Conservatives were con- tent with their institutions as they were, but were quite willing to adopt the legislation according to the wants of the day. Workingmen were beginning to see that Conserva- tives had done their best, by passing and consolidating the Factory Act, greatly against the wish of the Liberals, to preserve the health of women and children, and to improve the sanitary crulition of their homes. The Liberal party failed to take account of their responsibility for the increase of the national expenditure from 40 millions in 1840 to 89 millions last year. He repudiated the charge of obstruc- tion, but asked, when the Conservatives were in office and the Irish party tried to make party government impossible, on which side Mr. Chamberlain and Sir Charles Dirac were found. He believed the result of the Uovernment policy in India would be that Mr. IlbErt's bill must be withdrawn, and that Lord Ripon would have to resign. A vote condemning ' the policy of the Government was passed.

On Monday evening some men shrimping on the sands near Southport found the body of Atc'eib tld Hawley, the young Prestoe architect who was drowned a week previously whilst surveying the Ribble banks in connection with the Navigation Bill. The rigorous search for the body had been abandoned for sonic days, as it was thought to have become imbedded in the sand. A i oUFPCYSED MURDER AND SurctreE.—The bodies of refine Maria Getfield, nineteen years of age, and her illegitimate child, aged nine weeks, have been found in the river Colne, at Twickenham. It is reported that the girl had an alterca- tion with some of her friends relative to her past conduct, when she left her home in a passiem, saying she would destroy herself and her child, and did not again return. ILLICIT DISTILLATION OF WHISKY.—At Hanley, on Tues- day, John Mayer, potter, was fined £25, and sent to gaol for three months' hard labour in default of payment, for having in his possession a quantity of illicit whisky, together with various articles used in the illicit whisky trade. Ann Bailey, widow, is in custody at Leek on the charge of having a large still, in which the arhisky was manufactured, in her possession. The Wesleyan District meetings commenced on Tuesday. The comparative returns presented showed the following numerical differences :—Manchester District, increase 110; Bolton District, increase 276 ; Liverpool District, increase 1,037 ; Macclesfield District, increase 818; Leeds District, increase 489; Halifax and Bradford District, increase 1,372; Sheffield District, increase 392. The returns so far made up show an increaseein the Connexion during the year of up- wards of 13,000 members. A BOGUS ADVERTISING MEDIUH. At the Dorchester Police Court, on Tuesday, Charles William Blake, alias Frank Monceta, artilleryman, was again charged with fraud on Messrs. Wright and Round, publishers, Liverpool. Prisoner was also charged with frauds in various towns. The prosecutors had sent the prisoner a £1 cheque for an adver- tisement in and a subscription to a magazine called Mire, of which the prisoner professed to be the editor. His pros- pectus stated that the magazine was dedicated by permissioe to Prince Edward of Saxe-Weimar, and was under the patronage of over 8,000 officers. The magazine, however, never appeared.—Prisoner was again remanded for a week. BOAT ACCIDENT AND Loss OF FIVE LIVES.—A sad boat- ing accident occurred on Tuesday afternoon, at the Saltpans, on the river Stour, between Ramsgate and Sandwich. The river tug was proceeding from Sandwich to her moorings at Saltpans, and eight young men, all sons of tradesmen be- longing to Sandwich, went on board for an excursion down the river. On arriving at the Saltpans the party got into tug's boat, and were proceeding to the shore, when one of them stepped on the gunwale, capsizing the boat. All the youths were thrown into the water, and only three of them, named Warman, Chapman, and Page, managed to swim ashore. The other five, named Field, Reynolds, Uden, Nash, and Bushel, were drowned. The bodies of Nash, , Uden, and Reynolds were subsequently recovered, but the I other two bodies are still missing. The sad fatality has cast a gloom over the town of Sandwich. The inquest took place on Wednesday afternoon. The facts adduced were similar to those already' given, and the jury returned a verdict of "Accidently drowned." Tula QUEEN'S BIRTHDAY.-1118T Majesty Queen Victoria attained her 64th birthday on Thursday, an age which has been exceeded by only 11 of the Sovereigns of England, dating from the Norman Conquest, viz. :—Henry 1., who lived to the age of 67 Years; Henry 111., 65 years; Edward 1., 67 years; Edward 111., 65 years; Qaeen Elizabeth, 69 years; James 11., 68 years; George L, 67 years; George 11., 77 years; George 111., 82 years; George IV., 68 years; and William IV., 72 years. On the 20th of June next her Majesty will have reigned over the United Kingdom for 46 years, a length of reign which has been exceeded by three of the Kings of England only, viz. :—Henry 111., whose reign extended to 56 years; Edward 111., whose reign lasted 50 years; and George 111., whose reign extended to the long period of nearly 60 years. The Queen has now been a widow for nearly 22 years, the Prince Consort having died on December 14, 1861. Her Majesty has had a family of five daughters and foiir sons, all of whom are alive except the Princess Alice, Grand Duchess of Hesse, who died on December 14, 1878. MR. GLADSTONE ON THE STATE OF BUSINESS IN PAR- LIAMENT.—The following letter has been received by Mr. R. D. Holt, president of the Liverpool Liberal Association, in reply to the resolution and memorial forwarded from the Liberal meeting held in Liverpool on Friday last :—" 10, Downing-street, Whitehall, 22nd May, 1883.—Dear sir,— Mr. Gladstone is obliged to you for forwarding to him the resolution and memorial adopted at the recent meeting of the Liberal party in Liverpool on the subject of the present position of affairs in Parliament. In reply he desires me to assure you that he is very sensible of the weight to be at- tached to the representations of so important a body, and he will take care that such representations are made known to his colleagues, who mav be relied upon to join with him in endeavouring to the utmost in overcoming the legislative difficulties in the House of Commons. He himself looks forward hopefully to the principle of devolution by Grand Committees as affording means of promoting the despatch of public business, and he believes that by other new rules of procedure extreme powers of abuse have been somewhat re- strained. As regards the recent words about obstruction at- tributed to Sir Stafford Northcote, I am to observe that it I is to be presumed that if he spoke them he must have taken I into account the responsibility he was incurring by the use lof them.—l beg to remain, dear sir, yours faithfully, E. H. HAMILTON.—R. D. Holt, Esq." THE CONGESTION OF PARLIAMENT.—" A Ridical Mem- ber" makes the following suggestion in the Pall Mall Gazette :—" May I suggest to the Liberal members who have prescribed for the congestion from which the House of Commons is suffering that sooner or later a more thorough remedy must be adopted? The House must learn to take up its business at the beginning of one year at the stage at which it left that business at the year before. It is no use disguising the fact that nowadays there are as many sub- jects of interest crowding for discussion in one session as formerly occupied the attention of a whole Parliament. It is equally useless to stifle their claims by unreasonable adherence to empty usages. What is the significance of prorogation? It was once the means by which the Crown cheated the people of redress and grievance. It is now the process by which Parliament unwittingly and uselessly allows to be imposed upon itself the burden of weary wasted nights of damnable iteration. Let prorogation cease. Let each House at the end of the current session adjourn to some convenient day early in the next year. The difficulty will then be solved. The bills of the last session will proceed through their remaining stages. All notices of motion will come to a hearing. Obstruction will become ineffective, and therefore obsolete. By a slight modification of the Standing Orders, Supply and Ways and Means, with their attendant bills, can be arranged for each year. The only sufferers by the change will be the proprietors of 'annuals ' —the members who cultivate the same bill or motion session after session, to the exclusion of others who are less lucky in the ballot for a place." TIIE LABOUR MARKET.—The Whitsun holidays have in- terfered with the activity of the labour market, in some places the whole of the week being devoted to holiday- making, and many factories have been partially closed. Strikes have not entirely disappeared, and the colliers' strike in North Staffordshire seems likely to contieue, although seine of the men have resumed work, hut the majority now out, although non-unionists, are promised support until the old rate of wages is restored. In most districts engineers and shipbuilders are full of work. Ironworks, as a rule, are busy, and many collieries are on full time. At Birmingham, all classes of manufactures are busy; plenty of orders are coming in freely. At the Hartlepools labour is plentiful. At Middlesbrough steel-making is rather quiet, and the Eaton Works have been laid off this week, owing to a wages dispute which is being actively carried on by the men. At Sunder- land ard Wolverhampton trade is very active; and at New- castle-on-Tyne collieries are busy. At Sheffield many houses are very busy completing American orders for de- livery before July 1, when the new tariff comes into oper- ation. The fine weather has given an extra impetus to building operations and railway and tramway con- struction, and all classes of workmen are in great demand. The textile trades are :somewhat quiet, although at Man- chester, spinners arc better employed, and at Leeds many manufacturers are receiving full time; and hat and cap making is also showing signs of reviving. At Leicester and Nottingham, the hosiery and lace trades are steady. At Dundee, jute-yarn spinners are fairly employed. At Kidderminster, the carpet factories are fairly busy. The verious centres of the boot and shoe trades are full of work, I and tailors and painters are in great demand in London and the provinces. Emigration continues active, especially in the direction of Canada.—Labour News.

THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES.—The dis- organisation of basiness caused by the holidays has scarcely yet disappeared, and the iron market on Tuesday had only partially resumed its normal condition. There was a fairly good attendance, but business was quiet, and very few tran- sactions of any importance were reported. So far as prices are concerned there is no change, and on the part both of pig and finished iron makers a strong disposition is displayed rather to do less business than to take orders at lower rates. For Lancashire pig iron makers still quote 458 for forge and 46s for foundry lees 2 delivered equal to Manchester: at a little under these figures offers are made, but these are not accepted. For Lincolnshire pig iron quotations are about 448 103 to 45810 d less 21-. F for forge and foundry delivered here, but with very little doing, and the blowing out of some of the furnaces is in contemplation. Other irons are practically out of this market as competing brands. Finished iron makers are in most cases kept going, and still hold for £6 5s for bars delivered equal to Manchester, with hoops quoted at .£6 12e 6d, and although orders are difficult to get makers are not disposed to come lower.—At many of the collieries in the Manchester district the Whitsuntide holi- days have extended pretty well this week. In other dis- tricts stoppages of alnut three days have been pretty general, and businees has been practically suspended more or less during the week. As yet orders are only earning in very irregularly, and afford little or no indication as to the legitimate requirements of trade. In prices there is a little cutting here and there where colliery proprietors are com- pelled to seek orders, but generally a steady tone is being maintained. The average prices at the pit mouth are without change, and may be quoted as under :—Best coal, Os to Os 61; seconds, is to 7s 6d ; common house-fire coal, 63 to 16s 6d ; steam and forge coal, 5s 6J to 5s Pd; burgy, 4s 9d to s; ordinary slack, 3s 3d to 3s 6d ; and better qualities, 3s 9d to 48 3cl per ton. The recent more favourable weather appears to have brought about some improvement in the shipping trade, but the business doing generally is still only moderate, and orders are competed for at low figures, 78 to Is 6d per ton being still about the average price at which ordinary Lancashire steam coal can be I bought delivered at the Garston docks, or the high level, Liverpool.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-MONDAY.

1 Intsit AFFAIRS.—The House reassembled on Monday after the Whitsuntide recess, and the Irish members promptly resumed their favourite practice of proposing questions to the Chief Secretary.—ln the course of his replies, Mr. TREVELYAN stated that it was expected that nearly all the applications under the Land Act would have been *dealt with by the end of June, that there was a grati- fying diminution in agrarian crime, that no further procla- mations would be issued under the Crimes Act than were necessary for the public peace, and that it was not the inten- tion of the Government to continuethe system of special resi- dent magistrates longer than was absolutely necessary.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for IRELAND assured Mr. Harrington that there was no foundation for the allegation that Patrick Delaney was induced to make his statement incriminating Timothy Kelly in the murder of Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke on an understanding that his own life would be spared. SUPPLY—In Committee of Supply, on the vote of 1 £95,000 for acquiring a new site for the War and Admiralty- offices, Mr. DILLwrN moved the rejection of the vote, , which he objected to as an unnecessary expenditure of pub- lic money.—Mr. SRAW-LEFEVRE defended the site chosen, and asserted that the rejection of the suggested plan would lead to great delay. The estimated cost of purchase of land and the erection of buildings was £765,000, the interest on which would be £22,500, but this would be more than com- pensated by the savings which would be involved in the proposed changes. After considerable discussion Mr. BILLWYN withdrew his motion, and the vote was agreed to. —On the vote for Post-office telegraphs there was a short discussion on the Parcels Post.—Mr. FAWCETT repeated his belief that in the first year the receipts would cover the ex- penditure' and that the postal service in the rural districts would be benefited by the introduction of the new business. —An appeal for a new post-office for Liverpool met with the reply that there were demands of a much more serious nature from Bradfcr-cl and other towns, and the Government could not hold out any hope of great operations being carried on in Liverpool for some time.—Several other votes were agreed to. _

Biros BURIAL BOARD —The President of the Local Government Board was asked to give an opinion on the action of the Rhos Burial Board in passing a resolution against the consecration of a portion of the burial ground at that place. Sir C. DILKE'S reply was that the Board had not acted illegally, though they had gone beyond their powers. He added that the Home Secretary had been ad- vised that the obligation by law to divide .burial grounds into consecrated and unconsecrated parts still continued. THE DERBY DAY. Sir H. MAXWELL moved that the House, on its rising, should adjourn till Thursday. Mr. lIENEAGE seconded the motion, on the ground that the Derby Day was the one day on which members considered themselves free to do anything they liked.—Sir WILFRID LAWSON opposed the motion and objected to the adjourn- ment of the House for any other than a national object.— Mr. LABOUCHERE said it was most undesirable that the ac- tion of men like Sir W. Lawson should be considered a part of the Radical creed. The constituencies were not such fools as some people took them to be.—The House divided, when there voted for the motion, 18:5 ; against, 85. THE INDIAN BUDGET.—Mr. Alderman FOWLER raised a discussion on the practice of postponing the consideration of the Indian Budget until within two or three days of the end of the session. The hon, member urged that two or three nights should be devoted to the discussion of the im- portant affairs of India at a period when all hon. members , could take part in such discussion. Sir G. CAMPBELL thought, as Indian finance was a matter which now involved more difficulties than European finance, the only useful way of dealing with the Indian Budget would be to refer it to a Select Committee of capable men, who should sit and review the accounts and then report to the House.—Mr. J. K. Cuoss called attention to the circumstance that an hour before, when the Derby was being discussed, the benches on both sides were filled, but when the affairs of the great dependency of India were under debate the House was nearly empty. The UNDER SECRETARY pointed out that one great obstacle in the way of bringing forward the Indian Budget was the want of progress in the business of the House, and be was willing to accept the proposal of Mr. Fowler that the Indian financial statement should be made at a period of the session when it could be fully discussed. The motion was then agreed to without a division. COUNT OCT.—The Customs and Inland Revenue Bill, the • Unien of Benefices Act (1860) Amendment Bill, and the Poor Law Conferences Bill were read a second time.—Mr. WARTON was speaking in opposition to the motion or the , second reading of the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sun- day (No. 2) Bill, when the House was counted out at half- past seven o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY.
The House met to-day for the first time after the Whit- suntide recess. Several bills were advanced a stage, and their Lordships adjourned after a twenty minutes sitting.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.—nrunspAy.

THE FIGHTING IN ZULULAND. - Mr. E. ASHLEY stated, in reply to Sir H. Holland, that the Government did not in- tend to interfere in the quarrel now going on within the borders of Zululand, any more than they did before the Zulu war.

MESSRS. HEALY, DAVITT, AND QUINN.—Mr. TREVELYAN, referring to the imprisonment of Messrs. Healy, Davitt, and Quinn for refusing to find bail, remarlied that the ease was not an ordinary one for remission, as the prisoners could at any moment obtain their release by complying with the I law. He was, however, willing to promise that the Lord Lieutenant should communicate with the judicial authori- ties with a view to seeing if any remission was advisable. MISCELLANEOUS.—Lord E. FITZSIAURICE announced that communications had passed which gave hopes of the early resumption of diplomatic relations between this coun- try and Mexico.—Mr. SHAW-LEFEVRE expressed an opinion that enough was not known of electricity to justify him in talking measures for lighting the National Gallery and the British Museum by means of the electric light.—Lord E. rITZNIALIRIcV., :72',..`1.71:2; 19 Mr. A Arnold, admitted that it was the intention of the Russian Choiernment to impose ad- ditional duties upon British cotton manufaciurei !tiel other , goods in transit for Persia, and that difficulties wei-;; threatened in the method of transit.

MR. ERRINGTON'S MissioN.—Mr. Cowen was informed that Her Majesty's Government had never proposed to estab- lish a diplomatic resident at the Vatican. Mr. Errington was not in any sense the channel of communication between the Foreign Office and the Vatican, and having received no appointment would not receive any remuneration.—The UNDER-SECRETARY added that the Pope's censure of the Archbishop of Cashel was not issued at the request of our Government, and no congratulations had been addressed to Rome regarding it.—Mr. Cow EN gave notice that he should on Monday ask whether Lord Granville had written to Mr. Errington thanking him generally for his services.

„ THY: SOUTHPORT FORESIC/E.—Mr. DODSON, upon being questioned as to the present position of the Southport fore- shore dispute, expressed a hope that what he was doing in the matter would ultimately lead to an amicable settlement, as both parties had accepted his good offices. THE TENANTS' COMPENSATION BILL.—The PRIME MINI- STER held out a hope that Mr. Dodson would be able on Tuesday to propose the second reading of the Tenants' Com- pensation Bill. A PROTEST.—Lord E. FITZMAURICE informed Mr. A. Arnold that a note had been received from the Porte stating that it was their intention to levy forthwith an ad valorem duty of 8 per cent. on all imports, aud this duty was now being enforced. A formal protest had been addressed to the Porte on the subject. FRANCE AND MADAGASCAR.—Mr. FORSTER : There is a rumour that the port ef Majunga, in Madagascar, has been bombarded by the French ships, and I wish to know if it is true.—Lord EDMOND FITZMAURICE : In reply to this ques- tion, I think I cannot do better than read to the House a telegram which was handed to me a few minutes before I left the Foreign Office. It is from Colonel Miles :—” The bombardment of Majunga took place on the 16th, and lasted six hours. A force was then landed, under cover of guns, and took possession. The novas suffered great loss; the French none. The admiral returned to Mayotte, leaving a garrison." I may explain to the House that Majunga is a port on the north-west coast of Madagascar, and Mayotte is an island in the possession of the French. The proposal to abolish imprisonment for debt meets with the strong disapproval of one of the oldest County Court judges, Mr. Hastings Ingham. In the course of some re- marks made in his Court at Barrow-in• Furness, he said it was a common thing in the iron districts for young men earn- ing wages varying from 30s to £3 per week to be boarded and lodged by poor women who ran into debt at small shops to get food Gr them, and for these men, to disappear or plead utter inability to pay. No doubt most of their wages were spent in drink, and if imprisonment for debt were abolished it would be offering a premium for drunkenness and dis- honesty.

ARREST Or 14yrrrro— MEN.-At Newcastle, on Wednes- day, a large number of men being suspected of being en- gaged in betting were arrested by the police. The appre- hension took place in two public houses, wherein 39 persons, including the landlord, in one, were arrested, and 20, includ- ing the landlord, in another. The whole of the men were brought before the magistrates, several being discharged, and the rest I ernanded on bail.

EXCESSIVE. VACCINATION DISTRAINTS. At Leicester CGunty Court, on Wednesday, Judge Barrow gave an irn- portant decision in a test case brought against four police officers for excessive distraint under the Vaccination Acts. The police seized £l2 worth of goods for non-payment of a of a few shillings, and hence the action for damages. The judge strongly deprecated the agitation against the Vaccination Acts, but condemned the action of the police, awarding £7 damages. A CURIOUS PLEA.—A young man, named Thomas Keane, who said that he came from Manchester, was charged at the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, with being drunk at St. Helens.—A police-officer said that he found defendant staggering about Church-street on Satur- : day night, and he was so helpless that he could neither sav who he was or where he came frcm.--Defendant admitte'd having been drunk, but thought the Bench ought in impos- ing a fine to take into consideration the fact that he had , paid 1113 train fare from Mane,hester.—He was enc.(' 53. and I costs.

THE STATE OF IRELAND. HOW CAREY BECAME AN INFORMER. A Dublin correspondent says :—"lt has often been won- dered at that James Carey was accepted as an approver when the Crown authorities had their choice of so many. It ap- pears, however, that the circumstances presented no alterna- tive. The statement that James Carey was precisely a quarter of an hour before Curley is not literally exact, but he was indeed before him. In fact Peter Carey had made a statement which was accepted by the authorities a week or 10 days before James Carey became an approver. This fact explains some points which were before perplexing. It was found that Peter Carev's information was not sufficient, and it was necessary to get another prisoner as approver who wa, an eye-witness of the murders. The authorities, having their choice then of James Carer and Daniel Curley, chose the former, wliJs, life had in 'fact been bargained for on those terms by his brother Peter, who still kept his position in the dock for a considerable time afterwards, and received the praises of his fellow-prisoners as being a true man, unlike the traitor James. How Peter Carey came to give his first state- ment is a matter involved in a little romance, if such a terns can be applied to transactions of the kind. The circum- stances, which are very curious and interesting, may at some time not far distant be made public."

The correspondence between Mr. Pryor, counsel for Tynan at New York, and the representative of the British Consul, is published in the Times New York telegram. Mr. Pryor wrote to Mr. F. F. Marbury, counsel to the British Consulate :—" Dear Sir,—From newspaper reports, pub- lished apparently by the authority of the British Minister at Washington, it may be inferred that the British Govern- ment would cause the arrest of Patrick Tynan if he could be found. I am instructed by Mr. Tynan to inform whom- soever it may concern that if he has not obtruded himself upon public notice, neither has he been in hiding, and that on intimation to the undersigned he will promptly present himself to the Marshal to do and abide whatsoever the laws of the United States may require of him." Mr. Marbury replied as follows :—" Dear Sir,—ln answer to your letter of this date, I have to state that I have no information or knowledge whatever respecting your client Patrick Tynan. I certainly have received no instructions to take proceedings for his arrest, and no warrant, therefore, has been applied for. Thanking you for your courteous offer to produce Mr. Tynan whenever he is called for, I beg to state that if occa- sion should arise I will further communicate with you.— Yours truly, F. F. MARBURY. P.S.—There is another Tynan of whom I have seen some notice in the papers; but as he him I may also say that I have re- ceived no instructions, nor taken any proceedings." Mr. Pryor, at an interview, stated that Tynan first appeared to him forty-eight hours before, and that his client had lived at New York quietly for mouths with his wife and eight children.

The papal circular to the Irish bishops has given an im- petus to the Parneli fund A number of members of Parlia- ment and others met in Dublin on Saturday, and passed resolutions in protest against the document.

Two men who were -arrested on board the steamer Cana- dian, on Saturday, were charged at Galway on Monday, one with the murder of the Lydons, and the other with the mur- der of Constable Kavanagh, and were remanded till to-day (Saturday). The body of a man named Quinn, formerly steward to Mr. Brown, of Rahins, near Castlebar, was on Saturday dis- covered by a fisherman in Islandcady Lake, near Westport, with a chain round his neck. Quinn mysteriously disap- peared about four months ago. Eight men implicated in the Crossmolina conspiracy—to murder landlords, agents, and others—were on Wednesday brought before the magistrate at Castlebar and remanded. The prisoners seem disposed at present to treat their position with levity. As they were being marched under a strong escort to the court-house, one of them, described as fashionably attired, mockingly assumed the command by giving the order "right turn," and his comrades solemnly obeyed him. _

Arrangements are being made for the despatch of the in- formers Kavanagh, Smith, O'Hanlon, and Peter Carey to Australia. James Carey and Farrell, the first informers, are to be retained until the next cammission in order that if Tynan, Sheridan, and Walsh be extradited, they will be re- quired as important evidence, so that they cannot be yet sent out of the country. Several persons assembled outside James Carey's late residence on Saturday night, thinking that a report that he had been released was well founded. Patrick Delaney's sentence has been commuted to penal servitude for life. The prisoner was informed of the fact officially early on Saturday morning. He had been supplied with the convict dress which the others sentenced to penal servitude already wear. It was Delaney who was told off by the Invincibles to murder Judge Lawson. No doubt is ex- pressed of the truth of the man's story that in order to re- move himself from the influence of the murder gang he allowed himself to be captured upon that occasion, and made no real attempt to execute his mission. The six convicts, Patrick Delaney, Edward O'Brien, Edward M'Caffery, William Moroney. Thomas Doyle, and Laurence Hanlon, the first-named convicted on the capital charge, but whose sentence was commuted, the next four convicted of conspiracy to murder, and Hanlon, convicted of the attempt to murder Mr. Field, were on Tuesday removed from Kilmainham Prison to Mountjoy Convict Prison, where they will undergo the first portion of their terms of penal servitude, 'Mr, only men who are under similar sentence now who have not yet been removed from Kilmainham are Daniel Delaney and James Mullett. The United Ireland of Thursday says :—The letter of ' Daniel Curley, executed last Friday, to his wife was written , on the 16th of May, and was delivered to Mrs. Curley on the 18tb, after she had read it in the papers. Mrs. Curley stated that she would not have published her husband's letter, and she is convinced her husband did not intend it for publication. She is painfully grieved at the conduct of the Government in violating the sanctity of a private letter written under such solemn and distressing circumstances. Mr. Trevelvan should by called upon to give a reason for this infamous proceeding.

Both at Dublin and Kingstown Archbishop Croke has been , received with enthusiasm on his return from Rome. The demonstration of public feeling in his favour is an expres- sion of antagonism to the recent Papal circular, but Dr. croi, r,:i.neated at Queenstown what he was reported to have said when passing :hrough Paris. He was summoned to give his opinion on the state Of I"land, J-1( c,-;`,7! opinion, and it was received with the greatest pzuble atten- tion, and he had nothing to complain of in any way. reports, be said, had been circulated about his visit, and subsequently, in answering an address from Wicklow, be remarked that when the Pope understood matters better the efforts of himself and the priesthood on behalf of the Irish people would be crowned with success. Dr. Croke has evi- dently come from Rome as he said, "unchanged and un- changeable; " but meanwhile he advises submission to the Vatican.

ARREST FOR THE MURDER or MRS. SMYTHE.—A tramping blacksmith, named Robert Elliott, whom the police have been searching for ever since the murder of Mrs. Smythe, was arrested on Tuesday evening on a charge of complicity in the brutal outrage. He was on Wednesday brought before Captain Borleau, R.M., at the Mullingar Constabulary Barrack and remanded for eight days. The soldier who was present at the late private investigation has identified Elliott as being the actual murderer. Elliott admitted having been present at the locality at the time of the murder. Two women are also giving information. It is believed the authorities have some very important evidence.

THE B MBE MONUMENT.—A monument, subscribed for ; by the resident magistrates of Ireland to the memory of the late Mr. T. H. Burke, was erected on Monday in Glasnevin Cemetery, where the deceased gentleman is interred. The monument consists of a pedestal, with panels, on which are engraved in relief the coat of arms of the Burke family and the deceased's monogram. The pedestal is surmounted by a column, finishing with a cross, and on the base is the follow- ing inscription. "To the memory of Thomas Henry Burke. Under-Secretary to the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland. Assas- sinated in the Phcenix Park, May 6, 1882. This memorial is erected by many friends among the resident magistrates in Ireland as a mark of their appreciat of his high character and eminent public services." A guard of police has been I detached for the protection of the monument. There is no truth in the report that Daniel Curley left a written statement about the Invincibles. However, the authorities are now aware that not alone were the Park murders originated by the Invincibles, but that the organ- isation spread south, west, and east. They have reason to believe that the murder of Mr. Burke and the wounding of Mrs. Burke, and the murder of the soldier who was on guard, were planned and c wried out by the Invincibles from Dublin. Mrs. Smythe's murder also had its origin from the Invincibles. The murder of Mr. Herbert, the magistrate, outside Tralee, and the murder of the youth Boyd in Kil- kenny are also attributed to the Invincibles. Different officials in authoritative positions boast that they have evi- dence that branches of this organisation existed in Dublin, Westmeath, Galway, Clare, Kilkenny, Kerry, and Roscom- mon. The Invincibles in Dublin are stated, when the organisation was flourishing, to have numbered 200, includ- ing members from the provinces. They are now, owing to the prosecutions and convictions, reduced to fifty. one of the fifty are considered, as far as the authorities know, to be dangerous characters. THE POPE AND Mn. PARNELL : ANOTHER CIRCULAR.— Another document from the Propaganda, supplementary to the Encyclical to the Irish bishops has been despatched. It is what the Curia calls Reservatissinto. It enforces the injunc- tions of the Encyclical, and supplies the solutions of sundry cases of conscience such as may he supposed to arise out of the position of the Irish clergy. Many of these solutions I are in reply to questions addreseed to Rome from Ireland. ' The proofs of a remarkable pamphlet, printed in English at the Propaganda Press, and entitled "Ireland 'and the Holy See; a Retrospect from 10t36 to 1833," have been issued. The object is to show, especially from the writings of i Cardinal Cullen, that the teaching of the Church as regards secret associations in Ireland has always been the same. "God grant," says the writer, "that the publication of these extracts may serve to disabuse those ignorant persons who think they can remain good Catholics while they join secret, seditious associations, which the Church has never ceased to condemn." The pages of this short pamphlet con- tain several passages singularly and strikingly applicable to, recent events in Ireland. Their publication abundanthr proves the absurdity of the contention that the Pope is cot correctly or sufficiently informed upon Irish affairs.
A Batavia telegram date-d Thursday says :—A. violent eruption has been going on since Sunday last on the Island of Krakatoa, near Anjer, in the Straits of Sunda..

......_.....--_.,. WAR IN MADAGASCAR. • I CONIMENCEMENT OF THE FRENCH OPERATIONS. IFrom Paris it is announced that a French force under Admiral Pierre has captured the military posts established by the Queen of Madagascar on the Sakalava territory, and ' that the Custom House at Majunga has also been taken pos- session of by the French. The news was confirmed in the House of Commons on Thursday night. by Lord E. Fitz- maurice, who said that on May I.6th Majusga had been bombarded for six hours, after which the French landed and took possession.

The Central News learns that the landing of French troops in Madagascar has taken the Hovas completely by surprise, and the Madagascar Embassy now in London know nothing of the matter beyond what has appeared in the Press. Their Excellencies, however, are in no way dis- concerted. They state their people will fight the French invaders to the deatb ; and several members of the Embassy will hasten their departure in order to take part in the de- fence of their native land. Liberal offers of men, money, and arms have been tendered to the Malagasy authorities by prominent Americans and by many Englishmen. The Malagasies claim that all they require to maintain a suc- cessful defence is a sufficient supply of modern breechloaders and ammunition. Several thousand stand of rifles have been recently purchased, and are now well on their way to Madagascar. The Queen of Madagascar will immediately call for a loan for the purpose of purchasing the necessary munitions of war.

A great fire, by which many dwellin: houses were de- stroyed, took place on Monrl7, at ludesheim, Germany. A special train left Ballaghaderin on Thursday morning with eighty emigrants from the Ballina Union and thirty from Swinford, all bound for Canada. Herr Lasker, the former leader of the German National Liberal party, comes to England next week, and hence to America on a visit to his brother. The Vicomte Dart, a relation of a former Imperial Minis- ter, has been run over in Paris by a carriage at a crossing of the Avenue de l'Opera and the Rue Louis le Grand. He was carried hume in an alarming state. A telegram from Alexandria says :—The sudden resigna- tion of Ismail Pasha Eyoub is involved in mystery. Rumours are current that he was found to have accepted bribes.

The Central News states that M. Challemel Lacour on Thursday informed Count Hoyos that M. Waddington would be French Ambassador at Vienna. Count Hoyos re- plied that the appointment would be an acceptable one. An Exchange Company's Paris telegram states :—lt is reported in diplomatic circles that the Sovereigns of Ger- many, Austria, and Italy, will meet at Gastin when the German Emperor, who will be accompanied by Prince Bis- marck, is there to take the waters. The Durban correspondent of the Standard transmits a report that the Swazis have taken the field against the Boers, and that the Dutch militia are in laager at Luneberg. The report has not been confirmed. If it should be true, another element of difficulty will have been introduced into the situation in South Africa.

A Lloyd's telegram received from Sourabaya (Java) states that the ship Agir, 1,383 tons register, whilst loading at Kraakan for the English channel, took fire in port and was totally destroyed. At the time of the outbreak the vessel had on board .1,400 tons of sugar, valued at £50,000, all of which is lost. The crew of 45 men were safely landed before the vessel sank.

GREAT FIRE IN A RUSSIA'S SHIP-BUILDING YARD.--• According to intelligence received at St. Petersburg from Sebastopol, a disastrous fire broke out there on the 20th instant, in the shipbuilding-yards of the Russian Naviga- tion Company. The buildings, containing machinery and models of vessels, were completely destroyed, as was also a workshGp which was being built for the construction of ironclads. The remaining worshops were saved. A SECOND SrEz CANAL—The Suez Canal Company has, the Standard Paris correspondent says, asked the British Government to support it in an application to the Khedive for additional land to enable the construction of a iecond canal parallel to the first. The company is prepared to commence the works at once, and estimate that the new canal will be completed in four years. The company has also submitted a proposal for the reduction of the tariff at fixed dates and for providing an effective control ever the trafgc.

Baron Sequard, the eminent physiologist, was giving a lecture at the College of France on vivisection, and produced a young monkey, on which he intended to perform experi- ments. He had not proceeded further than to tie .isp his patient, who, not liking the preliminary operation; uttered piercing cries, when a lady elegantly dressed stepped for- ward and struck the professor on the nose with her parasol. lie was ungallant enough to call her "an old fool;" and ordered her to be removed. At the police office she said sho had only properly acted on the Gramont humanitarian law. The correctional police must decide whether this plea justifies an assault.

'IRE FIGHTING IN Z ULULAND.—I n tel I i gen ce was received at Cape Town shortly before the mail left on May 1, front which we gather that the defeat of the Usuto party in Zululand is fully confirmed. The Zulus say that in few of their battles has their loss of life been so great, certainly not in any with the English. On the authority of the corres- pondent of the Natal Mercury, it is stated that Cetewayo, without any attempt at concealment, is raising a second army, and threatens that those who do not join him will be treated as enemies. The journal adds that he is collecting men from the reserve territory as well as from other parts of the country, but in the meantime arrangements have been completed by Mr. Osborne, resident commissioner, for main- taining order in the Reserve. He has definite powers and a force of armed police at his disposal. RUSSIA AND ARMENIA.—Tbe Daily News publishes a letter from its special correspondent at Tiflis, in which he gives an account of the Russification of Trans-Caucasia. He says that although the Russian forces have not been in. creased, it does not follow that the fears of a Russian inva- sion of Turkish Armenia are groundless. "The momentous step," he says, " may be forced at any moment upon the Russians by the fatuity of the Turkish Government in Erzeroum, and the feelings of bitter, irreconcilable enmity between the Christians and the Mussulmans of that unhappy province. When this takes place, it will be easy enbugh lot" Russia to push forward without a day's delay a third of her farms army in the Caucasus, which at present numbers r 14000 men, Already, too, the Russian staff officers know i every Inch of groue. of their future operatong, in o f4r they can know this by means of maps. The great bridge between New York and Brooklyn was formally opened on Thursday, amidst great enthusiasm. The Brooklyn-bridge is the largest and longest suspension bridge in the world. Its main span, which forms the bridge proper, is 1,595 N feet in length. The land spans between the towers and the anchorages are each 930 feet. The length of the viaduct leading to the anchorage on the New York side is 1,562.'2 feet, and that on the Brooklyn side is 971 feet. The entire length cf the bridge from the starting point near the City Hall in Brooklyn to the other terminus near the City Hall in New York is a little over a mile (5.989 feet.) Work was begun upon it January 3rd, 1870. The cost has been 15,000,000 dollars. Between eight and nine o'clock in the evening there will be au elaborate dis- play of fireworks from the top of the bridge towers and the centre of the bridge and the shipping in the river. THE RECENT dTCLONF.S : GREAT Loss or Cyclones which swept over Wisconsin, Minnesota, Illinois, and Missouri, on Friday night, committed terrible ravages. No fewer than 83 persons are already known to have been killed and at least 400 injured, many of them fatally. The scene at the town cf Racine, in Wisconsin, was awful in the extreme. Dark clouds were seen whirling in the air, and they approached the earth in a pillar of cloud crowned by vivid flashes of lightning. The cyclone struck the town with inconceivable fury, clearing a path 400 yards wide and half a mile long. Every building which was in the direct path of the terrible cloud fell in ruins. The whirling cloud passed over Lake Michigan, into which were precipitated vast numbers of animals and moveable objects of all kinds which had been., swept from the face of the earth. From Dakota, in the extreme West, we have a repot that the town of Deadwood has been partially destroyed by a flood.

A NEW RAILWAY IN EGYPT.—A Cairo telegram in the Standard states that the engineering representative of the proposed company for the construction of a railway from Suakin to Berber was summoned on Monday before the Council of Ministers, and although no definite decision has yet been arrived at, the general inclination of the Egyptian Government appears to be favourable. The Government, however, is still somewhat reluctant to guarantee the 4 per required on the estimated capital of two and a half millions. The promoters undertake to complete the railway, whose length would be 300 miles, in one year and a half, and claim for their scheme that it would at once open up the whole of the Soudan, there being already a waterway to Berber. It is further claimed that the railway would, after the first veer or two, add several millions yearly to the Egyp- tian revenue, and the promoters offer to put tlle comp my under Government control, and convey troops or Government supplies at half rates.

THE FIGHTING IN AFGH&NISTAN.—The Government has received the following official account of the Ameer's victory over the Shinwarris :--`"rhe A meer's troops join il their levies at Peshbolak on April 26. Next morning the troops started for Deh Sarak, which was the principal Shinwarri settlement, and contained several forts. The pass was diffi- cult to force. Two of the principal forts were manned with the flower of the Shinwarri fighting men, and the surround- ing positions were strongly entrenched. The attacking party formed two columns, the right consisting of an flerati 'infantry regiment an& a regiment of cavalry, with two guns ; I the left of the Cabuli infantry and some Turkestani cavalry, with four guns. Both advanced simultaneously, shelling the position, and a party succeeded in blowing open the gates of the forts. The cavalry of the left column carried the entrenchments, notwithstanding a heavy tire from both forts, and the positions wete at length captured. The action lasted one hour. The settlement was burnt. The prisoners The enemyel 1 e n lostt e If reoenta. 15101 teo K3hoOv.. state that on their side 32;000 men wen engaged. The casualties among the Amber's troops amounted !o 133 killed and 73 wounded.
