ITILE REV. S. H. R.l2vrelscßorT, OF RUNCORN, IN SOUTH A ERICA.—At the South African Conference of Wesleyan I Methodists, which met at Capetown last month, we I learn that the Rev. S. H. Revenscroft, late of Runcorn, was, among otners, recommended to be received into full connec- tion with the British Yearly Conference. BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOL, RuNconer. —The annual sermons in behaif of this school were preached in Bethesda Chapel, on Sunday, by the Rev.W. Hubbard, of Manchester. Good congregations were present at each of the three services which were held, and the collections amounted to £ll 10e. During the day specially selected hymns and anthems were sung by the choir and scholars under the conductorship of Mr. F. Fairhurst, and Mr. Ravenscroft presided at the organ. • THEFT OF BACON AT PRESCOT.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, a respectable looking old man named Thomas Harrison was charged with stealing a piece of bacon, worth 61, the property Mr. Glendellen, grocer, Derby-street, Preecot. On the 21st inst. the prisoner entered Mr. Glendellen's shop. After his departure, the bacon which had been lying on the counter was missed, and P.C. Simms subsequently found it in a basket which the prisoner was carrying. The prisoner admitted his guilt, but pleaded for leniency on account of his age, which he stated was 70. He was sentenced to seven days' imprisen- ment. RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD AT WORIC.—Mr. BOWYer, the school attendance officer, prosecuted at the Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, the following persons for neglecting to send their children to school :—Bartbolornew McLoughlin, Cooper-srreet ; Richard Clynch, Percival's-lane ; Martha Hillidge, Granville-street; Joseph Wilson, Mill-brow; Jno. MacDcrield, King-street; Samuel Asbbrook, Canal-street; John Hill, Wellington-street; Joseph ISlannering,, Cooper- street; George Rowles, Canal-street; John Henry Moly- neaux, Ross-strut; and George Lee, Spring-street. The usual fine of 58. was imposed in each case. A warrant was ordered for the apprehension of Thomas Conway, Parr's- square. AN ABSCONDING PAUPER AT WIDNES.—Mary Small, a young woman, was charged with 'Absconding from Prescot Workhouse ; and also with stealing a snit of clothes of the value of 17s 61, the property of the Guardians.—The pri- soner, who had been apprehended on a warrant, pleaded guilty.—Mr. Hartley said on the 26th December last, the prisoner was permittel temporarily to leave the house, but when her leave of absence bad expired she did not return, and had not been in the House since. She was wearine clothing at the time, and these she had sold to a woman who lived in Lugsdale-road.—Mr. Bicknell, the master, having given evidence, the prisoner was sent to gaol for 21 days' hard labour.

RUNCORN Y.M.C.A. His-ronicAL SpclE-vv.—The last meeting of the present session of the society was held in the reading-room, on Thursday evening, when Mr. T. Glover read a paper on "Myths and folklore." Mr. W. Handley, the president of the society, occupied the chair. Mr. Glover, in a clever and interestineway, dealt with the myths of the Aryan races, and asserted that they had a common origin in natural phenomena. The paper was a most exhaustive one, and was listened to with great delight by the audience which had assembled. The usual votes of , thanks were passed, and it was announced that the society will re-open its meetings in October next, when Mr. Pink, F.R.H.S., has promised to deliver a lecture. MAINTENANCE ORDERS.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on , , Wednesday, James and Patrick Kevill, brothers, were sum- , moned to show cause why they should not contribute towards the support g their father, who is an inmate of 1 Prescot Workhouse. Mr. S. ii: Hartley, represented the , Guardians, and stated the facts of the Cage. Tbo Bench I made an order for 2s 6d upon James, who is a single man; and of is dtlper week upon Patrick, who has a wife and t vo children.—The Bench also made an order for is al per week upon Frederick and James Moore, whose father is chargeable to the common fund of the Union.—Nicholas Gillen was ordered to contribute Is 6d per week towards the support of his mother, who is a pauper; whilst Edward Bennett, whose wife is an inmate of Rainhill Asylum, was ordered to pay 2s per week towards her maintenance. DLM/GING THM Nsw 'COCKS AT WIDNES. Before Mr. B. K. Muspratt and Mr. G. Pilkington, a boy named John Carrol was charged on the information of Christopher Sharp with wilfully damaging the new dock works at Widnes. In course of construction at West Bank, below the railway bridge, are the new docks of Widnes, round which a mud 'bank has been male. On Thursday night there was a rumour in the town that two boys had been drowned lathe river, and a great crowd collected near the dock works. As the people were dispersing the defendant took hold of a wheelbarrow, which he ran for a distance of about 20 yards, and then tip- ped it down the bank. In its descent the barrow was smashed, and the bank was damaged to such an extent that it took a man five hours to repair it.—Christopher Sharp, the watchman, and another man gave evidence to this effect, the former stating that lads like the defendant were a source of great annoyance.—Superintendent Barker said the defendant was the worst lad in Widnes. He had been twice committed to take his trial at the sessions, and had been several times convicted at the Petty Sessions.—The Bench sentenced him to 14 days' hard labour. SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST WIDNES MARINE STORE DEALERS.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Paul Kerley and Owen Kerley, father and son, marine store dealers, were charged with purchasing a less quantity of brass than was allowed by Act of Parliament.—Mr. Knowles appeared on behalf of the son, but the father did not appear, and Superintendent Barker in consequence asked for the case to be remanded. He need scarcely point out the im- portance of this case. The defendants had purchased sillas. of brass, whereas they were prohibited from buying that metal in less quantities than 561bs. The defendant was , remanded for a week.—John Richard Holden was then put ' in the dock to answer a charge of stealing 5-1-lbs. of brass. IP.S. Robinson on the 161 h inst. apptehended the prisoner , on suspicion of having stolen the "brass step" produced, I but up to the present an owner had not been found. From 1 Information in hi ,esession, he had no doubt that he should be able to do so; and a remand was asked for. The prisoner had sold the brass steps to the Kerleys. Prisoner was remanded for a week. I PRESENTATION AT RUNCORN.—As a token of the esteem and regard in which they hold Mr. James Littler, the managing clerk to Messrs. Brundrit and Co., Runcorn, the captains of that firm on Saturday presented that gentleman with a handsome gold watch and att address. Captain Wm. Jones made the presentation and read the following ad- dress :—" Dear Sir,—On behalf of the captains in the employ of Brundrit and Co., I have pleasure in asking you to accept this gold watch as a token of the respect and esteem in which you are held by them, and as a mark of the friend- ship and good feeling existing between is and yourself. Hoping you may be spared to live a long, useful, and happy life, I am, yeurs faithfully. WILLIAM Rums." The watch, which has a hunter 'case and chronometer balance, bore the : following inscription :—" Presented to Mr. James Littler by ! the captains in the employ of Messrs. Brundrit and Co., 1 Runcorn, May, 1883, as a token of their esteem." Mr. ; Littler suitably returned thanks for the gift, and expressed I the hope that the kindly relations which existed between him and the captains would long continue. GALLANT RESCUE FROM DROWNING AT WESTON POINT.— Mr. W. Green, of Weston Point, who has saved many per- sons from drowning, rescued his son from a similar fate on Saturday last. In attempting to jump from a flat to the canal bank the boy fell into the water between the flat and the bank. His father, who was near, leaped into the canal without divesting himself of his clothing, and luckily seized the drowning youth before he was drawn beneath the barge, and brought him to the bank. The boy would inevitably ' have been drowned but for his father's bravery. We have heard of another instance of Mr. Green's gallant conduct. About three weeks ago two boys were retiring from school, when one slipped into the canal. His companion who attempted to save him, also fell into the water, and both cried loudly for help. Mr. Green. who lives in the vicinity, ran to the canal bank, and seeing the position of affairs leaped into the water. Taking a boy in each arm, he managed with difficulty, although an expert swimmer, in getting them to the bank, and both were saved. Mr. Green's gallant deeds deserve recognition, and we think he is a At subject for the Humane Society. . PROPOSED ALTERA/110N TO RUNCORN TOWN HALL.—The inadequate accommodation and defective arrangements of Runcorn Town Hall have often been commented upon, but the much needed alterations are likely to soon be carried out. Negotiations are proceeding between the County Police Au- thorities and the Commissioners for the purchase of the Board's offices, and when these are concluded, the in- ternal conformation of the Town Hall will be arranged. At present when prisoners are to be removed from the police station to the cells they have to be taken into the street and exposed to the gaze of a gaping crowd, besides chances of escaps, being afforded, before the cells can be reached. The plans make provision for direct communication between the office and the cells, which will be a great convenience and obviate this objectionable practice. It is also contemplated to give the solicitors and the Press increased accommodation, an improvement much wanted, and proper provision will be made for the officials ; whilst the magistrates' bench will be made more comfortable. The present defective ventilation of the court-room, which is filled with a most poisonous at- mosphere every sessions day, is to be remedied, and alto- gether the building will be made more satisfactory and con- venient to those who are in the habit of transacting business ' there. RTINCORW FREE LIBRARY Co3nurrEE. The monthly - meeting was held at the Town Hall, under the presidency of Dr. Steele. There were also presentt—Messrs. Simpson, Handley, Lake, Meadowcroft, Riley, and Brookes (secre- tary).—The Secretary reported that during the month of April 1,206 books were issued from the Library, classified as follows :—Tbeology 24, philosophy 13, history, travels, ttc., 194, science and art 38, poetry and the drama 18, prose and fiction 850, miscellaneous 69. The sum of £1 3s lid had been received in fines.—Accounts amounting to £3 2s 9d were passed for payment. The committee sanctioned the purchasing of a considerable number of new books.—lt was resolved, on the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Lake, that the Commissioners be asked to transfer to the committee the balance of the unspent library rate, amounting to £4B 7s Id.—On the motion of Mr. Handley, ' seconded by Mr. Meadowcroft, it was resolved that "The ' Library Committee, haying met the sub-committee, res- oecting the appropriation of rooms at Waterloo House, sug- t-ested the desirability of the Commissioners appropriating alter rooms on the north side of the house giving the re I - auired accommodation, and they respectfully ask the Com- o grant the use of the rooms suggested. and empower the T.ibrary Committee, in conjunction with the Commissioners, to carry out the necessary alterations."

If they wished they could suggest what the proprietors could do to prevent any similar occurrence in the fature.—After about 10 min- utes consideration the jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased died through injuries received by the ac- cidental fall of the gate, which they considered was impro- perly constructed, and ought to be at we remedied.
DROWNING FATALITY AT WIDNES.

Mr. T. W. Barker, the coroner, held an inquest at the West Bank Hotel, Widnes, on Tuesday afternoon, touching I the death of Annie Platt, 11 years of age, who was found drowned in St. Helens Canal on Sunday evening. She was sent to Widnes Alkali Company's wurks about five , o'clock with her father's tea, and after performing her I errand returned home along the canal side. It is surmised that the deceased slipped and fell into the water, for her dead body was found in the canal about seven o'clock the I same evening. There is no suspicion of foul play. The fpllowing evidence was given :—Edward Platt, chemical labourer, 2, West Bank-street, said the deceased was his daughter, aged 11 years. She was in the habit of taking I his meals to the Widnes Alkali Works. She took him his tea about a quarter to five on Sunday afternoon, and stayed about ten minutes. She left him about five o'clock. She had a basket and can with her. She asked his permission to return home by the canal, but he told her to go by Newtown, as the other way was dangerous near Muspratt's works. The pathway on the canal bank at this part was very narrow, and especially when wagons were standing there. It was called the St. Helens canal, and belonged to the London and North-Western Railway Company. About six o'clock he saw a number of men standing on the canal bank. He went to them, and learned that they had found his child's hat in the canal. Shortly I afterwards her body was taken from the water.—P.C. Murray said on Sunday evening information was brought to the police station that a basket and hat was floating in the canal. He went there, and at a quarter to seven the body of the deceased was recovered. There was only a footpath two feet wide where the body was found. There wera some pegs, or as they were called" mushroom tops" at one part of the path, which was private property, and the deceased might have stumbled over them.—The Coroner remarked that there • was no snspicion of foul-play in the matter, and, on Lia sug- gestion, the jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned"
LATEST NEWS.
The Gazette announces a number of appointments to Indian orders.

The funeral of Dr. William Chambers took place yester- day, and was of a public character. The appointment of the Rev. George Kitchin, Oxford, to the deanery of Winchester, was gazetted last night. The death is announced of M. Edouard Laboulaye, a mem- ber of the French Senate and director of the College of France.

The strike at the Albert Colliery, Hollinwood, through which over a hundred miners 'nave been unemployed for five weeks, has been amicably arranged. The men will resume work on Monday. Mr. John 'Henry Morris, Bengal Civil Service, is appointed Knight Commander of the Star of India; and the decoration ot the Imperial Order of the Crown of India is conferred upon the Countess of Kemberley and Mrs. Grant Duff. At Kildysart, on Thursday evening, John Behan, corres- pondent for %Vest Clare district for the Irish World, was arrested, charged with intimidating Considine Ennis while driving the mail car between Kildysart and Labasheeda. He has been remanded.

An Exchange Company's telegram, dated Vienna, Friday stys :—News has been received here that Osman Pacha is to be replaced in the Ministly of War by Sussein Husni Pacha, who is now Turkish Ambassador at Berlin. Said • Pacha is likely to become Grand Vizier. An Exchange Company's telegram states that it is re- ported in Paris from the Upper Alps that there has been a terrible fire at the village of Vars, half of it having been destroyed. Fifty houses have been entirely burnt down, several persons perishing in the flames. At the Liverpool Police Court,yesterday,Patrick O'Brien, Michael Hynes, and Patrick Slater, were charged on re- mand with conspiring and confederating together, for the purpose of defeating the ends of justice, and publishing and circulating certain documents. Mr. Marks intimated that he was not in a position to proceed into the case yes- terday, and asked for a further remand which was granted until Wednesday.

div.head: HARTLAND MEMORIAL CHAPEL, WIDNES.
div.p: THE HARTLAND MEMORIAL CHAPEL, WIDNES.

The Methodist of last week has the following eulogy on Mr. W. Hartland's honoured connection with Widnes Wesleyan Methodism :—" Honour to whom honour is due." The President of the Conference in his speech at the annual meeting of the Metropolitan Chapel Building Fund referred to the Hartland Memorial Chapel, Widnes. Ministers who have travelled in that circuit will never forget William Hartland, tall, well-built and withal of a ruddy countenance, a good local preacher, and a most successful class leader. Whenever Mr. Hartland occupied the Widnes pulpit he always attracted a large number of workingmen, who were seldom seen at the chapel on other occasions. He was of a most amiable disposition, and led a blameless life, and won the respect of employers and employed alike. He was always in his place, whether at the Sabbath services, the class meeting, or the prayer meeting. His earnest and fixed attention as a hearer was always encouraging and even in- spiring to the preacher, whoever he might be. Widnes fourteen years since was truly what the President would call "a dark spot on the river Mersey," and was notorious for filth, drunkenness, and poverty. The place swarmed with Irish of the lowest class. Very few of the streets were paved, and they were but inadequately lighted, and their sanitary condition must not be described. The opening of several new works brought large numbers of workingmen to the town and the place became so overcrowded that it was said that the beds in which the men slept were never cool. Cock- fighting and rabbit-chasing were winked at, and it was no uncommon thing on the outskirts of the torn at night to stumble over men "dead drunk." In the midst of all this moral darkness William Hartland "let his light shine," and did noble service for Christ. That his employers should contribute £l,OOO to the erection of a chapel as a memorial of this model workingman, is a splendid testimony of his real worth. I do hope that we shall hear from the friends on the spot more of him and of the changes for the better which have taken place. Local preachers sometimes think that they work hard in the cause of God under great dis- couragement, and their services are not valued and recog- nized. William Hartland in past years might have thought the same. I have just heard of two local preachers in a northern circrlit who have had an unexpected windfall. An aged member of society who died recently left them £5O each. One is a miner and the other is a platelayer. The reason that she assigned for the bequest was that these brethren "had done her good, and had stuck well to the canes." There are thousands of our people who cannot con- tribute £l,OOO to a memorial chapel, nor bequeath £lOO, who set the highest value on the work the local preachers of Methodism are doing for Christ.
PRESENTATION TO THE REV. J. E. HUGHES, FORMERLY OF WESTON.

We extract the following from the Newport and Market Drayton Advertiser :—A very interesting meeting in con- nection with the departure of the Rev. J. Hughes, to take charge of the living at Cheswsrdine, was held in the Schoolroom, Hales, on Friday evening in last week. Daring the time Mr. Hughes has been incumbent of Hales the way in which he has discharged his ministerial duties has won for him the respect and affection of all his parishioners, and his many efforts pro bono public° have resulted in mach good. When be was first inducted to the living the only educational institution in the parish was a dame's school'. but in the course of two years, he was successful in having the school put under Government inspection, and a certifi- cated teacher was engaged. The school, under its new aspect, kept on improving until it was found necessary to "lengthen et ehraer, gwee er ef thelying li vai about, ge u, tt hi ne the cords and strengthen the stakes," and a new class room wa s baptismal,bui mWa rhr ang Me Mr. Hand udgeha sh troeogki the vestry of the Church at the mercy of anyone; the Communion plate was kept in a box lined with newspaper' minus bags, and washrought from the churchwardens' house on Sacramental days. Feeling that this state of things would not do, Mr. Hughes induced the leading parishioners to sub- scribe for a safe, which was placed in the vestry wall some years since, and the valuables above mentioned are now kept therein. Mr. Hughes also used his influence and was suc- cessful in inducing the postal authorities to place a pillar letter box in the village—a boon which is duly appreciated. Above all the retiring Incumbent's care for the welfare of his flock so endeared him to his parishioners that when they heard he was leaving the cottagers set on foot a subscription and purchased a beautiful oak writing table, and the other parishioners subscribed for a handsome gold watch, both of which were presented to the rev, gentleman on the evening in question, together with an address bearing 83 signatures. The meeting was largely attended by all classes of pari- shioners, and Mr. Joseph Meadows, of Oakley Villa (agent to P. Buchanan, Esq.) presided. It is interesting to note that an the occasion of Mr. Hughes leaving Weston to ci.mp to Hale, the churchwardens and parishioners of St. John Op Evangelist's, at that place, presented him with an address and a silver salvia as a token of their esteem and respect.

div.head: FIRE AT MIDDLESBOROUGH: A PERILOUS LEAP.
div.p: FIRE AT MIDDLESBOROUGH: A PERILOUS LEAP.

Fire broke out late on Thursday night at Middlesborough, in the premises of Mr. Robinson, leather merchant. Much damage was done to stock. A man named Meridith, who entered an adjoining honse to save the furniture, was com- pelled to leap from the upstairs window, and sustained serious injuries FATAL ACCIDENT AT OLDHAM.—CHAPEL TRUSTEES CENSURED.

On Thursday, at an inquest held at Oldham, on the body of a boy who was killed by a gate falling oti him, the jury censured the trustees of the Unitarian Chapel for permitting the gate to be in a dangerous state; and the coroner was in- structed to communcate with the Town Clerk on the sub- ject.

div.head: SERIOUS FIRE IN LONDON.
div.p: SERIOUS FIRE IN LONDON.

Yesterday afternoon, Messrs. Bowley and Bon's oil refinery and drysaltery storesion the banks of the Thames at Battersea, were destroyed by fire. The burning oil ran into the river and set fire to two barges laden with parafin, which were also destroyed. The fire at one time threatened to attain terrific proportions, but was ultimately mastered. The damage la roughly estimated at £lO,OOO. DISPUTE IN THE BOLTON COTTON TRADE.

For some time the spinners in the employ of the Bolton Union Spinning Company, Limited, have complained that the quality of the work upon which they were engaged has affected their earnings to a considerable extent. Failing to obtain an improvement the men tendered fourteen days' notice to cease work, and as this notice expired on Thurs- day without any effort on the part of the company the em- ployees left. A HERD OF CATTLE ACCIDENTALLY POISONED. On Wednesday the Earl af Haddington had a compound duly labelled " poison" used on a portion of the carriage drive to his seat at Arderne Hall, Tarporley, Cheshire, for the purpose of killing weeds. Shortly after, the fine herd of cattle grazing in the park showed symptoms of illness. A veterinary surgeon was immediately sent for, and despite his skill two most valuable cows died from poisoning. The others will probably recover. THE BRIGHT CELEBRATION AT BIRMINGHAM.

The forthcoming celebration in honour of Mr. Bright'i 25 years political service as representative of Birmingham, promises to be the grandest and most enthusiastic demon- stration ever held in the borough. In addition to every town of any importance in the United Kingdom being influenti- ally represented, letters have been received from America and many continental cities expressing an intention to be ' present on the occasion. The arrangements are rapidly approaching completion. ANO TREK ANTI-JEWISH OUTBREAK IN RUSSIA. Intelligence received at Berlin from Rostoff on the Don states that a violent outbreak of popular feeling against the Jews occurred there on the morning of the 22nd inst. The killing of a Russian by a Jewish publican is alleged as the cause of the riot. The mob robbed, burned, or otherwise destroyed several Jewish houses and shops, and the disturb- ances continued until late in the evening. Three sotnias of Kuban Cossacks brought into the town proved powerless to restore order, and fresh riots were apprehended.

div.head: DECORATIONS FOR LADIES.
div.p: DECORATIONS FOR LADIES.

Last night's Gazette announces that the Queen has con- ferred the decoration of the recently-formed orders of the Royal Red Cross upon the following :—The Princess of Wales, the Crown Princess of Germany, Princess Christian, Ptincess Beatrice, the Duchess of Connaught, the Duchess of Teck, Viscountess Strangeford, Lady Lloyd Lindsay, Miss Nightingale, Mrs. Deeble, Miss Caulfield, Miss Stewart, Mrs. Fellowes, Miss J. A. Gray, Miss Norman, Miss Jerrard, Miss Cannel!, Miss Jones, Miss Story, Mies Airey, Miss Wheldon, Miss J. M. Gray, Miss Langlands and Sisters Louisa, Pea, Celestine, Camella, Carmela, Ludevica, Ben- detta. and Orpheline. ELECTION EXCITEMENT IN THE ISLE OF MAN. Considerable excitement has prevailed in Ramsey since Tuesday in connection with the election of a member to represent the town in the Manx House of Keys. The poll- ing took placa on Thursday. Messrs. William Crennell and Robert Tears were the condidates, and the coatest was fought solely on local questions. The Ballot Act not yet being in operation, the open system of voting prevailed. The hourly returns created much party feeling. Crennell polled 180; Teare, 130. On Thursday night a crowd assailed the successful candidate with flour bags, and be had to seek refuge in a friend's house. The police acted with modera- tion, thereby preventing more serious disturbance. Order was not restored until darkness set in. " THE PERUVIAN BONDHOLDERS.

_ The Centr4l News understands that the Peruvian bond- holders have received a letter from the Chilian Minister in Paris stating there are delicate matters connected with the distribution of the money now in hand on account ot bond- holders which he has deemed it necessary to submit to the consideration of the WIWI Government before taking final s'eps in regard to the funds. Liquidation, so far as accounts of cargoes are concerned, being now finished, his Excellency encloses an extract therefrom which shows that the amount in hand lying at interest is £261,208. The contract with the Pacific Financial and Commercial Company is now in force, and the company have already paid into the Ch'lian Government's account for five cargoes of guano the sum of 445,167. AN EXTRAORDINARY CASE.

A singular Case was beard in Liverpool Court of Pas- sage, yesterday. William Clarke sued Martin O'Connor and his wife to recover £lO on a document given under ex- traordinary circumstances. The plaintiff and the female defendant were the relatives of a man named Trainor, who bad considerable wealth, and it was believed that they and other nephews and neices would, when Trainor died, suc- ceed to his property. However, circumstances arose which led to the belief that one of them would be left out of the will, and it was expected that that one would be Mrs. I O'Connor. A meeting of all the relatives was called, and each signed a document agreeing to give £lO to whoever was left out of the will. Clarke turned out to be the un- lucky one, and all the parties paid up except the defendants. His Honour said the agreement was signed by Mrs. O'Con- nor, before the Married Women's Property Act came into operation, and the plaintiff must therefore be nonsuited. THE DISPUTED SECULARIST'S WILL. An Adjourned application of a remarkable character was made before the judge of the Bradford County Court, Mr. Daniell, Q C., yesterday morning. In August, 1872, died John Thorp, confectioner, of Leeds. By will he left some hundreds of pounds to be applied to the propagation of secularism by the payment of lecturers, services, advances in aid of the establishment of secular halls, and by pur- chasing books. The executors and trustees appointed by the testator were Mr. Bradlaugh and four others of the same school. In 1873, however, Mr. Bradlaugh and the other executors renounced all right to the execution f the will. Mr. Scott, solicitor, of Bradford, Ipplied on behalf of the next of kin that the portion 0. r ho will in favour of secularism should be &el trod void as aitainst public policy. His Honour, when the apn i cation was first before him, thought it be'ter to adjou ai• .q:o that Mr. Bradlaugh and the other executors mig •t b • communicated with. Yesterday morning Mr. bCot rrid a

letter from Mr. Bradlaugh, in which the writer made a fur- ther disclaimer, and said the grounds for his taking that course were that he did not want to take from the next of kin any portion of the small property of which the testator died possessed, and the interest of which was not enough for her maintenance. Mr. Scott said he had received fresh disclaimers from only two other executors. His Honour expressed himself satisfied as to the absolute nature of the renunciation of the executors, and upon the contention that the will was void as against public policy, decided against Mr. Scott, saying that a mart had a right to entertain secu- larist views or any other views which his intellect, with or without conscience, led him to adopt. The property, there- fore, goes to the next of kin.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
THE LATE LAW CLERK'S BILLS.

A special meeting of Widnes Local Board, was held at Al- I forde Chambers on Wednesday, for the purpose of passing a I cheque for the payment of Mr. T. Beasley; (the late law clerk to the Bcard) accounts. Mr. T. Handley presided, and there were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. E. Carey, D. Forster, D. Wright, J. Midwood, F. Pankhinst, S. Sadler, J. Martley, and J. T. Allen (clerk ).—The CHAIRMAN explained that the Finance Committee found that there was a balance owing to Mr. Beasley's trustee of £585 13s id, exclusive of a bill amounting to £213 for parliamentary work done in the ses- sion of 1881, for which the Board had not yet received the sanction of the Local Govern- ment Board. The Clerk had received the following letter : "1, South John-street. Liverpool, May 17, 1883.—J. T. Allen, Esq.—Dear Sir,—Re T. Beasley, a bankrupt,—We find the patience of the creditors in this m Itter is becoming ex- hausted, and further proceedings in the bankruptcy are threatened. This morning a letter was received by us from the Comptroller in Bankruptcy requiring an immediate ex- planation why no dividend had. vet been declared and any assets recovered. It therefore becomes irmyrative that the the accounts between the bankrupt and the Local Board should be settled without any further delay. Under any circumstances we fail to see what possible ground of ex- cuse there can be for postponing the immediate payment of all the costs other than the last parliamentary bill. This sum would provide us at once with funds to declare an immediate dividend, and we are most anxious to receive at least that portion of the costa not later than Monday next. Failing this sum you must not complain if legal proceedings are instituted against the Board, as we cannot resist the pressure which is being brought to bear upon us. It is useless to continue the correspondencee, and you must accept this as a final notice. —Yours truly, Ginsom and BoudoTn."—The Chair- men went on to say that he was consulted by Mr. Allen on the subject. He advised Mr. Allen to go to Liver- pool and have a personal interview with Messrs. Gibson and Bolland, and he did so. Mr. Gibson informed Mr. Allen that he must have the cheque by Wednesday, and in conse- quence a meeting of the Finance Committee was called. The committee had inquired into the whole matter and re- commended the Board to pass a cheque for £585 13s Id. The accounts were all in order, and had been passed by the taxing master. He had pleasure in prsposing that the committee's recvnmendation be adonted.—Mr. WRIGHT se- conded the motion.—ln answer to Mr. Martley, the CHAIR. MAN said the accounts had been before the Finance Com- mittee for 12 months, and the matter had been discussed meeting after meeting. The committe9 unanimously re- commended that the accounts be paid.—The motion was carried unanimously, and the members separated.

div.head: PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Wednes- day. Mr. W. L. Evans presided, and there was also present Messrs. Hall, Goldswortb, Sanders, and Cross (clerk.)—ln accordance with a resolution obtained by Mr. Hall at the last meeting, Mr. Baylis, school attendance officer, sub- mitted a return of the number of children residing in the township of Prescot attending tbe following schools : Board schools, 429; Church schools, 239; Grammar school, 93; Yew Tree school, 310*' private adventure schools, 112; Huyten and Whiston schools, 19; and Lane Ends, 10. Number attending private schools as follows : MissTyrer's, 20; Miss Hindie's, Market-place, 12; Miss Scarisbrick's, West-street. 23; and Miss Scarisbrick's, Atherton-street, 35. All the teachers at these schools kept, registers; but Miss Riley, Market-place, did not, and re- fused to give him any particulars. From a conversation which he had with her, he ascertained, how- ever, that the number would be somewhere abeut 20. Dissatisfaction was expressed at Miss Riley not keeping a register, and Mr. Baylis was instructed to ascertain as well as he could who went to Miss Riley's Echool, so that he could have an eve upon their attendance. Complaint was made that a number of children staved away from school habitually two half days a week, their parents haring an impression that they were entitled to keep them away o'• those hail dlys, and Mr. Baylis was instructed to notify them that such was not the case, and to summon the parents whose childrep did not attend regularly.

div.head: INVASION OF MADAGASCAR.
div.p: THE INVASION OF MADAGASCAR.

The Central News learns that the so-called Custom House at Mayunga, on the Madagascar coast, is a mere out station under the control of local chiefs, who exact dues in the name of the Queen. There is no defences, and the natives belong to no regular military organisation. There are no posts of any kind at the place, and the six hours bombard- ment by the French fleet must have been directed against the huts of natives who could be in no position to offer re- sistance.

div.head: CORONATION OF THE CZAR.
div.p: THE CORONATION OF THE CZAR.

It is stated that several of the foreign princes assembled at Moscow for the coronation will subsequently visit St. Petersburg to witness the military parade and manoeuvres to be held at Krasnoje Selo, and to attend the court fes- tivities there. The following are expected :—The Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh, the Prince of Bulgaria, the Prince of Montenegro, Prince Waldemar of Denmark, and some of the German princes.

div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.

Lord NORTHBROOK moved the second reading of the Naval Discipline and Enlistment Acts Amendment Bill. The Bill, he said, would simplify the constitution of Courts Martial and the punishments to be inflicted for naval offences.—Lord SIDMOUTH thought the Bill contained some I„,eneticial provisions, but there were others of which he did not think so highly.—The Bill was read a second time.— The Customs and Inland Revenue Bill was read a second time, and the House adjourned.

div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

THE PARCELS POST. Mr. FAWCETT said he could not alter the rates to be charged when the parcel post came in- to operation in order that a small increase in the weight might be allowed in regard to coverings of parcels. _ _

MR. ERRINGTON'S MISSION.—Lord E. FITZILIUMCE said that on the 14th filf February Earl Granville denied that Mr. Errington had, or would receive any remuneration from the Government, or any member of it, for services rendered. That answer was equally true at the present time.
ZULULAND.—Mr. ASHLEY replvinz to Sir M. H. Beach, said nothing had yet transpired in Zululand which called for_the interference of Her Majesty's Government.

GOVERNMENT AND THE SUEZ CANAL—Mr. GLADSTONE Slid it was true that communications had passed between the Suez Canal Company and the Government. He would take steps to ascertain whether these communications could be made public. The opinion of the House would certainly be taken before any important step was finally adopted. THE AGRICULTURAL HOIDINGS BILL —Mr. GLADSTONE said the second reading of the Agricultural Holdings Bill would be moved next Tuesday evening. Till EGYPTIAN HEROES —Mr. GLADSTONE said full op- portunity would be afforded for moving amendments to the new financial proposal that was to be made in favour of Lords Wolseley and Alcester. REFORMS IN ARMENIA.—Mr. BRYCE called attention to the neglect of the Ottoman Porte to carry out the reforms in Armenia and Macedonia provided for in the treaty of Berlin. He at some length dwelt on the dangers to peace in the East so long as these reforms were delayed, and moved the following resolution: "That the House trusted Her Majesty's Government would, in conjunction with the other powers of Europe, signatories of the treaty of Berlin, continue to press upon the Ottoman Porte the duty and necessity of forthwith carrying out effective reforms in Armenia and. European Turkey, conformably with the stipulations of the sixty-first and twenty-third articles of the treaty of Berlin. He expressed the firm belief that the only way of making Turkey carry out her obligations was , a strong pressure being put on her by other great powers; but he had no desire that war should again break forth, or at England should become involved in fresh entanglements. Ha believed Turkey could be brought to the fulfilment of !her treaty obligation, short of war; if strong pressure was put upon her by the Great European Powers. Lord E. FITZMAURICE said that in February, 1882, Turkey had pro- mised to carry out a scheme of reform for these provinces which had been drawn up by the English and Russian Am- bassadors; but that promise had not yet betn performed. Lord Dufferin had used his utmost efforts on behalf of the sufferings that oppressed this population of Armenia, and he had re- ceived promises from the Porte which time only could show whether they were better than these promises and parker constitutions that had hitherto been given. The English 1 Government had lost no opportunity of pressing on Turkey the great importance of fully carrying out her treaty obliga- tions, and he really/eh we were at the beginning of abetter !state of things. Turkey, he did not believe, intended waiting until it was too late before she com- menced putting her house in order. She had a nobler duty to perform than wringing revenue from oppressed provinces and suffering populations.—Mr. Asu- MEAD BARTLETT condemned the conduct of Russia, and said the present was not a time to press reforms on Turkey.— Mr. GLADSTONE condemned the observations of Mr. Bartlett, and said Turkey's worst friends were those who told her she had no need to make reforms. If the words in the resolution referring to the other Powers were omitted, he would accept it.—Mr. BRYCE at once consented to omit the woris, and the resolution was agreed to.—The House was counted out at 8-40.

div.head: AD BATHENG FATALITY AT THE NEWTON REFORMATORY SCHOOL.
div.p: AD BATHENG FATALITY AT THE NEWTON REFORMATORY SCHOOL.

A bathing accident, and one which is surrounded with cir- cumstances of a very sad character, occurred at Newton, On Wednesday evening. In the grounds adjacent and belong- ing to the Liverpool Reformatory Farm School is a large open-air swimmin4 bath, especially constructed for the use of the lads who are committee', to the institution. The bath varies in depth from two feet to six feet, the asphalt° hot- , tom being on an incline. It seems that for some time a number of the lads other than those residing on the premises have had an idea that they could go and bathe just as they desired, and accordingly on We,linesday evening, ceveral residing at the Vulcan, Eariestown, proceeded thereto to have a hithe. Among the lads were John Shipman, Alfred Astall, Thomas Baker, Charles Maynes, and Henry Piatt, and together they un- i dressed and entered the water. This would be about half- past seven o'clock. Not many minutes had elapsed before it was noticed that Platt, who could not swim very well, was struggling in the deepest part of the bath. Some of the lads at once went to his assistance and made an effort to rescue him, while one of their number ran to the school and gave information that a lad was drowning. Platt sunk to the bottom, however, and for a few minutes his body was unrecovered. Some of the best swimmers from the school quickly entered the water, and after one or two efforts one of them named Joseph Jones succeeded in bringing the body to the sur- face. The utmost efforts and exertions were put forth in order to restore animation; and the body was carried to the school, where a bed was quickly prepared. Hot bricks, kc., were applied to the feet; several of the schoolboys rubbed the body with flannels, and Mr. Atty, the school governor, who gave the various directions, deserves the warmest thanks for his exertions. A messenger was des- 'o the surgery of Dr. Watkins, and Dr. Jones, the assistant, quickly put in an appearance, but all was too late, as the poor lad was then quite dead, lie was nearly 16 years of age and had been employed as an anpren- tice•machinist at the Vulcan Iron Foundry. He was the ton of Mr. William Platt, and resided at 5, Sheffield-row, Vulcan. The news of the sad occurrence came with such suddenness upon the deceased's mother that she fell to the floor unconscious, and remained in that condition for some hours. The grief of the poor woman knew no bounds, and it was at one time feared that serious results would follow. The deceased's father has been ill for many months past, and unable to follow his occupation; while another son, a few months older than deceased, had one of his feet amputated about twelve months ago owing to a disease in the bone. He, too, has been unable to follow any work, and there is now but one son about 20 years of age out of seven children bringing in any wages. The event has cast quite a gloom over the district, and many expressions of sympathy and sorrow for the bereaved family have been expressed. The body of the deceased was removed to his late home the same evening, and an inquest will be held.

It appears that from some unexplained cams°, a bed in the children's sleeping apartment became ignited, and the flames spread to the floor and several boxes and articles of furniture which were in the room. Assistance was soon obtained, and the fire brigade sent for, but, although they were promptly on the spot, their services were not re- quired, the fire having been extinguished by means or buckets of water. div.p: LYNN,

DRUMM. tNESS.—At the Lymm Petty Sessions, yesterdey —before Messrs. Norris, Juynson, aud Gill—John shore, in the employ of Mr. Rigby, was fined sa. and coats ler having been drune at Booth's Hill. CRUELTY TO A MARE AT LYMIL—A. farmer named Fdwiu Massey, Lynnn, was summonEd at Lymm Petty &salon& Yesterday, for having cruelly ill-treated a mare.—Defen- dant pleaded not guilty. Inap2etor Harper, of the R.S.P.C.A., said that on the Bth inst. he found defetes!ant's 1 cart stet:dine in the yard at Lymrn Station, arid on eaetnin- ing the mare in it found a wound about the size of a five- shilling piece on the hack, under the saddle. The attention of defendant, who was on the platform, was called to it, aud he said he knew the animal wanted rest —A fine of 5s and casts was imposed. ALLOWING A DANGEROUS DOG TO Row AT LARGEI.—Wsa. Gibson, farmer, Thelwall, was summoned at Lymm Petty Sessions, yesterday, for that he, being the owner of a dangerous dog, did not keep it under proper control, on the 6th inst.—Norman Taylor, a gardener living near the defeue dant, stated that defendant was the owner of a large dog, which was well known in the neighbourhood as being a savage one. On the 13th ult. it bit his (complainant's) boy in three places when he was leaving school. He spoke to defendant about the matter, and the latter expressed his sorrow for what had taken place, sucked the wounds made by the dog, and promised to keep the animal up. But about a week after the dog was ageirs running at large, and he (witness) was afraid that if it was not kept up his boy might be attacked by it, and thereby, receive some permanent injury. Consequently he had an interview with P.S. Harrineton who caused defendant to be warned. However, on the 6th instant the dog was again at large, and hence these proceedings.—Defendant: Yen'ro not doing this out of spite ?--Complainant : X', , I have not the slightest ill-feeling towards you.—Defendent con- tended that the doe.' was not a dangerous one, and csdisell Wm. Ellison, blacksmith, and other witnesses in support of his assertion.—Defendant said he had done all he could to keep the dog undm. control. At the time it was stated to be at large he had unchained it becinse it was pining ; an then it was not at liberty very long. He had now, how- ever, got rid or the doge—The Bench made an order that the dog be kept under proper control, remarking that it was all the better for defendant if he had got rid of the animal.

div.p: Wettev% to the Ottitor.

raE coNDIrioN OF THE CORPORATION LAMPS. Sir,—Can you inform your readers who is supposed to clean the glass on the gas lamps throughout the town ? They seem at the present time to be waiting for something to drop from the clouds to give them a good washing. Ido not remember ever seeing them in such a neglected state as they are at present, and it is pitiful to see the excellent Bray's lamps trying to throw a decent light through the smoky inside and dusty outside glees which encases them. Surely someone is respensible for seeing the glass kept clean, bat there appears to be no regularity in cleanina them.— Yours, dcz., METEOR. Warriugton, May 24th, 1883. THE PROGRESS OF LEGISIATION. Sic,—Since that terrible event, the dieestablietiment of the Irish Church, we have gone on at such a break-neck pace, that there is no wonder at Lord Bramwell taking up his pen, and, with all the strength and energy that belongs -to the judicial mind, deprecating all present and future legislation. Like Earl Russell he is disposed to "rest and be thankful." Unfortunately we have not yet arrived at the fnillenium. When eilier that blissful period or the one anxiously looked forward to by the Christadelphians does came upon us, we may surely hope that such phrases as "unearned increment" will be consigned to the limbo of all political and theological terms. Lord Bramwell and Earl Weaves, along with a few other Tory magnates have combined together, and under the high sounding, but en- tirely misleading title, viz.," The Liberty and Property De- fence League," seek to stay all further legislation. We can well understand this anxiety to defend property; it is equally clear as to what is meant by liberty; but all the same, we distinctly refuse to accept these sapient "men of light and leading." Mr. Chamberlain, speeking of those who toil not neither do they spin, touched the sote round which all the inflammation is gathering; and as sure as the sun will rise to-morrow will this sore have to he pricked. Liberty from a Tory's point of v:ew is apt to be one-sided; consequently selfish. 'Like an example. Mr. Warton is quite at liberty to aspire to the position of chief bleaker in the Howse of Commens ; but his selfishness in that particular is robbing other members of the liberty they ought to possess of placing measures before the House. So when the question is one of property. A miser who hoards his money is condemned by all except the heir; a landlord who clears his land of tenants, so that he may have good shooting, is quite within the statute law; but he is certainly breaking a higher law. In like manner, when he neglects to farm it to the public - good does be by so much injure the public. A manufac- turer's positien and a landlord's differ very much. The one to prosper must be Argus-eyed, constantly on the alert, or woe be to him. On the other hand—that is up to the present time—the lendlord may quietly stand by, watch his tenants labour. and invest their bit of capital on property that is not their own, then quietly and repeatedly extract it all for his own ealieh purposes by means of what is termed rent. We see by thie it is quite necessary that the people should not be led away even by such an authority as Lord Bramwell. No doubt there is a tendency in the present day towards radical Rad drastic legislation, and we need not be surprised at the large amount of bad temper, and I may say bad tanguege, that our friends the Tories use towards the teformers. Wier° Is howlynge and sehowlynqe, all cast in a dump, With whey/ling and pewling, as though they had lost a trumps; • Mjghing and sobbing, they weep and they wayle, marvel in my mind what the devil they ayle. We can, out of our inner consciousness, conceive what must be their chagrin and dismay at seeing one pet theory after smother so completely smashed and pulverized. After the Irish Church was placed on an honest basis there was to be something really dreadful occur. An entirely unbiased inig..?„. the Americen Consul, tells us a different tale to-day. A:fter the Burials Bill, I suppose it is matter for wonder that dee Nonconformists, who have since been interred, remain tender the sod peaceably. Purchase in the army and other reforming questions have been laid hold of by the Reds, and still, someleow or other, England stands better to day dui at any other time in her history. Nay, if the Tories had any belief in their own talk—it cannot be called argu- nrent—l am sure they must see that their belief is blinding their intellect. Take the Bradlaugb question. Now, many prophecies have been delivered since that gentleman was elected. From Randolph Churchill down to Cardinal Man- ning, and thousands upon thousands of clergymen, have all warned us of the consequences of a godless Par- • liament, yet, that he will sit in the House of Commons is a certa:nty. Had there been no oaths two years since, Mr. Bradlaugh would before this have dealt with the pension list from his seat in the Howie. Dare our Tory friends assert that for this period the prayers of the chap- fain would have been unavailing, and that inconsequence of Mr. Bradlaugh having a seat in that pious assembly the Almighty would have retired defeated ? If not, where is their honesty? But eon this, as on all other questions, they are making a great mistake. Instead of injuring Mr. Bradlaugh, they are not only benefiting him but the society- of which he is the respected president; and if the Oppoei- den goes on much longer, strollers in Fleet-street, London, .may see joining to the Christiait World Office another grand building with a splendid gilt sign— Teeethinker Office. —I am. dm., H. W. Warrington, May 24, 1883.

div.head: CORONATION OF THE CZAR.
div.p: THE CORONATION OF THE CZAR.
THE IMPERIAL ENTRY INTO MOSCOW.

On Sunday morning the Emperor and Empress of Russia, with their children and the Grand Dukes, left the Gatschina Palace for Moscow. Their Majesties reached Moscow shortly after six o'clock on Sunday night, and met with an enthu- siastic reception. The "Holy City" presented a wonderfully splendid and picturesque appearance on Monday. Western princes, noties, and diplomatists arrived in quick succession to at- tend the coronation, and from the eastern extremities of the empire and its vassal states there Came deputations of all ranks of people. The State entry of the Emperor and Empress into Moscow took place on Tuesday. The whole route traversed by the Imperial cortele from the Petroffsky Palace to the Kremlin, , a distance of four-and•a-half miles, was gaily decorated, banners waved from hundreds of Venetian masts, and the windows and balconies of the houses were hung with bright:y-colottred material. The route to the Kremlin was densely packed by an exceedingly enthusiastic multitude, whose cheer was again and again taken up as the Emperor and afterwards the Empress in their respective positions in the procession passed. The pageant included nearly all the members of the Imperial Family, the high nobility, repre- sentatives of the various corps d'elite of the army, Ambassa- dors, Turcoman vassals, and Russian municipal bodies. The Czar, who left the Petroffsky Palace at noon reached the Kremlin at 25 minutes past one o'clock. Although the weather in the early part of the day was fine, there was a slight fall of rain during the procession. The Emperor and Empress will reside at the Alexancirovsky Palace until the day of the coronation, which is definitely fixed for to- morrow (Sunday ) Festive as the city is, and loyal as are the people, strict preciutions are being taken to guard against evil; and the foreign newspaper correspondents are each provided with askeass, to which a photograph of the bearer is attached. -

The ceremony of blessing the Imperial flig was performed at noon on Wednesday in the Kremlin Palace, in the presence of the Emperor and Empress, the Princes and Princesses of the Imperial family, and the members of the Emperor's military household. The Emperor and Empress drove to the Kremlin on Wednesday morning from Alexandrous`xy Palace in an open carriage without escort. A telegram from Moscow on Thursday says :—The fes- tivities are proceeding in a very orderly manner and with every expression of popular satisfaction. The solemn pro- clamation of the Emperor's coronation on Sunday next was made this morning with great ceremony by the Herald-at- Arms, attended by several dignitaries and a numerous es- cort of infantry and cavalry, under the cemmand of a general officer. Ihe ambassadors were formally notified of the date by the masters of the ceremonies, who called upon each of them in State carriages. The Emperor and Empress, who are engaged in devotions preparatory to coronation, will not quit their seclusions in Alexandrovsky Palace until the day after the ceremony, except to receive the visits of foreign Princes. Until Sunday the public _Pies will be in a great measure suspended.

div.head: CROWNING HIMSELF.
div.p: CROWNING HIMSELF.

The Czar is the only sovereign in Europe who is not crowned, for the reason that be crowns himself. When the day comes on which special correspondents have to describe the actual ceremony in the Church of the Assumption of Moscow, whose gilded walls are so much less conspicuous than those of any other metropolitan church, it will be observed that the Czar then appears not merely as titular but as the real head of the Russian Church, th,..t in that capacity His Majesty is himself the principal and solitary flgure in the ceremony of his coronation. He will, as priest and Emperor, recite aloud the confession of faith ; he alone on his knees will offer before and on behalf of the splendid congregation the prayer of intercession for the Empire ; he will place his own crown on his own head, and in his sacre- dotal character His Majesty will thm enter alone through the sacred door in the screen panelled with jewelled pictures, and taking the elements of bread and water with his own hands from the altar, will himself proceed to ad- minister the most sacred rite of the orthodox Russian Church. Before all His Majesty will salute with his lips the picture, atttibuted to St. Luke, of " thi Holy Virgin of Vladimir," an attribution which no foreigner will credit, but which may have helped in bringing to it the £50,000 worth of jewels, including an immense emerald, with which its tinselled framework is adorned. RUMOURS OF A PLOT TO ASSASSINATE.

There are again rumours of a plot to assassinate the Czar on the occasion of the coronation. An officer who is under arrest has revealed the names of several officers of the Guard, quartered in St. Petersburg, who, he says, are mem- bers of a revolutionary club, which is not connected with the Nihilists, but has objects of its own. This statement is said to have had a very painful effect upon the Emperor, who was at first disposed to postpone the coronation, but was dissuaded from doing so. Several officers of the Guards have since been arrested. Another account says that a plot has been discovered to alarm the Czar's horse, and to take advantage of the confusion that would result to make an attempt upon his life. It is difficult to say what amount of lll.mortrce should be attached to these reports, but anxiety will exist until the coronation festivities have been con- cluded.

llntelligence received from St. Petersburg' at Berlin on Tuesday says that a report was current, though not then confirmed, that prior to the departure of the Emperor and Empress for Moscow an exploSion occurred in the Empress's 1 dressing room, apparently proceeding from under the wash- ing stand and the fireplac.e. No one was iniureu. The Emperor and Empress wero in the dining 1%.)0rn at the time. The Officio/ Messenger of St. Poteremarg states that the recent explosion occurred opposite the Palac:t, and was due te. 3n escape of gas.

ALTRINCHAM UNION RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting of the above Authority was held on Wednesday, present—Messrs. McKenzie (inspector), and Joseph Toft (assistant clerk). The Assistant Clerk laid before the Authority cer- tificates from the engineer (Mr. Newton) for the payment of £2OO and £lOO on account of the coutracts for Knutsford drainage. A letter was read from the Local Government Board sanctioning the payment of £lOO to the clerk to the Rural Sanitary Authority for the year ending March last. The Inspector informed the Authority that there had been no fresh outbreak of infectieus disease since they last met. He also submitted several plans, which were dealt with, and the business concluded.

div.head: ASHTON.
div.p: ASHTON.

ODDFELLOWS MEETING AT ASHTON. An ordinary monthly meeting of the members of the Loyal Triumphant Lodge of the Independent Order of Oddfellows, M. U., was held on Saturday evening last, at the Gerard's Arms, Ashton. There was a very fair attendance, and Prov. C. S. John Hodgkinson, officiating as N. G., presided. The Secretary (Bro. C. Ifodgkinson) stated that he had succeeded in ob- taining the remission of the income tax paid by the society on their _property. and investments during the past three years, attounting to .£3 83; and after some discussion it was decided that he should be paid for the extra services he had rendered. The receipts during the month amounted to nearly £2O, and the disbursements to a little over £l3. 013ANGEISM AT ASHTON.—A meeting of the Ashton-in- Makerfield District, Group GS of the Loyal Orange Institu- tion of England, Liverpool province took place on Saturday last at the L.O.L. 29 meeting-room, Ashton-road, Ashton-in- Malierfield. There was a very numerous attendance of delegates from Lodges 14, 29, 37, 282, and 490. The chair was occupied by the W.D.M. Bro. Jas. Egan, the Provincial Grand Master Bro. J. W. Ballard and Bro. F. Morgan, Pro- vincial Grand Secretary, being also present. The W.D.M. Bro. Egan having retired, the chair was taken by the P.G.M. Bro. J. W. Ballard and, the following brethren were elected officers for the district :—Bros. J. Egan, W.D.M.; B. Prescot, D.D.M. ; W. Kenyon, D.T. ; and J. Wood, D.S. The P.G.M. Bro. J. W. Ballard impressed upon the brethren the necessity for taking steps to increase the number of the various lodges in the district by having public meetings, and by inviting brethren down to deliver lectures in exposition of Orange and constitutional principles, and by various other means to bring the influence of an enlightened public opinion to bear in support of the Protestant cause throughont the king- dom. After other business the lodge was closed, and the brethren having reassembled sat down to an excellent tea, to which ample justice was done. A vote of thanks was then passed to the P.G.M. for his attendance, also to the P.G.S. Bro. F. Morgan. Bros. Egan, Gibson, Wood, and Arrowsmith also spoke with reference to the above. The P.G.M. Bro. J. W. Ballard and P.G.S. Bro. Morgan having acknowledged the compliments paid them, the meeting was clesed.

TEE ASHTON YEOMANRY CAVALRY: ANNUAL DINNER. —After having undergone a week's training at Southport, the local troop of the Lancashire Hussars Yeomanry Cavalry returned on the afternoon of Monday week, and on the following Thursday evening the memters of the " A " (Ashton-in-Makerfield) and "B" (Moss-bank) troops were entertained to their annual dinner at the house of Mr. Charles Rose, the Gerard Arms Hotel. Ashton. The dinner was very kindly provided by Captain Gerard, and was a re- past which reflected the utmost credit upon the host and hostess. There were about 130 persons present, including Lieut. Walmsley (of Westwood), Major Relf, Surgeon- Major Dr. Beansan, Veterinary Surgeon Dixon, Mr. Hutton Wright, Mr. Jas. Daplyn, Mr. W. Melling, Mr. W. Painter, Mr. Ferguson, Mr. Ambrose, and Mr. J. Rigby, Sen., Low Bank. All having enjoyed the good things provided, Lieut. Walmsley was unanimously called to the chair, Quarter- master-Sergeant Livasley occupying the vice-chair. The toast of "Her Majesty the Queen " having been given, the toasts of "The Prince of Wales," "The Royal Family," "The Army and Navy," &c., were similarly honoured, after which came "The Health of Colonel Legh," which was ap- propiately proposed by Major Relf and enthusiastically re- ceived by the company. The Chairman gave "The health of Captain Moreland," coupling with the toast the name of their late adjutant, Major Relf. The toast was received with cheers, and the band played "For they are jolly good fellows." Major Relf, in reply, thanked them for the manner in which they had honoured the toast. On behalf of Captain Moreland, who unfortunately could not be with them that night, he could only say that if he spent his term of five years as happily among them as he (Major Reif) had done, he would have nothing to regret. For him- self he could only wish that he might be allowed to take another lease of five years, but of course the authorities thoughtdifferently,and he must submit. He was indeed sorry to leave them, but he hoped to have the pleasure of coming amongst them from time to time for years to come. (Cheers.) Surgeon-Major Beaman regretted he had not been able to propose the health of Major Relf, but he would ask them to drink the health of Mrs. Relf and all the little Relfs. (Laughter.) The toast was heartily given.—Major Relf replying, proposed the toast of the "Band," remarking that he knew of no better cavalry band anywhere than that pos- sessed by the Lancashire Hussars, of which he felt truly proud, and he begged to couple with the toast the name of Mr. Hugh Roberts, who had served with the regiment for 34 years.—The toast was duly honoured, after which Mr. Roberts (in the unavoidable absence of Mr. Batley, the bandmaster) responded and thanked them for the honour they had done him by coupling his name with the toast, and ex- pressed the hope that the band would long occupy its present position of honourable mention.—During the even- ing a number of songs were given, and the company dis- persed at 11 o'clock, after the customary votes of thanks had been accorded.

TRESPASSING A.T Crtoyrote.—Thomas and Richard Wright were summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, to answer a charge of trespassing on land at Cronton owned by Mr. Grace, doing damage to the extent of 13.—A fine of 23. 6d. and costs .was imposed.

POOR RATE FOR CRONTON.—The assistant overseer for Cronton asked the magistrates at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, to sanction the laying of a poor rate for that township of Bd. in the pound to realise £l2l 2s. 41. Only £3 53. 91. of the old rate was uncollected.—The rate was sanctioned.

GOOD TEMTLAIIT AT Crtolcrom.—About 30 members of the Hope of Appleton 1.0.G.T. lodge, accompanied by several friends, paid a visit to Cronton 'fhtemperance Society on Monday evening, and gave an entertainment in the Wes- leyan school-room, which was well filled. Mr. J. P. More- wood, W.T., presided. and a varied programme consisting of songs, recitations, dro., was gone through in good style. The Widnes hand-bell ringers gave several selections in their best manner. Addresses were delivered by the chair- man and Brother T. Treacy. The latter gentleman contended that teetotalism aught to stand in the front rank of all moral agencies, not excepting religion, because he considered that a man unless he had adopted teetotal principles was likely to sin although he might be a Christian. A vote of thanks was unanimously passed to the visitors for their excellent entertainment, which was much enjoyed, and the chairman replied. DITTON.

DEFECTIVE SCALES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wed- nesday, before Mr. E. K. Muspratt and Mr. G. Pilkington, Thomas Cane, coaldealer, Ditton, was summoned on a charge of having his scales out of balance.—Superintendent Barker said h 3 visited the defendant's place of business on Satur- day, the 19th inst and examined the scales which were used to weigh coal. On the weight end of the scale was placed a loose piece of iron weighing B,lbs, which the defendant could take off and put on at will. The iron made the scales balance, but if by chance it should be left off the purchaser would be the looser. It was against the law to use loose pieces of iron on the scale.—The defendant was fined 20s and costs, or in default a month's hard labour.--John Gardner, grocer, Ditton Junction, pleaded guilty to a similar charge.—Superintendent Barker said on the 19th inst he found three pairs of scales in the defendant's shop out of balance against the purchaser, and they were fixed in such a position that a person buying con': not possibly see whether they were proper weights or not. On one of the scales was a piece of wire, evidently to make the weights in favour of the seller, because when he took it off the scales were correct. The scales used for weighing butcher's meat were raised with a piece of loose iron weighing about half a pound. One scale was three drachms against the purchaser, and another two drachms. The son of the defendant said the loose piece of iron mentioned was put on the scales by the maker. Superinteneent Barker said this could not be so. The whole of the scales were a disgrace to the establishment. He never saw scales in a worse condition.—Mr. Muspratt said the magistrates considered this a very serious c see, and fined the defe:dant in the total sum of .£3 and casts, or in default two months hard labour._

div.head: HU Y 1 ON QUARRY.
div.p: HU Y 1 ON QUARRY.

A MAN STABBED BY HIS FATHER.—At Prescot, on Tues- day, an elderly man named William Knox, a gardener by trade, was charged with unlawfully wounding his son Samuel Knox. It appeared that the two men, with other members of their family, lived together at Huyton Quarry, and that frequent disputes arose between them in con- sequence of the prisoner's propensity for drinking and failure to contribute towards the support of the family. A quarrel of this kind took place on Saturday night, when Samuel Knox, who is a collier,attempted to eject his father from the house. A struggle ensued in the back yard, and the prisoner taking a knife from his pocket stabbed his son in the side. The attention of P.C. Hall having been attracted to the scene by the screams of some women, he at once went into the back yard and arrested the prisoner, who was standing in a small crowd that had c Alected. The wounded man was carried into the house, and Dr. Gorst was sent for, when it was found that he had received a deep and dangerous wound. The prosecutor being unable to appear the prisoner was remanded for a week.

div.head: LEIGH.
div.p: LEIGH.

CLEVER CAPTURE or A BURGLAR AT LEIGII.—On Thurs- day morning week Police-constable Wilkinson, of the county constabulary, stationed at Bedford Leigh, made a clever capture of a burglar. About half-past three he was on duty in the neighbourhood of Bedford Hall, Leigh, occupied by Mr. Johnson Mills, auctioneer, bailiff of the Bolton County Court, when he saw a man emerge from the breakfast-room and proceed across the lawn, apparently looking for an ac- complice, or that the coast was clear for escape. Finding everything to his own satisfaction he returned to the house, but was instantly followed by the officer, who closed with the man as he entered the room, securing him without much difficulty. The inmates were aroused, and an inspection of the dining-room showed that all the most valuable plate had been packed ready for removal. Had the capttare been effected in this part of the house it is probable a most des- perate struggle would have ensued, for the burglar was pre- pared for any surprise, having weapons of a deadly charac- ter planted so as to be ready for any emergency. The prisoner was taken to the police station, where he gave the name of George Mills, of Chester. He is 29 years of age, though he looks much older, describes himself as a tailor, and is 4ft. 10in. in height.

GOTERNMENT INQUIRY AT URICSTON. - On Wednesday afternoon an inquiry was held at the Church Schools, Urmston, before Mr. Arnold Taylor. inspector to the Local Government Board, into the application of the Barton Rural Sanitary Authority for sanction to borrow £5,200 to carry out certain street works in the townships of Flixton and Urmston. Of the above amount £7,500 is for Urmston, and will be expended in sewering, forming and channelling streets.—Mr. Price, surveyor to the Authority, submitted plans and sections of the proposed works. Several owners attended and raised objections, and Mr. Whitworth (clerk) handed in letters from absent owners in favour of and against the proposed works. The Inspector reminded the opposition, that in a general scheme of street works, such as the one submitted, the Authority could not make fish of one and flesh of another, and carry out the works to suit the wishes of all parties. He suggested that the term of repayment of the loans should be as short as possible, so that the Authority might not experience any difficulty in collecting the street apportionments.—The Inspector then visited the several streets in company with the various per- sons interested. He will lay his report before the Local Government Board in due course. WINSFORD.
SERMONS AT WlNsFonn.—The annual sermons of the Wesleyan Sabbath School were preached by the Rev. James Kent, of Sandbach, last Sunday, when the collections amounted to £1.4 153.

TIM NATIONAL SCROOL, WHAIITON.—In aid of this school, sermons were preached or. Sunday last; in• the morn- ing by the Rev. Canon France-Hayhurst, rector of Daven- ham, and in the evening by the Rev. H. G. Youard, vicar of Whitegate. The collections realised the sum of £33 ss. BRINE SCALDINO AT WINSFORD.—CharIes Threadgold, while engaged last week at what is called as "topping a pan," accidentally fell into the boiling brine, and was so sadly scalded that on Sanday last he died, leaving a widow and nine chitdren.

BOILER ACCIDENT AT WINSFORD.—At the salt works of Mr. John Thompson, situated at Meadow Bank, a boiler burst last Saturday, but the accident fortunately occurred when the men were away loading a barge. Mr. Cowley, junior, who had charge of the machine, heard a fizzing noise, but was unable to find out where it came from. After a short time the boiler blew up, the boiler house was thrown down, the fly wheel broken, but beyond this no serious damage was done. _

LAND SEBSIDENCE AT WmFonn.—The raid upon un- safe property by the Winsford Local Board surveyor has caused differences in one or two localities. It will no doubt be necessary to put others right before long, for the salt works when in more active operation will cause an increase of brine pumping, which will soon make a perceptible differ- ence in parts. The landslips continue to extend, and that of Marton and those near Whitegate show signs of progres- sion every time they are visited.

div.head: ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.
div.p: ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.

TIM ALLEGED INCENDIATIISM AT UPTON—Michael Gal- lagher, labourer, Upton, was brought up on remand at the Chester County Police Court on Saturday, and charged with having wilfully set fire to a number of stacks of bay, straw and corn at Upton Hall Farm. The evidence not being sufficient to warrant a conviction, the accused was discharged. The ravages of foxes among farmers' bencotes, is, it is sunposed, le ding to a war of extermiaation, as a fine vixen and two cubs have been found poisoned in the woods on Captain Massey's estate at Worleston, and four cubs belong- ing to another litter have mysteriously disappeared. Foxes have recently inflicted serious losses on farmers, but these have hitherto been liberally covered by the members of the Cheshire Hunt.

The whole of the men employed at Neston Colliery have come out on strike. Round and small coals were paid for separately, but the masters, becoming dissatisfied with the amount of slack included, appointed a person to examine the coals as they came to the pit's mouth, with the result that a large number of boxes were disqualified. The men then offered to get round and small coals at is lid, and struck work on being offered Is Bd. Both Mr. James Totnkinson and Mr. David Duncan speaking at Neston, on Wednesday night, advocated the acceptance of the Government's Agricultural Holdings Bill, but were in favour of introducing improvements into it during its passage through Parliament. This is the general attitude of farmers towards the bill, and if it be not improved, it will not be their fault. Whether improved or not, however, thev would be sorry to see it rejected. THE CHEsuIR VOLUNTEERS.—The 3rd Cheshire Volun- teers were under canvas last week in Tattoo-park, the seat of Lord Egerton. About 750 men went into camp, and splendid weather favoured the operations of the week. The camp broke up on Saturday, the battalion having beenin- spected by Colonel Hall, of the Chester district, who was accompanied by Major Wylie. The commanding officer paid a high compliment to the men for the admirable manner in which they had gone through the evolutions, and promised to forward a good report to the general in command of the Northern District. Colonel Marshall said that the men had greatly improved in drill, and he was proud to say that not a single case of insubordination had been b-Jore him the whole week. The health of the men during the encampment was excellent. Among the officers present at the inspection were Major Fox, Major Braddell, Captains Davies, Marsland, Cheshire, Turner, Butler, Haworth. and Jones.

ALLEGED KIDNAPPING IN CHESHI Rl4 —On Tuesday, at Crewe Sessions. Herbert Williams, a middle-aged man, was charged with stealing and carrying away from her home, a -little girl named Mary Jane Tilston, aged ave years.—Superintendent Leah stated that the child was found wandering about the streets of the town at nine o'clock the previous evening. He ascertained that she had been brought to a lodging-house in Crewe by some man whose name she did not know, and who, she said, had car- ried her away from her home and her parents. She gave her name as Mary Jane Tilston, and said her father's name was George lilston. The result of inquiries lea to the ap- prehension of the prisoner, who at first said that the child was his, but then admitted that was untrue, and said that it was the child of a parson at Tunstall with whom ha had been living several years. He said, however, that he clkl not know the name of the girl or her mother. The ch'ild pereisted in her story that the irean had stolen her from her home, and said she mule her escape from tbe lodging-Iwnise at Crewe where the prisoner took her. The police found her wandering in the streets crying bitterly. Prisoner, who made several contradictory statements as to how he. became nossessed of the child, was remanded in custody pending inqnries. The police believe that the object of thai prisoner was to train the child for begging.—Williams: was again charged on Thursday with stealing a little girl named Mary Tilstene, aged four years. The prisoner alleged that the child belonged to himself, but the girl's parents, who live at Tunstall, Came forward and identified her. They missed her on Sunday, and the prisoner was seer, in the streets of Tunstall about that time, begging. Tha child was found in A common lodging-house at Crewe. The prisener waahanded over to the North Staffordshire pole, conveyed to Tun.stall, and committed for trial. A large crowd assembled at the police office, and were with di!nc,,ll.';'y pre7etted tram mob- bing the pri.souer,

From Mackeson's Guide to the London, Churches, just issued, we learn that in London and its immediate suburbs there are :

Commenting on these figures, the Reformed Church Record says By comparing the figures, under the years 1873: and 1883, the Ritualistic advance can at once be ascertained. We particularly observe that in no less than 304 London churches the 'eastward position' is adopted. The signifl. canoe of this fact cannot be over estimated. The eastward position' of the priest is intended to impart teaching which we at least cannot distinguish from the Romish dogma of transubstantiation. With such a list as is given above,, we base abundant evidence of the growth of Ritualism, dospite all the money which has been expended in law Sy the Church Association. So soon as the common-sense GI Eng- land learns that the Established Church is praatically becoming established Romanistn, the ballot box,.it silent but effective language, will liberate the State from, an un- holy alliance with the doctriaes and practices o;"e apostate formalism, and allow the establishment no:, only to play with but to play for, her popish trumpery and abomi- nations."
