WESLEYAN DISTRICT MEETING. LIVERPOOL DIaTRICT. During this week the annual rueeting of Wesleyan Ministers in the Liverpool District has been held in Preston. The proceedings of the District Conference were ushered in with a great demonstration of the temperance workers of the town, held on Monday night, in the school-room of the North-road Wesleyan Chapel. The proceedings were of the most hearty character. The president (the Rev. Charles Garrett) presided, anta his able and earnest address was received with great enthusiasm. Among the speakers. were

The Rev. RICHARD HARPER (Whines), who said tat he addressed a Preston audience some 20 years ago, and it was a great pleasure for him to appear that evening in support of the glorious and progressive work of temperance. He had watched with pain for years the vast evils which the drink had done, not only in their pulpits, but in their con- gregations, schools, and workshops 7 and he knew that the drinking customs of society were the cause ef nine-tenths of the crime of the country. The drinking custvms of society had been fostered by the Legislature :ler the nke of revenue. It seemed to him to be a short-sighted police, and not only short-sighted but sad, that revenue shculd be raised from the sale of that which demoralised and s'aorteneel. life. They knew that this would before long be altered. Public opinion was changing, and they showed this by th 3 monstre petition they sent to the House of Commons a short time ago. (Ap- plause.) They had to thank God and take courage. They bad still a great work to do, for there was a vast amount of money spent in intcTicants. The money spent in drink far exceeded 0,000,000 per week. That amount would give an order for £lOOOOO to 20 manufactnr era If divided amongst our staple industries it would give an. order to Manchester for cotton goods, to LeeS and Trow- bridge for broadcloth, to Rochdale and Welchpool for flannels, to Witney for blankets, to Dewsbury for shoddy, to Norwich for poplins and bombazine, to Bradford fin merinos and alpacca, to Spitalfields and Macclesfield for silk, to Coventry for ribbons, watches, and bicycles, to Sheffield and Birmingham for hardware, to Stafford and Northampton for shoes, to Eurslem and Worcester for china, to Paisley and Shetland for shawls, to Barnsley and Belfast for linen, to Nottingham and Leicester for hosiery and lace, and to London for books. (Applause.) That could be re- peated three times in the year, so as to give an order for £lOO,OOO worth of goods to 1,030 manufacturers and, merchants, and also to place a copy of the Word of God in the hands of every person in the British Empire. (Applause.) I Once shut up the liquor shops and there was no telling , where their benefits and blessings would end. What I quarterly collections they would have! (Laughter.)l What improvements in their churches and chapels they would effect. Then let them all unite in an effort to rid the country of this great evil and bring about the time when men should no more be destroyed by the great enemy —strong drink. (Applause.)

The Rev. J. A. BEEr (Warrington) observed that he noticed there were a great many people in the world who did this, that, and the other for no reason whatever except that another man did it. He was sure that this applied to the use of stimulants. He had noticed again and again that if one man said "No " it had its influence on others. If a man took stimulants it had its influence on others, and if he be a good man to wham people looked up that influence became a great deal stronger. It was easy to reply that these sort of people were weak brethren, but he had a great deal of sympathy for weak brethren, for he was weak himself, and he remembered that for these weak ones Christ died. He found this, that if he took stimulants others would. Some disposed to be a total abstainer would be kept back because he was not one and people might take a glass less if he took none. Even moderate drinking was to a vast number of people exceedingly perilous, and the damage done by it was greater than anybody could conceive. Look at the number of people spiritually damaged by strong drink. He felt cer- tain that even if he were a moderate drinker he would be doing something to lead people along this perilous path, and it was almost certain that some would fall over. The time would come when they would see the result of their own unconscious influence, when they would have to re- gard this unconscious influence in the light of eternity. Now, he was not prepared to place in eternity the results of moderate drinking. He was certain that abstinence would give no results; he could not conceive of persons be- ing worse because he took cold water. (Hear, hearo, It was difficult for him to conceive but that, if he was a moderate drinker, some people would 1p worse. The first argument in favour of moderate drinking 'was that these drinks wzre plea- sant. Admit that, and admit that ministers had no right to forbid pleasant things in which there was no harms But though these drinks were pleasant, were they useful or good? Were they not dangerous? Put the pleasure into one scale and into the other the possibilities of the revelation of the Great Day. Now weigh them up. In one they had'all the pleasure they could conceive, and in the other a single per- son who had finally fallen from God through moderate drinking. Look at that scale in the light of eternity, and was there one of them who would not be glad to leave heaven itself that they might come and undo the result of that moderate drinking? (Hear, hear.) The speaker then pro- ceeded to say a few words on the medical aspect. Med:eally, he found he did not need it, but he did not say, theoretically he never should take intoxicants, though when he saw the damage it caused he s hould be very critical about the gain The Rev. G. HACK (Runcorn) commenced an interesting speech by relating an anecdote of the rev. president. Whilst they were at a table in Scotland a noble lord told Mr. Gar- rett that he had got a cold, and that drink he heard-was good for a cold. Mr. Garrett replied, "My lord; I have heard of men smoking to cure corns," (Loud laughter.) He testified to the great temptations that were apt to he put in the way of ministers to take drink, and he expressed'his thankfulness that tho Tcniperanco benctuient was becoming more widespread. He said that Joseph Livesey anC:l his brethren would stand out distinguished in our history as having commenced the total abstinence movement, anel he hoped that the spread of Temperance principles- would in the years to come be more rapid than it had been in the past.. (Applause.)

The Rev. T. RIPPON (Warrington). speaking of his plea- sure at seeing the President in the chair, said that in Preston he had made some of his best triumphs for God and humanity. He thanked God for the temperance sentiment that was prevailing in the country, and for the great.pro- gress that was being made. He expressed his pleasure at the progress of the coffee tavern movement, and•at the spread of temperance principles in great branches of ser- vices. The Canard Company had stopped the supply of intoxicants to their seamen, and the London and North- Western Railway Company had bought GOO cows to supply their refreshment rooms with the " genuine cratur." His great joy was that the churches and the schools of all de- nominations were taking their right stand.on this question. In their body t*o-thirds of their ministers were total abstainers, and a return which he had just received from their training institutions, showed that out of 129 students 110 were total abstainers. He referred to the great impor• tance of a good example being set, and of their propagating the principles of abstinence from all intoxicants at every opportunity. He exhorted the Methodists of Preston to be proud in the remembrance that here was born the great temperance agitation which had made such wonderful strides, and to relax no effort to bring about the happy day when all people shall be both sober and good. The meeting then ended with the Benediction. The sessions were commenced on Tuesday, in the Assembly-rooms of the Corn Exchange, under the pre- sidency of the Rey. Charles Garrett, the president of the conference. The Rev. W. H. Tindall, of Southport, was unanimously elected secretary, and the Rey. John Horne- brook, of Waterloo, was requested to act as assistant- secretary. All the ministers of the district, except about half-a-dozen, were present, and to the absentees leave of absence was given on the around of sickness. The usual questions as to moral and religious character, belief of Wesleyan doctrine, and observance of Methodist discipline were satisfactorily.answered. The Rev. J. S, Wor!sman, of Chester, and the Rev. Joseph Rippon, of Fleetwood, re- quested permission to be allowed to become supernumeraries (the former, for twelve months) at the ensuing conference, and the meeting agreed to recommend their request. The Rev. Edward Lloyd Jones, who has been supernumerary at Rhyl during the year, reported improved health, and the meeting agreed to recommend that he be restored to active work at the next conference. div.head: – WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: - WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

IP'he monthly meeting was held on Thursday in the eards Otlics, Victoria-road. Mr. T. S. Timmis presided, seil there were present the Rev. Fathers Clarke and Finne.- gen, 'Messrs. R. dradslaaar, John Brock, H. 121runu?.r. if. IA . .11:a4on, R. Snail, W. Hartland, R. if, Davies, and U. H. 1111,14:7 (clerk ), •111111 scaour. 011 COOKERY: INTERESTING DISCUSSION. Tao Rev. Father FINNEGAN Said he had to submit a sreprtrt on the tetehing of cookery in schools, a question that CAA occupied the attention not only of the committee, but atilt) Board, for in any years. 'The fact that a cookery school had been built for five years, and not yet been lolled, proved that the Board had not been quite unanimous with regard to the use they wished tb biildin put to. It was only natural and past that die Board should ask what VUlti to be dime with this building that had been erected a, a SCIIOOI of cookery; and the committee, in order to get ,eoine information on this ociblect, lied visited Liverpool onca or twos. He would refer to one school in particular, the Walton-road school of cookery, belonging to the Liverpool 011ehool Botrd. On the occasion the committee visited this school there were about eight or nine girls receiving instruc- tion. Tneae girls were cnietly if not entirely drawn from the :;choolia hi the north end of Liverpool, near Stanley-road, sod he must say that although on the whole pleased with the lastruction given, which appeared to be simple, and also of the kind that was like!y to be useful in the homes from which the children who were then receiving instruction were taltsn. he thought the committee were rather disappointed in eliag that in Liverpool there were comparatively so few pupils. He spoke at all events his own eadividual opinion in saying that he felt disap- whited. The facts the committee had ascertained were tIW the salary received by the teacher in the 'school mentioned, and tie believed by the other teachers I instructiois in Cookery in Liverpool, was .£BO a year fff me Widnes School Board were to employ a teacher of cookery, he did not think they could expect to expend less than that. This amount, however, secured the teacher's services for the whole wJek ? It appears that if they were to adopt the system that many members of the Board wished in their own schools, where they said there Was scarcely work for a teacher all the week, they could engage one for three &lye At 1.23 Gil per day. But the Committee had come to the conclusion that it would be quite as well to secure the servites of a teacher for the whole of the week as three days per week at 12s 6d
per Jay would atnouot to the SAMS sum per year. The fact before the Board was that if they employed a_tßacher, the salary could not be less than _ .

AO a year To this mast be added the actual expenses in- curred in carrying on the school, and on this subject Mr. ID:;,•by had furnished him with some figures. He wished to draw a distinctlon between the figures of Mr. Danby- and his own opinion. Mr. Danbv thought the expenses would be £lO a year. He (Mr. Finnegan) only need to say that that would make a total sum of DX), and be could only hope that if the cookery school was opened, that Mr. Danby was correct, and his own opinion false and wrong. With re- gard to the number of children they might hope to draw from their own schools into the school of cookery, the clerk bal furnilhed him with some figures. He might bst e I.Bl:Lurk that they had been in comma-
_ Etic%lion with the denominational schools in the district, but there appears to be at present no

ie c i nation amongst the niinagers of these establishments •ither to assist or take part in any way in the project if it eirAm carried out, so that as the CABO at present stood the ischool ofpekery would have to depend on the merits of the tio,rd's own school. and on their own schools alone. The

Ci.'rk hoped that 167 children would be sent from the three iflifnient qchools to learn cookery at Siam's Cross. Ile (Mr. e,..agan) hoped that would be 30, out he questioned it. But aupposing ld7 children were te attend to pass the examina- tion and earn the grant of 1.40, the charge on the ratepayers would only be £5O per year. Mr. Danbv's figures might be perfectly right, but he scarcely agreed that they would get Much large classes. The committee made no

recommendation, but merely gave the Board faithfully the information the had gathered dur- ing the last few months; and left the Board to decide what bad been done on this subject.—The CHAIR- mot : I m inclined to think that the clerk has rather a:der-estimated the expenses. I quite think you are right *but that.—Mr. BRUNNIKR said he 'Resumed the £lO which had been named was simply for fuel, wear and tear of pots and pans and the replenishment of any articles that right be broken.—The CHAIRMAN: And possible loss on the articles cooked ?—Mr. BRUNNER, continuing, said at all cookery schools, so far as the committee had seen, they bad always been able to sell any cooked food at such price ac to cover the expenses of the food purchased and the articles used in the preparation of the food. The committee found that the Liverpool schools got a great deal of things which they used in cooking given to them. Ono shopkeeper in the neighbourhood sends them a sack of potatoes, while another down town would give them a sack Øf rice, and so on. The Liverpool schools of cookery got a great number of articles given to them, which they in Widnes could hardly hope to get, and he therefore agreed with Father Finnegan that the estimate of cost given by.the clerk was rather law.—Mr. DAVIES moved "That cookery be taught in our Board schools, and that the School Manage- ri,..at Committee be instructed to recommend to the Board a suitable teacher for appointment, and make arrangements for the les.;ans to cornr.,.,--e ;n October." r Davies endorsed all that Father Fine-

gan had said, and remarked that the committee had spent a great amount of time in considering the subject, and had visited several schools. He specially, 'mentioned Roman Catholic school in Liverpool, and ob- served that wh,rever cookery classes had been established, they were found to be a ',neat success, and Acknowledged to be of great service. In almost every case the amount received fur corked food was larger than the amount ex- pended in raw tuaterial, and in all schools there had been ne difficulty in disposing of the cooked dishes. He thought ev!ry member of the Board was anxious to promote the crank education of the scholars, and he d:d not think they Could adopt any study not already taught in the school i which would be of more practical use to the scholars than cookery. (Hear, hear.)--Mr. Brunner was about to second the motion, when Father FINNIIGAN rose to a point of order, and the Chairman ruled that Mere such a motion could be considered notice retest be given.—Mr. DAVIES then gave notice that he would bring forward the resolution at the next meeting, and Fattier Ftererso ex formally moved the approval of the report tie had given.—Mr. DRACON remarked that if they engaged a teacher ot cookery for her whole time, they could hire her .04e vices out for the two days they were not n quired by the Board.—Fat,her FINNEGAN said the committee had endea- voured to get tt. Helena, Warrineton, and other veighbouting -towns to join the Board in using the ' .services of the teacher.—Mr. DEACON sue,gested that the re- v;rt should he printed and circulated amongst the members. The CHAIRMAN ol,served that even if the coat of the school cook.ry was £lOO a year, he did not think the Board could spend the money in a way which would bring better 4e.3u1t8 than by teaching cookery. Lie understood that the (vet lesson was to teach the scholars how to scour a sauce- or a frying-pan. Well, to a child who came from such cottages as they had in Widnes that was an educational 4;eson.—Mr. BROCK : Do they teach them to use soap. (:.e.eghter.)-I.The CrietoareeT : That is rol; a matter of c,okery. (Renewed laughter.) He pointed out that Frod- st,am would very likely join the Boanl in the matter if asked, and concluded by secondine; the adoption of the re- pert.—Father FINNEGAN said in presenting that report he bad not given his own opinions on the subject, but he had strong reasons for thinking that a report gut in Liverpool would not hold in Widnes.—Tire report was approved.

div.head: DISTRICT ERUDITION COMMITTER.
div.p: DISTRICT ERUDITION COMMITTER.
Thia comtnittee reported that during the month of April, there wete..l39 applicAtions for scoot fees, which were
granted to 114 persons. Thcre were 268 persons before the committee for contravention of the Education Act. Of these 45 were prosecuted, and convicted by the inAgistrates.
TILE SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION QUF.STION.

Mr. BROCK moved the adoption of the minutes of the Sites and Building Committee, who rec)le itended "that, subject to the approval of the Education Department, that to provide for the detic;ent school accommodation for in-

rants in the south district, they be empowered to negotiate for the hire of Oakland-street Wesleyan School Chapel, and that to provide for the deficiency in the west district they be authorised to obtain estimates to cArry out the plans sub- mitted by the architects." The first pert of the resolution was first considered, and Mr. Bacx:x remarked that

there were strong objections td extending West 13 ink school as they would have to take a clnsiderable portion of the already smill playground; and the Government inspector had been approached en the sub- j ct of hiring Oakland-street Wesleyan school. .He was willing to give the Board power to arrange if they could with the trustees for the hire of that building for the accom- modation of the infants.—The CHAIRMAN said the nem-

mittee was unanimous in its desire not to encroach on the playground, and thought that the plan recommended was the most economical-14r. DEACON: Can Oakland•street - School be hired ?—The CHAIRMAN : Yes, the trustees are Willing- Referring to the extension of Simms Cross school, a•ei Chairman said he was at first in favour of utilizing Warrington-road school, an! the railway company .'_•,onsented to erect a bridge over Bradley crossing fir the convenience of scholars, but he was surprised to find that it weld be cheaper to build at Sit:lllles Cross.—Father FINNEGA.N remarked that the chairman's argument was un- tiaarsl of in education. He had Proved by figures that a school already built and ready to receive scholars would be more costly than to erect a new school. lie thought the chairman's premiss were false, and his conclusions must 3150 be false. He (Father Finnegan) contended that it was cheaper to fill schools a I ready built. The code fitated that children living within a radius of two tailes of illy school should bd compelled to attend that school. Now Warrington-road 171 s not more than three-quarters of a mile from Shum's Cross, and there was co difficulty in sending the senior boys and the senior girls from the latter school over the railway Grossing to the War- * ington-road school. H should hesitate before he compelled

infa-nts to cross the railway, but there could be no hardship, and he should have no scruple in forcing the senior boys t'ad girls from the neighbourhood of Albert and Deacon- goads to do so. The d anger was removed by the railway company's generous offer to erect a bridge, and as a matter r,f facf, the children the Board was so careful about crosscd these lines four and five times a day in going to the works. There was no cry about that 'llad there was no harm done that he Wild

see of. Father Finnegan referred to the fact that children from the outside townships were taught at SiMilli Cross, and he contended that the Board had no right to accommodate children from those places. He could not for the life of him see how it would be cheaper to build schools than to fill schools already in existence.—Mr. DEACON said Father Fine- gan had made an eloquent speech, but pointed out that the question was whether they should keep two head mastera.— Mr. SHAW remarked that for years the onervtic School Management Committee had endeavoured to fill Warrington- road School, but little progress had been made up to the present. It was therefore the wiser plan to provide accommodation where they knew it would bused, and he felt satisfied th it the only thing they could do was to extend Simm's Cross school.—Mr. BRUNNER said seeing that Warrington-road school was only partially filed, would the Education Department allow the Board to barrow money to enlarge the Simm's Cross school ?—The CHAIRMAN pointed out that the resolution said subject to the approval of the Education Department.—Mr. DeacoN observed that in future the Government grant would to a great extent de- pend upon the average attendance of the scholars, and it was probable that if Warrington-road school was utilised as sug- gested by Father Finnegan, the attendance of scholars would not be so good, and the grant consequently less. A loss would thus be caused.—After a little conversation the resolution was passed.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £414 13s. 7d. The school fees re- ceived during March were—Simms Cross, £44 12s. 2d. ; Warrington-road, £l9 O. 3d.; West Bank, £37 11s. 6d.— The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. SHAW, and the Bnard rose.

div.head: RYLANDS BREACH OF PROMISE CASE.
div.p: THE RYLANDS BREACH OF PROMISE CASE.
A NEW TRIAL GRANTED.

In the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court of Justice, on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Denman and Mr. Justice Manisty, the case was heard of Wilkinsan v. Rylands. This was the argument of a rule nisi for a new trial, recently obtained on b3half of the plaintiff, Miss Mar- garet Emma Wilkinson, of High Leigh, Cheshire. Origin- ally an action for breach of promise of marriage was brought by the plaintiff against Mr. Edward Glazsbrook Rylands, son of Mr. John Rylands, of Thelwall Lodge, near Warrington. The case was down for trial at Liver- pool on May 3rd, 1882, but, as was alleged by the plain- tiff, was compromised through the father of the defendant arranging to pay her £750 and costs, with a view to keeping the matter out of court. This, however, Mr. John Rylands denied, his contention being that he had never given any authority for such a compromise to be effected in his name. Thereupon an action was commenced against him to recover the money, and on the case being tried at Manchester in the early part of the present year the learned judge (Mr. Justice Williams) directed a verdict to be entered for the defen- dant. :,Subsequently a rule nisi for a new trial was ob- tained on the ground that the learned judge improperly re- jected the evidence of Mr. Ridgway, solicitor, of Warring- ton, when the plaintiff's counsel offered to call him. Mr. Charles Russell, Q.C., and Mr. Kennedy now ap- peared on behalf of the defendant, while the plaintiff was represented by Mr. Jordan. Mr, Russell, in showing cause against the rule, said there would have been no objection to Mr. Ridgway being called provided he had been called at the proper time. The action was, as he said at the trial, simply aa attempt on the part of the advisers of the plaintiff to extort from Mr. Jahn Rylands, by playing upon his fears of exposure, a sum of money for which be was not responsible. His learned friend Mr. Jordan at the trial at Manchester deliberately took his chance and closed his case without calling Ridgway, who acted as the solicitor to the defendant in the first action. Subsequently, however, he wanted to reopen his case and call Ridgway, and then the learned judge, after reminding Mr. Jordan that he had told him he would undoubtedly have to call Ridgway, and that notwithstanding that he had elected not to do so, refused to allow Ridgway to go into the box. That was a matter which clearly was absolutely within the discretion of the learned judge, aud he had to contend that in doing as he did, his lordship was acting within his power. Coming to the case itself they found that on the let of May, 1832. there was an interview between the father of the plaintiff and the defendant, Mr. John Rylands, at which, according to the former, the latter offered him much sympathy, and spoke of the disgrace that had fallen on him through the conduct of his son, while he offered to pay £25 a year for the child Wilkinson's daughter had had by his son. It was suggested at that interview that the matter should be settled by their solicitors, and according there was a meet- ing between Mr. Rideal, of Manchester, acting for the plain- tiff, and Mr. Ridgway, who represented Mr. Rylands. Ridgway then said he was instructed to offer £lOO to settle matter, and if it were not accepted then the case must go on, and so they parted. The next morning being the 3rd of May. the day of the trial, Rideal attended at the court. and there saw Ridgway, who, apparently, desired to avoid him. He, however, went up to him, and he was then in- formed by Ridgway that the case would have to go on. He understood his learned friend to have said, when moving for a now trial, that Mr. John Rvlands was in the court at Liverpool when the action was being tried. Mr. Jordan.—l never said he was there; in fact, he was I not there.

Mr. Russell said the learned counsel's language at all events bore that construction; but the fact was Mr. Ryland was neither in court ncr in Liverpool at the ti, e, and, tai e, could not have been present to give any tharity to Mr. Ridgway to make the arrangements for the £750 and costs to be paid. There was not, in fact, the slightest evidence to prove that Mr. Rvlands over gave his authority to Ridgway to first offer L:500 and then £750. Ridgway was the solicitor of defendant's son, and in a certain sense also acted for Mr. John Rylands. Subsequent to the pro- ceedings in the court at Liverpool, Rideal in June wrote to Messrs. Ridgway and Worsley, Informing them the costs had been taxed, and asking for a re- mittance. They replied the next day, stating they had had no instructions in the matter from Mr. John Rylands. Other correspondence followed, and in one of his letters Rideal remarked that the present defendant was in honour bound to pay. Messrs. Ridgway and Worsley then wrote back to plaintiff's solicitor, telling him that he was per- fectly well aware that on the day before the trial their Mr. Ridgway saw him and informed him what was the utmost Mr. John Rylands would do. At the hearing, the letter went on to say, they also informed him that the agreement was as against the defendant, and not his father, Mr. John Rylands, and therefore plaintiff's remedy was against the first defendant. The letter finally expressed a desire that the correspondence should there close. He submitted, on the facts he had put before their lordehips, that the rule ought to be discharged. Mr. Kennedy followed on the same side. Mr. Jordan, in support of the rule, said the fatker of the plaintiff was Mr. George Henry Wilkinson, was the head . cashier of a large firm in Manchester, and the family moved in a most respectable circle. A more disgraceful and d,s- honourable defence to an action was never set up than that entered by the defence in this case. The son, Edward Ry- lands, was in Australia at the time, and his address was not even known, and there could be no question that Mr. Ridg- way appeared at the Liverpool Assizes on behalf of the father and by his instructions. It was also equally certain that the compromise effected was arrived at with the sanc- tion and authority of Mr. John Rylands. When the girl was enceinte the father begged of Rylands and his son that the latter would marry her and save the family from dis- grace. Even then when she was in that condition the son, Edward Rylands, wrote a letter to the plaintiff suggesting that he should secretly keep her as his mistress in his father's house. There could be no doubt that the offer of £7OO at the trial came from Mr. John Rylands and from him alone, and he (Mr Jordan) was stopped just as he was in the midst of his address fo the jury. He had to submit further that the learned judge ought to have given him permission to call Ridgway. He, at the trial, was anxious not to call him if he could not avoid it, inasmuch as he was a hostile witness, and he thought he could complete his case without calling him. Certainly no client ought to lose a case be- cause of an error of judgment on the part of counsel when it was in the power of the learned judge to make good the mistake. Beyond all question Ridgway was instructed by Mr. John Rylands to negotiate on his behalf in this matter, and the offers, first of £5OO and then £750, came from Mr. Rylands, and Mr. Itylsnds alone. On these grounds he had to submit that the rule for a new trial ought to be made ab- solute.

Mr. Justice Denman said the case was a most peculiar and difficult one, and beyond all queetion Ridgway could throw considerable light on what took place. It was desirable that his evidence should ba given, and the rule for a new trial would consequently be made absolute. Mr. Justice Manisty concurred. Rule made absolute accordingly.

div.head: DUNHAM MASSEY.
div.p: DUNHAM MASSEY.

GARDEN ROBBERY AT DIINUAM ATMSEY. - Walter Clarke, a brickmaker, WAS charged at Lymm Petty Sessions, yesterday, with having stolen a quantity of vegetables, -valued at about 121, the property of Samuel Astall, market gardener, of Warburton.—Complainant said that on the 16th inst., he was concealed in a hut near a piece of land which adjoins the brickworks, Dunham Massey, and which is occupied by him as a garden, when he saw defendant pull- ing up a quantity of onions and lettuces. It was about nine o'clock in the evening, and jest growing dusk. He watched defendant about tql minutes, and then approached him and asked him how long he had carried on that game, and defendant begged to be forgiven.—Defendant, who pleaded not gu lty, said that complainant :ast yeargave him permission to pull as many lettuces as he liked.—Complainant denied this, out said that last year he gave that permission to the master of the brickworks where defAdant worked.—Defendant said there was anotber man with him in the garden, but cemplainant had received a sovereign from him to settle the case—Complainant admitted this, and said he gave hoth of them chance to escape being brought to the court by paying a little money to the Sunday school in the dis- trict, but defendant had refused to do this.—Deferdant was fined 20s.aad costs, 50 6d.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 26, 1883
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 26, 1883

The people of England were not groaning under the restrictions of the Germans, the tyranny of the Russians, and he might mention others such as the bigotry of Spain. Tbere was one great requisite to make life worth living and that was religion. He impressed upon them the duty and necessity of living a godly and virtuous life, and said there could be no happiness in the world like that of serving God.—The meeting was brought to a close in the usual manner.

SHOCKING OUTRAGE ON A MARRIED WOMAN AT GOLBORNE. COMMITTAL OF THE PRISONER. The reports of the shocking outrage committed upon a married woman, named Betsy Ball, at Golborne, on the night of 've hit-Monday, created a great deal of interest in the district, and when it was known that the prisoner, Robert Boland, was to be brought up at Newton Town Hall on Saturday forenoon last, a large number of persons assembled at the court, with the intention of hearing the details of the case. in this, however, they were disappointed, as the magistrate Mr. T. J. Gillispie, retired into an ante-reom, and it was stated that the case was not to be heard in public. Three representatives of the press presented themselves for admission, but the clerk (Mr. Buckton,) informed them that they would not care for reporting such a case as that, and it was to be tried in private. He there- fore asked them to retire, which they did. The pro- ceedings lasted upwards of fire hours, and we are enabled to give the following particulars. The prisoner, Robert Boland, who is a young man, apparently about 27 years of age, was defended by Mr. Lees, solicitor, of Wigan, and on being charged with the offence, he pleaded not guilty. The prosecutrix, Betsy Ball, was then called. She said she was 69 years of age, and was the wife of Sitneon Ball, re- siding in Ashton-road, Golborne. About ten o'clock on the previous Saturday night she went to the Golborne Inn for husband. She saw the prisoner sitting in the kitchen. She had not spoken to him for a long time past, although she had lived in the neighbourhood of his house. She asked her husband to go home, but he would not do so just then. He asked her to have some drink, and she said she would not, but he ordered some to be brouglet in. The prisoner then came into the room where she was, and sat down a little away from her. After waiting five or ten minutes, she asked her husband if he would go home, but he replied "not just yet." She accordingly started for home alone, and had to pass a place known as Boyden's farm. Just after doing se a man sprang out of the hedge and seized her. He then threw her to the ground, and she screamed for help, but the man put his hand over her mouth and stopped her cries. She struggled with him, but he at last overpowered her. He then committed upon her the assault complained of. He afterwards left her and got over a gate into the next field. She keew the prisoner very well by sight, and had seen him several times before. She had known him for four or five years, and she had no doubt about him being the person who assaulted her. She was sure it was him. After he had gone away she saw a policeman in plain clothes coming towards her. She did not at first know that he was a policeman, but he afterwards said so. She was severely in- jured.—Dr. Nathan Hannah (medical officer for the town- ship of Ashton) spoke to the marks and injuries be found upon the body of the prosecutrix on the morning after the assault. Mary Bent, servant of John Bent, landlord of the Golborne Inn, stated that she did not know what time the prosecutrix entered their house, as she (witness) had been out. She, however, saw prosecutrix about quarter-past 10. She asked her husband to go home several times in her (witness's) presence. The husband of the prosecutrix said he would not go just then, and prosecutrix left the hone° alone. The prisoner was in at the time, and he, too, left shortly after- wards.—Henry Battersby deposed that about half-past 10 on the night in question he heard the prosecutrix calling for help, and he went in the direction. When he got there he saw the constable bringing back the prisoner from a field. The prisoner was telling the constable that he was innocent. —P.S. Savage, stationed at Ashton, gave evidence to the effect that about half-past 10 on Whit-Monday night he heard screams for help coming from the direction pointed out by the previous witnesses. He saw the prisoner running away across a field, and ap- prehended him. He said he was innocent, and had not committed the assault.--Mr. Lees spoke at some length on behalf of the prisoner, and contended that not the slightest reliance could be placed upon the evidence of the pro- secutrix, who, he said, could not remember whether she drank a glass of beer or not, or whether her husband slept with her that night. He thought she must have been over- come with some giddiness, and when she awoke from it jumped to the conclusion that she had been assaulted. He maintained that the prisoner bad been directed to the spot by the screams, and that two men, who had committed the assault, afterwards decamped. He said that the woman had been examined by a medical gentleman, and asked why was not the prisoner similarly subjected to examination ? If he had been guilty be too would have had marks upon him. The charge was a very serious one, and there was a grave doubt as to whether the prisoner was the right man.—Mr. Gillespie then said that the prisoner would be committed for trial at the next Liverpool Assizes.

div.head: UTTERING COUNTERFEIT DECLARATIONS AT LYMM.
div.p: UTTERING COUNTERFEIT DECLARA- TIONS AT LYMM.

HE A V Y FINE. John Bradbury, Broom Edge, Lymm, was summoned at Lvmm Petty Sessions, yesterday, on a charge of having uttered three counterfeit declarations. The declaration forms are used by the cattle dealers who wish to remove cattle into areas declared to be affected with foot-and-mouth disease. The person signing them declares-1. That such animals have not been elsewhere than on the farm or lands from which the movement is to be made during the pre- needing 28 davi. 2. That foot-and-mouth disease had not existed'on such farm or lands, or on any adjoining farms or lands. 3. That no such animal has been exposed in any market, fair, exhibition, or public sale within tne last 28 days.—Mr. Moore appeared for defendant, and pleaded not guilty.—Sergeant Harrington said on the 12th inst. defen- dant applied to him for a declaration form, saying he wanted to send it to Whitchurch to be signed in order that he could remove some pigs from there into Cheshire. Wit- ness gave defendant the form produced, which was then blank, and on the following day (Sunday) witness received it back filled up as it now appeared, purporting to be signed by Charles Gregory. On this declaration he gave defen- dant a license to bring the swine, 30 in number, from Whit- church into Cheshire —Charles Gregory, pig dealer, Whit- , church, on examining the handwriting on the form referred I to, said it was not his writing. He did not sell the defend- ant 25 pigs about the 12th inst., nor was he the owner of that number of pigs.—The Magistrates' Clerk : Did you see him about the 12th ?—Witness: I saw him last Mon- day and spoke to him, but not about this transaction.— Cross-examined by Mr. Moore: He had employed William Bradbury, senior, and William Bradbury, junior, He had never given any oi the Bradbury's permiEsion to sign a de- claration in his name. Never since these orders from the Privy Council came into force had he signed a declaration. He had sold five pigs to William Bradbury, senior. They were free from disease, but he could not say how long they were in his (witness's) possession—some weeks. This closed the evidence in the first case, and Sergt. Harrington then deposed to the defendant applying for a declaration form on the sth inst.,and to granting him a removal license on the following day (Sunday) on his presenting the declaration form filled up and purporting to be signed by Wm. Bradbury, sen.—William Bradbury, sen., cattle dealer, Whitchurch, was then called. He gave hi S evidence in a very desultory fashion,rfrequently saying when asked a question that he was not a scholar, and that his son would be able to tell them when he came in. He also made fre- quent use of the words : "Ay, I doant knaw ; I knew nowt." The Bench cautioned him as to the seriousness of being sworn, and at one point ordered him to stand down, but he was again recalled, and Mr. Moore during the crosssexamination threatened him with proceed- ings for perjury. Witness retorted that the "defendant should pay him the money he owed him for the pigs." Witness, on examining the writing on the declaration bear- ing his name, said it was not his writing. He had sold defendant a number of pigs, and he believed the last lot he sold him numbered 15. These pigs had not been in his pos- session 28 days, as he bought them in the fair.—Cross- examined by Mr. Moore: He had given permission to defendant to sign declarations in his name once at Jones's Vaults, Whitchurch. He had authorised defendant to sign two or three, but he could not say when or where. He had signed one at his (witness's) house on one occasion.—William Bradbury, jun., son of the last witness was called. He said that the relationship between himself and the defendant was very slight. The writing on the declaration form shown to him was not his. Defendant had been in the habit of buying pigs from his father, and he thought defendant bought about 27 close upon the 6th inst. He remembered having sold defendant 15 other pigs, but he could not say on what date. He had never given defendant permission to write his (witness's) name.—Sergeant Harrington then gave evidence of having granted another license of removal to the defendant on the 20th inst. (Sunday) on another declaration form being presented to him, filled up, and purporting to be signed by Wm. Brad- bury. The two last witnesses were re-called, and said that the writing was not theirs.—Mr. Moore then addressed the Bench at some length, withdrawing the plea of not guilty in the first case. He admitted his client had committed a technical offence and had been guilty of great indiscretion, but he said be had not done it with the intention of evading the Act.—The Bench retired for a short time, and on return- ing into court said they looked upon these as most serious cases, and had no doubt that the regulations bad been put on one side and no attention paid to them whatever. In the first case—that of Gregory's—the fine would be £lO, and costs £2 12s; and in each of the other cases the costs would have to be paid, amounting in all to £l5 12s 61. In default of payment a distress warrant would be issued, and defen- dant failing that there would be a month's imprisonment in the first case, and 14 days' imprisonment in respect of each of the other cases.—Mr. Moore applied for time in which to pay the money, but the Bench refused to grant any, and the money was paid.

div.head: LECTURES ON CHRISTIANITY AND SCIENCE AT NEWTON.
div.p: LECTURES ON CHRISTIANITY AND SCIENCE AT NEWTON.

Mr. Thomas Cooper (the author of "The Purgatory of Suicides" and other publications) preached both morning and evening on Sunday last in the Congregation Church, Crow-lane, Newton, to large congregations. On Monday evening, a large number of persons assembled in the school- room to hear a lecture by Mr. Cooper, the subject being "Charles Darwin : in what his real greatness consisted, wherein his theory of Natural Selection' lacks proof; a protest against the grovelling and degrading doctrine that man comes out of the beasts." The chair was occupied by the Rev. James Allatt, pastor, and among those present were the Rev. J. M. Faifbourn (of Earlestown), Messrs. B. B. Glover, P. M. Campbell, J. Roberts, etre., and also Mrs. Evans.—After the meeting bad been opened with singing and prayer, the CIZAIRMAN said Mr. Cooper had again honoured them in visiting that district, and by services rendered in connection with that churc'e on the previous day. He knew those who had come together attracted by the name and fame of Mr. Cooper, and the interest attaching to his subject, would give to him that cordial attention which both he and his subject demanded.—Mr. COOPER commenced by remarking that what was called the civilised world seemed to be losing its celebrities, and in a most unusual way. Prussia had yet its Bismarck, but it was said he was confined to his bad; France had lost her Gambetta. Italy had lost her Garibaldi, and there was no one to take their place. I'Ve in this country had lost our Thomas Carlyle, Benjamin Disraeli, and Charles Darwin, and now there was but the grand old man, Mr. Gladstone, left—the last of the giants. Charles Darwin was a man very much thought of, and very much valued by scientific men a long time before he became to be celebrated, which he did in the year 1869, when he published his book "The evolution of species," and which set the world on fire. In alluding to Darwin'e early days, he said he studied nature in all its varieties, corresponding with geologists, botanists, mineralogists, zoologists, and all kinds of men of science. He studied everything that was passing in order to become thoroughly well acquainted with all science. He observed that Chas. Darwin in his writings had not given the slightest in- dication that lie had adopted Christianity, but they must not pronounce a final judgment upon the question before the volume of his last letters were published by his son. They mast be thankful that such a man had existed, who had searched the whole scope of nature and worked so diligently as he did. He was a true philosopher, and never stated anything as a positive fact but as his theory. They could not limit the mind of men, and did not know what he would vet do. He had done such wonderful things and manifested such a wonderful power that they could not tell yet what he would not do. The lecturer then proceeded to give a summary of the views of Mr. Darwin, remarking that the latter gentle- man had maintained that his system of "natural selection" came only into use when it became useful to the creature and improved its condition. In contrast to Darwin's theory, he (the lecturer) maintained that we had not descended from apes, that it was not said to an ape, whatsoever an ape soweth that shall he also reap. An ape had no conscience, and there was no evolution in plants, because they coald never change their real nature. Christ was crucifieel for men, but never for a gorilla or ape. We were responsible beings, and this earth was not our final state. We were here on pro- bation, and if we did not mind certain rules we should suffer in this world, but a more terrible retribution awaited us in the next world. It WM in vain to deny man's spiritual na- ture. God was a spirit, and it was said that they that wor- shipped Him must worship Him in spirit.—A collection was then made, and the meeting concluded with the Benedic- tion.

"Is life worth living " formed the subject cl Mr. Cooper's second lecture in the Congregation School, Crow- lane, on Tuesday evening. There was again a fair attend- ance, and the chair was occupied by the Rev. J. Allatt. The meeting was opened with singing and prayer, Immedi- ately after which the Chairman called upon Mr. Cooper to deliver his address. Mr. COOPER, at the commencement, alluded to the difference in the periodicals of to day and those when he was a boy, and said serious subjects were taken up now which were never thought of then, such as for instance the question "If life worth living—is life worth haring ?" If they asked that question of a really hippy man he would answer at once that it was worth living, as it was a very pleasant thing. Speaking of John Stuart Mill, he asked what had he to lead him to think that life wee not worth living. They found there were some people who thought that the very fact of death being in the world stamped a doubt • upon it, but it was sheer nonsense to think that God could not make life pleasant because there was death in the world. What a world this would have been ha.d no one died in it. There would not have been room for all who had lived, and what a sight it would have been to see huge creatures, dogs, and beasts crawling upon the earth, and human beings with palsied limbs and affected with all kinds of disease. Tngy must take life as it was, because they could not make it any better by sitting doe,n and weeping in time of trouble. They must gird up their loins and meet trouble. He maintained that the life of a child and youth were worth living, and said the thought came over adults that they would like to be young again. There was much to be done in youth if they would only do it, and a life worth living depended upon the liver of the ' life. Youth was the season of enjoyment if the youth went the right way about it, but it would not be the right way if he indulged in gambling, drinking, and such evils. There were many things in life to make it worth living. They should practice self-denial, for nothing could be 8cm:0111:shed

div.head: PARISH CHURCH TEMPERANCE SOCIETY, ST. HEL ENS.
div.p: PARISH CHURCH TEMPERANCE SOCIETY, ST. HEL ENS.

A well-attended meeing in connection with the Parish Church Branch of the Church of Englend Temperance Society was held in the school-room, Church-street, on Monday evening. The Rev. Canon Carr presided; and there were also present the Rev. R. H. Hammond, St. James', Toxteth Park, Liverpool ; Rev. J. Hurst, diocesan secretary to the society; and the Revs. W. T. Noble, H. S. Bolton, W. Chaplin, George Lakernan, A. A. Nunn, and W. Sweetnam. The meeting having been opened by payer by Mr. Chapman, the Chairman called upon the Rev. Mr. NOBLE to read the following report :—ln present- ing a brief report of the Parish Church Branch of the Church of England Temperance Society, it may be conve- nient to say a few words on the past, present, and future. The branch has been dormant since January, 1879, and was only resuscitated in November, 1882. Since then the work has been proceeding somewhat irregularly, and hence that degree of success has not been attained which more syste- matic and energetic operations might have accomplished. Still something has been done in preparing the way for future progress. S 3 much for the past. As regards our present position, we have 105 members on our books who have signed the temperance or teetotal pledge; we have an executive committee of eight gentlemen, whose work it will be to look after the general management of the society; we have a visiting committee of ladies and gentlemen, whose work it will be to visit absentees and backsliders and report to the executive committee. It is also arrange I that we shall have quarterly tea parties, to which all members shall be admitted free who have paid up their quarterly subscrip- tions as follows :—Adults, id. per week ; juveniles, id. per week. Those 15 years of age and upwards will be reckoned as adults, and all under 15 years as juveniles. The first quarter's contributions to begin from Tuesday, May 22,1883; meetings for juveniles and adults together to be held once a ortnight. According to the report of the committee of the Blue Ribbon Mission lately held in St. Helens, 1,000 per- sons, members of the Church of England, in the parish had signed the pledge, and out of these they had got a list of 072 names. Now, as they had only 105 on their books it was evident that over 560 persons are wanted to enrol them- selves as members of the Parish Church branch of the Church of England Temperance Society, and the gathering in of these should form a principal part of the present work of our visiting committee. Having noticed some of the causes of failure in the past and stated our present posi- tion and plans, we may now peep into the future. That it is possible to make this branch of the Church of England Temperance Society in the future worthy of the old Parish Church of St. Helens is a proposition which ought to be self-evident; that this object is worthy the united and earnest endeavours of every member of our beloved Church all will agree, but this end cannet be attained without the systematic and energetic support of all concerned, and, therefore, we ask for the enthusiastic support of all true- hearted men and women in this great cause. For the ac- complishment of that work the Church of England gives us a platform unparalleled in the world, at once Scriptural, practical, and common sense. On this platform the temper- ance man and the teetotaller can unite on equal terms and promote the cause of God and interests of man. (Cheers.) The Rove. J. Hurst, diocesan secretary, and R. R. J. liametoNn then gave vigorous and convincing temperance addr...sses, which were intently and intelligently listened to.

The CHAIRMAN then made several announcements as to future meetings and other matters appertaining to the societx, and, in doing so, said he should have been glad to have seen present more of those people who were generally called the better class. He thought they ought to give more encouragement to those meetirgs. (Hear, hear.) He should also have been very glad to see all their Sunday school and day school teachers there. (Hear, hear.) 'fhe meeting was afterwards brought to a close by hymns and votes of thanks.

THE ST. HEY.F.NS MINERS' AGENCY AND RELIEF FUND.— At a largely attended district meeting of representatives of the St Helens miners, held on Monday at the George Hotel, St. Helens, the question of appointing an agent was con- si.lered at considerable length. We have already stated that when Mr. John Cross took the management of the Red- gate Colliery it was informally suggested that he should resign, which he did, though apparently with reluctance. In appointing a successor each lodge may nominate a suit- able person, but as yet only one other person (Mr. Glover); seems to have been named. On Monday Mr. John Cross was again nominated, and he accepted the nomination, say- ing he would do all in his power for the miners, beThe7ing that he was in a better position to look after their itterests , than he had formerly been. There seems to be a feeling in fay.,ur of Mr. Cross retaining the position he has held for the last three years. The St. Helens miners havo shown in I a very practical manner their intention to support their fellow miners of Not th Staffordshire at present out on strike. The first levy in St. Helens and district to.vvards the fuwali' for the assistance of the North Staffordshire men was made on Saturday last, and as a result Mr. Lcin, secretary to the St. Helens and District Miners' Association, was enabled to forward on Monday R6O 121. in snu.ort I the object in view.

div.head: WARRINGTON NEWS,
div.p: WARRINGTON NEWS,

WARRINGTON CEMETERY.—The return of interments in the Warrington Cemetery during the week endhrig yesterday were: Adults, 9; children, 8; total, 17. CHESHIRE CHAMBER OF AGRICIILTURE. From an ad- vertisement in another column it will be Been that the half. yearly meeting of thi 3 Chamber will be held in the Town Hall, Chester, to-day (Saturday), when the report of the Council will be received, and the proposed Agricultural Holdings Bill, now before Parliament, disculsed. THE QUEEN'S BIRTHDAY. The Queen's birthday was observed in Warrington on Thursday in the usual manner. In the morning the church bells rang merry peals, and the municipal flag floated from the Town Hall. There was a parade of the 9th Lancashire Rifle Volunteers in the even- ing, and the "fire of joy" which they discharged in the field opposite the Post-otlice attracted a large number of spectators.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST Missrox Room, KNUTSFORD. ROAD, LATCHFORD.—The anniversary services in connection with the Sunday school attached to the above place of wor- ship were held on Sunday, and passld off in a highly satis- factory manner. Tha sermons, morning and evening, were preached by Mr. H. Dutton, of Warrington ; and in the afternoon an address to parents ani children was given by Mr. J. Ashley. of Runcorn. THE DRAMATIC LICENSE FOR THE PUBLIC IIALL.—Mr. M. W. Johnson, secretary to the Warrington Public Hall Company, applied at Warrington Borough Court, on Mon- day, for a renewal of the dramatic license for the Publie Hall.—ln reply to the magistrates, the Chief-Constable said he knew of no objection to the license being renewed ; he had not heard a single word against the license since it was granted.—The application was granted. FORTHCOMING SWIMMING MATCH AT THE BATHS. Local adepts in the natatory art will give exhibitions of their powers on Friday evening next, when a swimming match will be held at the Public Baths, Legh-street. Be- sides contested events, there will be displays of fancy swim- ming, and tricks will be performed under water by members of the Warrington Swimming Club. On reference to our advertising columns further particulars will be found re- specting the sports, which are under the patronage of his Worship the Mayor and other influential gentlemen. A COW IN A SHOP AT WAURINGTON.—The difficulty attendant upon the driving of cattle throuif.h the town was again exemplified on Monday afternoon. About half-past four o'clock a man named Henry Norman was driving two cows from the Eagle and Child yard to Proffitt's yard, Church-street, for Mr. Alfred Bowcock, butcher, when in passing along Mersey-street. opposite the shop occupied by Mr. John George, earthenware dealer, the animals were met by a horse and cart. The cows were thus separated, and one of them entered the earthenware shop, where damage to stock to the amount of £1 was done before the animal was got out.

- Lie um"' AT WALTON.—Mr. J. E. Worsley, deputy coroner held an inquest at the Stag Inn, Lower Walton, on Saturday, last, on the body of a child unknown. It seems that the body was found in the Old Quay Canal, near the turnbridge at Walton Inferior,on the 18th inst., by a woman named Mary Stringer. The body, according to the evidence Of Dr. Star- key Smith, was that of a fully-grown, newly-born male child, and had, from its appearance, been in the water from four to six days. There were no external marks of violence, and the doctor thought the child had died from want of at- tention at birth, as there were no signs of suffocation or drowning.—A verdict of "Found dead" was returned. DEATII OF AN OLD TANNRIS —James Painter came from Devonshire with the late Mr. \William Reynolds, in 1839, and remained with the firm in Mersey-street, until May Ist, 1853, when he was taken seriously ill and did not recover. He died on Saturday last, aged 81. He was buried at the Cemetery on Tuesday, and was followed to the grave by a number of his old fellow-workmen. He is believed to have never lost a day's work through sickness or otherwise, until November 21st, 1882 (43 years) since which time he has been ailing more or less. It was somewhat remarkable that during all this time he never revisited his native county. This is rather an extraordinary instance of long servitude. —Communicated.

WARRINGTON TEMPERANCE UNION.—We would c%II at- tention to the meeting announced for Wednesday evening next in connection with this society, which will be held in the Workmen's Club, Market Place. The Rev. Bennett Anderson, of Liverpool, who created such enthusiasm at the late Murphy meetings, and who is so deservedly popular with a Warrington audience, will deliver an address. The Blue Ribbon Choir is also expected to take part in the pro- ceedings The Rev. Thomas Rippon, to whom the success of the Blue Ribbon mission was very largely dee, will also speak. The chair will be taken by the Rev. Wm. Mules, and it is hoped that there will be a very large attendance.

ASSAULT UPON Tint POLICH.—A stonemason, named Joseph Golden, residing at Walton, was charged at Warring- ton Police Court, on Monday, before the Mayor and other magistrates, with being drunk and assaulting Inspector Berry and P.C. Cheney.—lnspector Berry was at Bridge Foot about eight o'clock on Saturday evening, and found prisoner with a crowd round him; and in spite of repeated requests from the officer prisoner refused to go away. He then took him into custody. Prisoner proceeded quietly with the officer afar as the ..as works, Mersey-street, when ef he became violent and refused to go any further. P.C. Cheney came to the assistance of the other officer, but pri- soner still "kicked and laundered about like a horse," ad was not effectually subdued until further assistance arrived.—Prisonor was tined ss. for being drunk and ss. for the assault.
THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINOTON.—For

week ending May 19th. The mean temperature was 49.5 Fahrenheit, and therefore 66 higher than the prrceding week. The maximum temperature 68 F. was recorded on the 16th inst., and the minimum temperature 32 F. on the 15th inst. The rainfall measured -15 inches. The general direction of the wind was north-west. During the week, which was the 20th of the current year, 40 births and 17 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 20 7 per 1,000, against 25 7 the average of the previona tour weeks, and agaiazt :19'6 eorroepoildiug week of last year. The deaths inelndAd 1 from chicken pox, 1 from pulmonary consumption, 5 from lung disease, 1 from heart disease, and 1 from old age.—Two cases of scarlet fever were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.—JoHN H. GonNALL, medical officer of health.

CORPUS CHRISTI PROCESSION AT ST. ALBAN'S CATHOLIC CHURCH.—The annual procession of this great feast of the Catholic Church took place on Thursday evening last,. in the above church. Soon after six o'clock a large crowd had gathered in Bewsey-street to witness the stream of carriages and cabs which conveyed the children who were to form the procession. At 7-30 prompt the preacher, the Rev. William Herbert Hickey, ascended the altar steps and spoke on the festival of the day, taking for his text the words from St. John's Gospel —"He came unto His own and His own re- ceived Him not." In a masterly and exhaustive discourse, occupying some 35 minutes, he showed the meaning of the feast, and the doctrine of the Real Presence as understood in the Catholic Church all the world over. He divided his subject into three parts : Christ the Saviour, Christ the Leader, and Christ the Good Shepherd. At the close of the sermon a procession was formed outside the church. It was headed by a cross-bearer, and some 80 or 100 children, varying from six to 14 years of age, took part in it. They were dressed in white, walked two a-breast, and each carried in his or her right hand a bouquet of dowers, plants, and the choicest shrubs, kindly given by members of the congregation. The whole service finished about nine o'clock.

How A TWENTY FOUND NOTH WAS FOUND.—The other day an ex-town councillor of this borough had the misfor- tune to lose a twenty pound note, and although he may be blessed with a fair share of this world's wealth ha felt in no humour to quietly forego his chance of regaining the missing flimsy representing so much of the filthy lucre. Accordingly he straightway made the acquaintance of the Chief Constable, and immediately a placard was posted offering a reward of £2 for the recovery of the note, the poster intimating that the number was known and the pay- ment was stopped. As a matter of fact, however, the num- ber was not known, and payment could not therefore be stopped. Meanwhile a little girl had casually picked the note up from the street, and without any scrutiny-L.- though it is questionable whether in this case a scrutiny would have been of mach avail—placed it in her school bag. For two full days it was there safely located ; but at the close of the second day the note by the merest accident dropped out of the bag while the child was learning her lessons, and it was lifted by an elder sister. The latter, not knowing its worth, in all simplicity told her mother that her sister had got possession of something belonging to the "Bank of England," and on the mother examining the note she seemed to entertain a strong opinion as to whether it was really genuine. On the father returning from his day's work, however, he set all doubts at rest. He was not long in discovering that the note was a good one, and he inwardly prayed that an owner might not turn up. As fate would bare it the first thing that attracted his notice on going out was the offer of, the reward, and as the father valued his honesty more than the pelf he at once took the note to the police station and received the Zf.,. RwnOVAL OF THE RF.T. FaTitEa FOZEI, or WARRINGTON. —The Rev. Father Pozzi, who for the laot 13 years has been stationed in Warrington, has just been. appointed successor to the Rev. Father Walker, who ha a resigned the charge Cl' Brownedge Roman Catholic Church, near Preston. The. Rev. Father Pozzi was for eight years in char.,,e of St. Albs. Church, Bewsey-street, and for the last five years he has- had the charge of St. Mary's, Buttormarket-street. Tho.rov: gentleman took great interest in.the work of the Warriagten branch of the League of the Cross, of which be was chap- laia. The neighbourhood to which the Rev. Father- Pmzi is about to remove is a very Catholie one as will be aemem-i bored from the monster procession, in which the Calholica were so strongly represented at the Guild ; and there are several other ahnrches there of the same order tc.which he belongs, that of St. Benedet. aezwnedge Roman Cathalic Church was for 36 years in charge of the Rev. Father Walk,e,r4 and during his ministrations a tower, spi;,e, and bells have bees added to the ?Acre edifice, the inter:ar of which. has also been enlarged and. bea4tified ; and tho presbytery has been much improvsd; and commo- dious schools erected. The Rev. Father Firth, who was seconft priest at Drownedge, as been renaayed to Liverpool, and he will he succeeded by the Rev. Father Craven, formerly Prior of Ampleforth College, Yorkshire, but who 'haa for a shod time assisted the rev. lather at Warringion. , The Rev. FaTher Sumner, of EgreAont. Cumberland, will ' succeed to the charge of St. Mary's, Buttermarket-street. The Rev. Father Pozzi's removal from Warrington is much regretted by his flock, who are making arrangements to present hint with a trAect cd Oz,e at,acwa in which hhoq by them,

RETURN OF AFGHAN HEROES.—On ThUrStl.l* 112 ex- pired service men from India, belonging to. ti.e King's Liverpool Regiment 2nd Battalion, arrived at Orford Bar- racks to be transferred to the reserve. The men took part in the Afghan campaign. WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.—Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkee, judge, held a sitting of this court on Thursday, but the cases were devoid of public interest. The cause list comprised 211 original plaints, 32 judgment summonses, 4 adjourned plaints, and 1 adjourned judgment summons. In the House of Commons, on Tuesday, petitions were presented against the Marriage with a Deceased Wife's Sister Bill by Mr. H. Tollemache from the Rural Deanery of Nantyrich ; for the repeal of the Contagious Diseases Acts from Burdon, Cheshire; and in favour of Sunday Closing from Bucklow Hill, Cheshire, by Mr. T. Egerton. THE BI3HOP or LIVERPOOL.—The faithful of the diocese, and, indeed, Catholics generally, will be gratified to learn that the Bishop, who has) been greatly benefited by his sojourn at Cannes, is expected to return home during the course of next week, actively to resume his episcopal func- tions. All will wish his lordship God-speed. Catholic Times. MILITARY FUNERAL AT WARRINGTON.—On Wednes- day the remains of Sergeant James Robinson, of the King's Liverpool Regiment, stationed at Orford Barracks, were interred in the cemetery with fall military honours. The entire troops of the garrison were present at the funeral, and the service was performed by one of the Catholic priests. The deceased sergeant was 30 years of age, and expired on Sunday last. TEMPERA.NCH MEETING. The weekly meeting of the friends of the temperance movement was held at Gallop's Coffee Tavern, Butternaarket-street, on Saturday night, wnen there was a fair attendance. Mr. Wm. Yarwood pre- sided, and a good programme was gone through. Some Lancashire recitations were given in good style; as also was the singing and readings, and after a very enjoyable evening had been spent the meeting was brought to a close by singing one of Sankey and Moody's hymns. After the vote of thanks to the chairman, and all who had in any way contributed to the evening's entertainment was carried, wo pledges were taken. A FEROCIOUS DOG AT LARGE AT LATCHFORD.—WiIIi3an Yarwoed, tanner, 14, Reynolds Buildings, Latchford, was summoned at Warrington Police Court, on Monday, fer suffering a ferocious dog to be at large unmuzzled, on the 11th inst. The complainant, Mrs. Collins, of Latchford, complained at the police office some time since that defend- ant's dog had bitten her boy several times, and the Chief Constable caused enquiries to be made with the result that defendant was ordered to keep his dog fastened up. How- ever, on the date named, the d)g was found running at large, and the circumstance was reported to the Chief Con- stable, who sent P.S. Bowen to see the defendant. In reply to this office, defendant said he intended to allow the dog to go at liberty, and proceedings were forthwith taken against him. It was found that the dog had also bitten a Mrs. Hartley's boy. Defendant now said that he had destroyed the dog, and called a witness in support of his statement. The Mayor said that as the defendant had destroyed the dog, the Bench would let him off on paying the expenses. OFFENDING LODGING-ROUSE KEEPERS.—Catherine Birch, 2, Hall-street, was charged at Warrington Police Court, on Monday, with having kept an unregistered lodging-house.— Defendant did not appear, but her brother came forward and stated that his sister was at work. She was only 18 years of age, and the house was kept in her name because their father had gone away.—Mr. Church, assistant inspec- tor of nuisances, said that on visiting the house he found it in a very dirty and untidy condition. There were eight persons living in it although it was only suited for five.—A fine of 55. and costs or seven days' imprisonment was im- posed.--Ellen Burke, who keeps a lodging-house in Lower Bank-street, was charged with having more lodgers than her house was registered for.—Mr. Church said that on the 14th , inst. he found nine persons living at the house which was only registered for six —The Chief Constable said it was a. question whether defendant was a fit person to keep a lodg- ing-house. From what he could learn the house was nothing better than a brothel.—Mr. R. Norman also gave the house a bad character. Defendant was ordered to pay 20s. and costs, or in default go to prison for a month.—At the rising of the court she asked the Bench to allow her to pay the money in instalments, but this they refused to do, saying that the case was a very bad one. A WOMAN ACCIDENTALLY STARRED AT WARRINGTON.— An underhand puddler, named James Morris, of 11, James- street, was charged before Major Cartwright and Councillor Monks, at Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, with having assaulted Margaret Larkin, Haydock-etreet, on the 7th inst.—lt appeared that prisoner went to prosecutrix's house on the evening of the date named. Drink was sent for, and during his stay a quarrel arose about his leaving prosecutrix's house, where he had been lodging. Prisoner, I who Was sitting on the sofa cutting tobacco with a pocket ' knife, called the prosecutrix a foul name, and this seems to have exasperated her so much that she struck him. Pri- soner, who, " fresh" with drink, immediately struck her in the face with hisopen hand. He then knocked prosecutrix into a corner, and wounded her twice—on the left temple (from which blood flowed profusely,) and on the forehead. The woman had since been under the care of a doctor, and had been unable until Monday to take proceedings against the prisoner.—Prisoner denied having the knife in his hand when he struck the woman, but several witteoses spoke to seeing him cutting tobacco with it previous to him striking the prosecutrix.—The Bench felt convinced that the wound had been caused by the knife, but considered that it had been done accidentally. They ordered prisoner to I pay 30s. compensation to complainant. IMPORTANT TO RAILWAY TRAVELLERS.—A case of con- siderable interest to railway travellers was down forbearing at the Manchester County Court on Wednesday last. A Mr. Thos. Hulme had sued the London and North-Western Railway Company for £5, for loss sustained and expenses incurred by reason of action taken by the company's ser- vants. On the case being called it was intimated to the learned judge that the matter had been compromised by the defendants paying three guineas, besides the costs of the UMW, and "... ....k fo. nr their servants. Judgment by consent was therefore entered for the amount named. The facts of the case, as laid down by plaintiff's solicitor (Mr. J. A. F. Eltoft), were as follows: —On March 17th last the plaintiff went to the London-road station, Manchester, for the purpose of proceeding to Leek in Staffordshire, near where he resides, and having taken a ticket for Leek he proceeded to the train, and took his seat in a carriage for that purpose. When the train was about to start, the ticket examiner went as usual to examine and snip tickets, and on the plaintiff producing his and hand- ing it over the official refused to return it to him, saying it had not been paid for. In consequence of this action of the railway authorities the plaintiff was unable to get home that night (this being the last train), and it was for the expenses incurre4 and the loss sustained by him that he took action against the railway company, with the result stated above. A SCROOLNOY DRUNK IN THE WARRINGTON MARKET- pr,Acs.—A deplorable case of boyish recklessness was brought to light at Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday'. A schoolboy named Jelm Conroy, 12 years of age, who resides at 2, Dolman's-lane, was charged with having been drunk in the Market-place at about 20 minutes past three o'clock on Tuesday afternoon. P.C. Halstead found the prisoner drunk and behaving himself in a disorderly manner by making a great noise and "kicking right and left" at a woman who was in charge of an ice-cream stall. It was now elicited from the boy that he along with three other boys bought a shilling's worth of whisky at Walker's Vaults, Scotland-road, and that they drank it without adding any water. They had earned the money by carrying parcels at the Ce'ntral station. One of the boys had run away from his work. Prisoner's mother, who was in court, said the boy had been birched at the police station for a misdemeanour on a previous occasion, and he deserved birching once a day, for "his father was never brought there for drunken- ness."—Alderman Chandley: You're willing that we should birch him?—Mrs. Conroy : Yes, and right down well, too.— Alderman Chandley: I suppose we have no hold on the people who served the liquor P—The Clerk: No; because it was bought to be consumed off the prem:ses.—The Bench said it was very wrong for publicans ta serve boys with drink in the careless manner in which it appeared these boys had been served. Prisoner would have to receive 12 strokes of the birch rod and be imprisoned,for the night, and receive six more strokes on the following day. He was just at the turning point in his life and might take up, but a great deal rested with the mother, whom they advised to look wcil, after him,

IN PARLIAMENT SESSION, 1883.— MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL. Resolution of Owners and Ratepayers passed at a meeting 14eld at the Public Hall, on the Bth day at May, 1883, approv- ing of a resolution passed by the Courcil of the Borough of Warringtcn on the 17th day of April, 1853, In opposition to a Bill in the present session of Parliament, intituled a Bill to au- thorise the cmstruction of a ship canal to Manchester, and for other purposes. That this meeting having considered the said resolat ion, and the Council of this Borough having been advised that the pro- visions of the Manchester Snip Canal Bill were prejudicial to the int rests represented by them, and the Council having on the 17th day of April last unanimously resolved to take all necessary proceedings as may be deemed expedient for the due protection of the rights and interests of the Borough of War- rington as represented by them, It is unanimously resolved : That the resolution passed by the Council at a meeting held on the 17th day of April, 1883, be approved and confirmed, and that the Council do take all necessary steps before Parliament in opposition to the Bill for the due protection of the rights and interests of this Borough, and that the coats, charges, and expenses incurred and to be incurred thereby be charged upon the Borough Fund and Borough Rate. Dated this 11th day of May, 1883. JOHN CROSFIELD, Mayor. WM. WY. BROOK, Town Clerk.

SAMUEL BRIERLEY, DECEASED.—Pursuant to the Act of Parliament, 22nd and 23rd Victoria, chapter 35, intituled An Act to further amend the law of Property and to relieve Trustees." Zf °Tics Is HEREBY GIVEN that all Creditors and other persons having any ca,Arms or nxmilms against the estate of SAMUEL BRIERLEY, late of Latchtord, in the County of Chester, wiredrawer, carter, farmer, and cow- keeper, deceased (who died on the Bth day of February, 1883, and whose will was proved in the Chester District Registry of the Probate Division of Her Majesty's High Court of Justice on the 14th day of April, 1883, by Thomas Tunstall and Thomas Birehall, the executors therein named), are hereby re- quired to send the particulars in writing of their claims or de- mands to us the undersigned the solicitors for the said Execu- tors, on or before the 23rd day of July, 1883. after wlich date the said Executors will proceed to distribute the assets of the said deceased amongst the persons entitled thereto, haying re- gard only to the claims and demands of which they shall then have had notice, and they will not be liable for the assets of the said deceased, or any part thereof, so distributed to any person or persons of whose claims or demands they shall not then have had notice. Dated this 24th day of May, 1883. ASHTON & WOODS, Warrington, Solicitors for the said Executors.

I published the following extraordinary epistle :—"Sir,--1 fl it my duty to impart to you information concerning a plot to Now up London, which, if carried out—and I have no doubt bu what it will be, and in the near future—will surpass anything, in point of destruction of both life and property, that has ever' been recorded on the pages of his- tory. Thousands, perhaps millions of your innocent citizens, before another April comes around, will be no more. It is a sad reflection, but we have been goaded to despera- tion, and while I must admit being an active member of the most formidable organisation in point of money and numberi that England hae ever had to deal with, I shudder from the idea of murdering women and children ; for men I feel little sympathy and no remorse. Our government or the government of our organisation, have plenty of men and material in your city, who have volunteered to do what- ever work is deemed necessary by our body. There are branch organisations all over the globe, and the public have not been able even to learn our name. I write you this simply that you may, if you choose, give warning to those unsuspecting victims, who are equally oppressed with our- selves, and that after receiving warning, should they still remain in London, and be mixed with the debris, as lime is with sand in making mortar, I can acquit my conscience of any guilt. Your recent explosion has not been even an ex- periment compared with what will surely take place. You will undoubtedly think very strange of me volunteering this information, but I am prompted in doing it from filial affection more than anything else. My parents are living in London, but I am ignorant of their address, otherwise I should never address these lines to you.—Respectfully yours, JAMES MACLEAN, Mineral Point, San Juan County, Colorado, April 29."
